a, Left: Confusion matrix, multilayer perceptron trained on SLEAP-derived features predicting manually annotated attack behaviour (balanced accuracy = 0.92). Right: Binary prediction of attack behaviours (red) against hand-annotated ground truth (black), representative example sessions. b, Occupancy (left), latency to first attack (middle), and persistence (average consecutive attack-bout length, right), early (first 2 days) versus late (last 2 days) sessions of the training period for EXP animals (n = 10 paired animals). Box plots: line represents median; box, 25th–75th percentile; whiskers, min/max within 1.5x IQR; points overlaid; lines connect the same animal across early and late sessions. Two-sided paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests: occupancy (paired t-test, t(9) = 0.702, p = 0.5003, n.s.); latency (Wilcoxon signed-rank, W = 6.000, p = 0.0273*); persistence (paired t-test, t(9) = 0.976, p = 0.3547, n.s.). c, Occupancy of attacks across days of the training period for EXP (orange, N = 10) and OBS (magenta, N = 9) animals (mean ± SEM). Significance brackets indicate days where EXP and OBS occupancy differ significantly (two-sided t-tests or Brunner-Munzel tests, FDR-corrected across all days; D1: Brunner-Munzel, BM = 2.808, p = 0.0305*; D2: Brunner-Munzel, BM = 4.289, p = 0.0059**; D3: t-test, t(17) = −2.937, p = 0.0246*; D4: Brunner-Munzel, BM = 4.216, p = 0.0059**; D5: t-test, t(17) = −2.666, p = 0.0305*; D6: Brunner-Munzel, BM = 2.308, p = 0.0393*; D7: t-test, t(17) = −2.499, p = 0.0307*; D8: t-test, t(17) = −1.745, p = 0.0991, n.s.). d, Occupancy of attacks during day 1, day 8, and the hard fight for EXP animals (n = 10 paired animals; box plots as in b, with lines connecting the same animal across the three timepoints). Omnibus comparison via Friedman test (F = 1.400, p = 0.4966, n.s.) e, Occupancy (left) and latency (right) of fleeing events during the hard fight by EXP (orange, N = 10), OBS (magenta, N = 9), and NON (grey, N = 8) animals. Occupancy: omnibus Kruskal-Wallis, H = 7.652, p = 0.0218; post-hoc two-sided Brunner-Munzel tests, FDR-corrected across comparisons: EXP vs. OBS (BM = 1.207, p = 0.2440, n.s.), EXP vs. NON (BM = 3.461, p = 0.0100*), OBS vs. NON (BM = 2.150, p = 0.0742, n.s.). Latency: omnibus Kruskal-Wallis, H = 1.662, p = 0.4356, n.s. Box plots as in b. f, Probability distribution of frames containing attacks found in each UMAP cluster during the hard fight. Clusters 2, 3, and 4 contain the highest proportion of attack frames, consistent with their designation as conflict clusters. g, Leave-one-session-out cross-validation balanced accuracy of group ID (EXP, OBS, NON) predictions using UMAP cluster occupancy as the classification feature, evaluated against a null distribution generated by a permutation test (1,000 permutations, group labels shuffled independently per session, one-sided; p = 0.0010***). h, Same as g but using pairwise transition probabilities between UMAP clusters as the classification feature (permutation test as in g; p = 0.0020**). i, Top: Same as g but using cluster persistence (average consecutive bout duration, seconds) as the classification feature (permutation test as in g; p = 0.0010***). Bottom: Persistence of all 13 behaviour clusters across groups (EXP N = 10, OBS N = 9, NON N = 8) during the hard fight (box plots as in b; one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test pending normality, post-hoc two-sided t-tests or Brunner-Munzel tests, FDR-corrected; full statistics in Table S1). j, Subset of averaged SLEAP-derived features across groups during the hard fight (EXP N = 10, OBS N = 9, NON N = 8; box plots as in b). Features shown: resident-intruder centroid distance, resident centroid speed, resident-intruder body overlap, intruder centroid speed. Full statistics in Table S1. For all comparisons, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001.

a, Schematic and mathematical descriptions of all SLEAP-derived features used for behavioural segmentation, organized by category. Distance features capture inter-animal proximity and approach dynamics. The bounding box category includes intersection over union (IoU), computed via Shapely polygon operations, which measures the degree of physical overlap between animal bounding boxes. Social orientation features capture the directed facing angle of each animal relative to the other. Postural features include within-mouse head angle (centroid–neck–head angle, indexing sniffing posture and body curvature) and within-mouse body length (tailbase-to-head distance, indexing body elongation). Speed features are computed as the rate of change (ROC) of position over a 4-frame window (100 ms), including within-mouse translational (centroid) speed and head-specific speed for both resident and intruder, as well as a summed speed feature aggregating across temporal lags spanning ±2 s. b, Unsupervised behaviour states resulting from watershed segmentation of the UMAP embedding, with descriptions organized according to the unsupervised hierarchical clustering results depicted in Fig. 1m, which segregates behavioural states into three discrete categories: conflict and aggression-preparatory states (red; clusters 1–4), investigative or social engagement states (gold; clusters 5, 7–9), and disengaged or avoidant states (green; clusters 6, 10–13). The behavioural content of each cluster is ascertained via a combination of manual curation of video frames across multiple sessions and animals and feature coding as shown in (c). c, Feature maps of all 13 behavioural clusters across all recorded SLEAP-derived behaviour features, including resident and intruder centroid speed, resident and intruder head speed, resident-intruder centroid distance, resident head to intruder head distance, resident head to intruder tailbase distance, intruder head to resident tailbase distance, resident-intruder orientation, intruder-resident orientation, resident-intruder body overlap (IoU), resident body length, intruder body length, resident body orientation, and intruder body orientation. Each map depicts the mean z-scored feature value projected onto the UMAP behaviour space, averaged across animals and sessions. d, Representative video frames depicting examples of each behavioural cluster, organized according to the same hierarchical grouping as in (b). Conflict states (clusters 1–4): mutual conflict, resident aggression, aggression preparation 1, aggression preparation 2. Investigative states (clusters 5, 7–9): huddled investigation, non-specific/orofacial investigation, mutual investigation, mutually facing investigation. Disengaged/avoidant states (clusters 6, 10, 11, 13): intruder disengages, intruder approaches/investigates, avoidance with resident movement 1, avoidance with resident movement 2, avoidance with resident scrunch/groom. Resident animals are indicated by cyan markers and intruder animals by red markers.

a, Schematic depicting the timeline of exposure training. In contrast to OBS animals, nonsocial exposure (XPO, N = 5) animals observed non-aggressive male cagemates for 8 days, and on day 9 were pitted against three rounds of CD1 aggressors. b, Leave-one-session-out cross-validation balanced accuracy of group ID (OBS vs. XPO) predictions using occupancy of UMAP clusters (left), persistence (mean length of cluster bouts, middle), and pairwise cluster transition probabilities (right) as classification features. For each metric, test balanced accuracy was evaluated against a null distribution generated by a permutation test (1,000 permutations, group labels shuffled independently per session, one-sided; occupancy, p = 0.0010***; persistence, p = 0.0010***; transitions, p = 0.0010***). c, Occupancy of a subset of behaviour clusters for OBS (N = 9) and XPO (N = 5) animals during the hard fight: clusters 2 and 4 (conflict), 5 and 7 (investigative), and 6 and 10 (asocial) — two representative clusters per behavioural category, selected a priori based on the category structure established in Fig. 1. Box plots: line represents median; box, 25th–75th percentile; whiskers, min/max within 1.5x IQR; points overlaid; individual points overlaid. Group differences evaluated via two-sided t-tests or Brunner-Munzel tests where no directional hypothesis existed, and one-sided tests where an a priori direction was established by the corresponding effect in Fig. 1: clusters 2, 4, 5, 7 tested one-sided (OBS > XPO) followed by FDR correction; clusters 6, 10 tested one-sided (OBS < XPO) followed by FDR correction. Full statistics in Table S1. d, Aggregate transition weights between behaviour-category clusters (as in Fig. 1o), OBS versus XPO, hard fight, for a subset of transitions of a priori interest from Fig. 1: conflict→conflict, conflict→investigation and asocial→investigation (one-sided, OBS > XPO); investigation→investigation and investigation→asocial (two-sided); and asocial→asocial (one-sided, OBS < XPO). N and box plots as in c. Tests: one-sided t-tests or Brunner-Munzel tests, followed by FDR corrections across comparisons in the same family of origin behaviours. Full statistics in Table S1. e, Classification strategy for determining EXP-like or NON-like behavioural tendency of OBS versus XPO animals during the hard fight. A support vector machine (SVM) classifier is trained on EXP and NON behaviour using cluster occupancy, persistence, or pairwise transition probabilities as separate feature sets. Each classifier is then applied to OBS and XPO animals, with individuals classified as EXP-like or NON-like based on the classifier output. f, Left: Distribution of P(classified as EXP) for OBS (N = 9, magenta) versus XPO (N = 5, cyan) animals, using cluster occupancy as the classifier feature (two-sided Brunner-Munzel test, BM = −2.956, p = 0.0193*). Box plots as in c. Middle: as in left, using cluster persistence (BM = −3.164, p = 0.0083**). Right: as in left, using pairwise transition probabilities (BM = −2.563, p = 0.0281*). For all comparisons, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001.

a, Representative GCaMP6f (green) or JRCaMP2b (red) expression across all 12 recorded brain areas. Scale bars 500 μm. Representative of fibre placement confirmed via histology in the majority of subjects per region (range: 8/12–12/12 for EXP; 9/9 for OBS; 8/8 for NON, across all regions); full per-region counts in b. b, Accepted fibre placements for every experimental subject across all 12 recorded brain areas. Coronal schematics are adapted from the Allen Brain Atlas51. Fraction of subjects per group with histologically confirmed placement, by region (EXP / OBS / NON): PrL, 11/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; vLS, 12/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; POA, 11/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; BNST, 10/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; AH, 10/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; MeA, 11/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; VMH, 12/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; PAG, 8/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; PMv, 9/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; LHb (excitatory only), 9/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; PA, 9/12 / 9/9 / 8/8; NAc (dopamine), 11/12 / 9/9 / 8/8.

a, Model architecture. Input clips of 20 frames (0.5 s) are passed through stochastic augmentations during training, followed by four 3D convolutional attention blocks, each consisting of a 3D convolution, batch normalization, max pooling, and a spatial attention module. The encoder output is pooled into a 512-dimensional feature vector and passed to a three-layer MLP classifier producing softmax probabilities over seven behavioural classes. The seven output classes are merged into four behaviour categories: attention (attention), self-directed (grooming, scratching), idle (still), and exploratory (investigate, rearing, turning). Fine-grained class colours are shown within each category in the legend. b, Spatial attention maps from the first three encoder blocks for four behavioural classes selected to span distinct postures (rearing, scratching, turning, attention). Each row shows a single representative frame from one held-out clip. Maps from the fourth block are omitted due to coarse spatial resolution. Within each panel, attention values are min-max normalized; brighter colours indicate higher attention weight. c, Row-normalized confusion matrix for the four behaviour categories, averaged across the 5 cross-validation folds. Cell values give the mean percentage of ground-truth samples assigned to each predicted category ± SD across folds. d, Example behavioural time series from three training sessions across the first 5 min of observation. Coloured bars indicate the classifier assigned behavioural category at each frame: attention (blue), self-directed (yellow), idle (grey), and exploratory (orange). Dark red dots mark demonstrator attack labels from an independent attack behaviour classifier (see Supervised behaviour classification in Methods). e, Behaviour category occupancy of OBS animals (N = 9 mice) during training period. f, Daily behaviour category occupancy for OBS (top, N = 9 mice) and XPO (bottom, N = 5 mice) animals across the training period. Attention proportion was modelled separately per condition by a linear mixed-effects model with day as a continuous fixed effect and a random intercept per mouse (occupancy ~ day + (1 | mouse), REML); significance is the two-sided Wald z-test on the day coefficient (OBS, β = 0.018 occupancy/ day, p = 0.002**; XPO, β = 0.011, p = 0.229, n.s.). Error bars, ±SEM across mice. g, Behaviour category occupancy (fraction of time occupied relative to total session length) compared between OBS (magenta, N = 9) and XPO (cyan, N = 5) animals during the training period. From left to right: attention occupancy (two-sided independent samples t-test: t(12) = 2.26, p = 0.044*), self-directed occupancy (two-sided independent samples t-test: t(12) = 0.166, p = 0.8713, n.s.), idle occupancy (two-sided Brunner-Munzel test: BM = 1.884, p = 0.0852 n.s.), exploratory occupancy (two-sided independent samples t-test: t(12) = −2.47, p = 0.0294). Box plots: line represents median; box, 25th–75th percentile; whiskers, min/max within 1.5x IQR; individual animal points overlaid h, Entropy (bits) of behaviour category occupancy distributions for OBS and XPO animals, computed as Shannon entropy across the four merged behavioural categories (two-sided independent samples t-test: t(12) = 2.248, p = 0.062 n.s.). Box plot and N as in g. i, Behaviour occupancy of OBS animals (N = 9) across attack relative time windows compared to a matched per-animal baseline. Windows: before attack onset (−25 to 0%), attack onset (0 to 25%), attack middle (25 to 75%), attack end (75 to 100%), and after attack offset (100 to 125%); baseline is mean behaviour occupancy across all training days. Error bars, ±SEM. Asterisks indicate significant deviation from baseline (two-sided paired t-tests with FDR correction, for full statistics see Table S1). j, Left: Average difference in behaviour category occupancy between attack and control periods across OBS animals (N = 9). Control segments were randomly drawn from non-attack frames across 50 independent trials, matched in total duration to attack segments (two-sided paired t-tests with FDR correction; attention: 0.0063**. Self-directed: 0.0083**). Right: Average mean latency to onset for each behavioural state during attack versus control periods across OBS animals (N = 9). Error bars, ±SEM across trials (two-sided paired t-tests with FDR correction; n.s). k, Average behaviour category occupancy at attack onset, before vs. after time-shifting across OBS animals (N = 9). A window of 2 s around attack onset is used for this analysis. After time-shifting, there is a significant increase in attention (p = 0.0098**) and decrease in idle (p = 0.0098**), and exploratory behaviours (p = 0.0372*) (two-sided paired t-tests with FDR correction). Error bars, ±SEM. l, Decoding performance (F1 score) for behaviour category labels in OBS animals (N = 9), comparing all recorded regions combined (filled bars), the best single region (outlined bars), and permutation-based chance (grey bars). The best single region was selected independently for each mouse and behaviour as the region yielding the highest mean F1 across cross-validation repeats. Error bars indicate ± SEM; dots show individual mice. Upper brackets indicate all regions vs. chance paired comparisons, lower brackets indicate all regions vs. best single region paired comparisons. P-values of two-sided paired t-tests with FDR correction are reported as (all vs. chance, all vs. best single region): attention (p = 9.54e-9***, p = 7.65e-4***); self-directed (p = 1.48e-6***, p = 1.87e-6***); idle (p = 3.28e-4***, p = 2.02e-4***); exploratory (p = 6.01e-7***, p = 8.89e-6***). m, Average SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values of signals’ contribution to decoding performance across OBS animals (N = 9), split by observer behaviour category. Error bars, ±SEM. For all comparisons, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001.

a, Overview schematic of the time-shifting process. Top left: A tensor of SBN activity is constructed with dimensions trial × attack window × neural population. Top middle: The model learns a population-specific activity template from the components of each recorded population. Bottom middle: The model learns the likely timing of activity on a trial-by-trial basis, yielding a distribution of per-trial time shifts ranging from −2 s to +2 s. Trials shifted in the negative direction are depicted in dark green and trials shifted in the positive direction in light green; unshifted trials are shown in grey-green. A negative skew in shift distribution (shifts <0) is evaluated via a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test (N = 1,115 trials, W = 258,136.5, p = 3.98 × 10−7***). Top right: The end result of the pipeline proceeds from unshifted signals through time-shifted alignment to attention-state filtering (ATTN+ versus ATTN−). b, Peri-event time histograms of excitatory (top) and inhibitory (bottom) SBN populations and valence areas for OBS animals, comparing time-shifted, attention-filtered (magenta) versus unshifted, attention-filtered (blue) attack-aligned signals (z-ΔF/F, mean, shaded area ± SEM). Shifted and unshifted signals are shown for each recorded region across the full network. For each population, post-attack mean activity (baseline-corrected) is compared against zero using two-sided one-sample t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests pending normality, with FDR correction across all regions. For full statistics, including N per population, see Table S1. For all comparisons, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001. c, To validate that time-shifting of neural signals does not spuriously generate neural activity, three control conditions were devised in which the same time-shifting model was applied to OBS animals. In the first condition, the model was applied to neural signals during randomly resampled behavioural events generated by a Markov chain trained to reproduce attack patterns (frequency and duration) at random time points not overlapping with real aggression (“synthetic,” light blue). In the second condition, the model was applied to neural signals during high resident velocity events unrelated to aggression (“speed,” dark blue-green). In the third condition, the model was applied to NON animal neural signals during random indices derived from real attack timepoints in OBS animals (“yoked,” grey). d, Peri-event time histograms (z-ΔF/F) of SBN and valence system activity for synthetic (left) and speed (right) control conditions (mean, shaded area ± SEM). Neural signals from each control condition are overlaid on OBS signals from Fig. 2j.

a, Illustration of the half-decay time metric applied to representative EXP (left) and OBS (right) subjects for VMHvl excitatory and inhibitory populations. Each trace shows the baseline-corrected, attack-aligned mean z-ΔF/F signal. The peak value (red dot) is identified within the post-attack window and the half-decay time t½ (yellow dot) is defined as the time from peak to the point at which the signal first returns to 50% of its peak value, estimated with sub-frame precision via linear interpolation. The baseline noise floor (2 × baseline SD) is used as a minimum threshold for valid peak detection. b, Half-decay time t½ (s) of attack-aligned calcium signals across all recorded excitatory (green) and inhibitory (blue) SBN populations, for EXP (orange) and OBS (magenta) animals during the training period. Box plots: line represents median; box, 25th–75th percentile; whiskers, min/max within 1.5x IQR; individual animal points overlaid. Regions are ordered with excitatory populations first, followed by inhibitory populations. For each region, EXP versus OBS comparisons are performed using two-sided independent samples t-tests or Brunner-Munzel tests pending normality, with FDR correction across all populations. For detailed statistics, see Table S1. c, Within-group comparison of half-decay time t½ between excitatory (light green) and inhibitory (light blue) populations for EXP animals, shown for each paired SBN region (VMHvl, PMv, AH, POA, MeA, PA, BNST, lPAG, vLS, PrL). Each point represents one animal; lines connect paired excitatory and inhibitory measurements from the same animal. Significance brackets indicate regions where excitatory half-decay time is significantly shorter than inhibitory half-decay time (one-sided paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests pending normality, with FDR correction across all regions). For detailed statistics, see Table S1. d, As in c but for OBS animals. For all comparisons, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001.

a, Average group-specific tuning curves (mean, shaded area +/− SEM) depicting the encoding of inter-animal proximity across hypothalamic and amygdala regions during the hard fight, shown as a function of binned proximity (close to far). Each tuning curve represents a set of GLM weights fit for each feature and each region independently, using a leave-one-animal-out cross-validation procedure, for EXP (orange), OBS (magenta), and NON (grey) animals. Boxed regions indicate representative neural populations selected for display. Highlighted areas in each curve denote the first five bins (blue) and last five bins (red) of each tuning curve, corresponding to low and high values of the encoded feature respectively. Tuning curves for which the cross-validated R² does not exceed zero are blurred to indicate poor model fit and low predictive power; region–feature combinations are only included in group comparisons if at least two groups show R² significantly greater than zero (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test). For full R² comparisons and pairwise group statistics, see Table S1. b, As in a but for resident self-speed (low to high). c, As in a but for CD1 aggressor speed (low to high).

a, Peri-event time histograms (z-ΔF/F) of inhibitory PMv, AH, MeA, and BNST populations, aligned to conflict bout onset (irrespective of attack direction) during the hard fight, for EXP (orange), OBS (magenta), and NON (grey) animals (mean ± SEM). b, Mean z-ΔF/F during the conflict period for each recorded population, excitatory populations and LHb (top row) and inhibitory populations and NAc DA (bottom row), EXP/OBS/NON. Individual animals shown as points; horizontal line indicates the group mean, error bar indicates +/− SEM. N per population in Table S1. Group comparisons: omnibus one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test pending normality, post-hoc two-sided t-tests or Brunner-Munzel tests, FDR-corrected within population; full statistics in Table S1. For all comparisons, *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001.

Schematic summarizing the relationship between inhibitory SBN ensemble activity and behavioural state across experimental groups. The x-axis represents the inhibitory ensemble state, indexed by population activity level and/or VMHvl coupling strength. The y-axis represents aggression preparedness, ranging from avoidant to aggressively prepared. NON animals, which lack social experience, occupy a high inhibitory ensemble / low preparedness state. OBS and EXP animals shift rightward and upward along both axes following observation and direct fighting experience respectively, reflecting reduced inhibitory tone and increased aggression preparedness. Reactivation of inhibition returns OBS animals toward the NON-like state, demonstrating that inhibitory ensemble activity is both necessary and sufficient to gate aggression preparedness in a novel aggression context.

#1383. Man United 3-2 Roma PLAYER RATINGS: Which star delivered their best performance in a red shirt? Whose physicality is something to marvel at? And who deserves 3/10 for their abysmal defending?

Published: 17:21 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 11:18 EDT, 4 November 2026

Manchester United pulled out an enormous win for Michael Carrick as they fought back from 2-0 down to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League.

Winless in nine games heading into this European night under the lights and United were staring at 10 without a win, a record that was last struck in 1978, when they were two down at half-time after a dreadful start.

But United conjured up spirit that has been barely visible so far this season as a brace from Matheus Cunha - who finished the night getting sent off - followed a penalty from Bruno Fernandes to seal the most crucial of wins.

What it means for Carrick's future in the medium to longer term remains to be seen.

Those upstairs at United have privately taken a lot of the blame and want to end the churn of managers carrying the can for poor player performances. Only time will tell how big a turning point this night can be.

Daily Mail Sport's NATHAN SALT was at Old Trafford on a frantic night to run the rule over the players...

Matheus Cunha rescued victory from the jaws of defeat for Manchester United against Roma

Made a big save low to his right on the stroke of half-time to prevent further embarrassment for United and, as it turned out, give them a fighting chance of getting the result they pulled out of the hat. His distribution seems to have really regressed this season with far too many aimless balls, though.

Made a huge recovery tackle to deny Rodrigo Mora a third and in a feckless first half it was he who bust a gut where others didn't. Yes, it's a low bar but Yoro has actually been one of, if not, the best United performers during this never-ending malaise.

A performance littered with mistakes that, in truth, looked to have been scrubbed from his game coming into this campaign. He's the leader of the back-line and he did everything but lead in a first half that saw positioning and decision-making leave a lot to be desired. His clearance that resulted in Roma's second goal was diabolical. Booked and was fortunate not to have been sent off.

Harry Maguire left a lot to be desired in a defensive performance littered with basic errors

Thrust into the side in place of Lisandro Martinez and his head will have been spinning when he gave away a penalty for a handball, which Donyell Malen converted. Booked for a lunging challenge that is becoming a worrying trend of tackling with studs up. May sound daft but he needs coaching by Jonny Evans or Jonathan Woodgate on a better way to slide tackle. Booked.

Abysmal defending for Roma's first goal as he committed to the attack like a winger and left Matias Soule the freedom of Manchester to score. Kept pushing forward – you have to assume by instruction – and kept being found wanting. Options are slim but he's not making any positive contribution to the team from left back. Needs a stop putting to it.

Got told to 'f**k off' by Bruno Fernandes in a fraught first half for a bobbly pass to tee him up on the edge of the box. Made a couple of smart bursts through lines but he's in the side to protect the defence and he didn't do it. Night cut short when he pulled his hamstring 60 seconds into the second half.

Will be disappointed with himself at how sloppily he gave away the ball in a turnover which exposed his defenders for the first goal. That error aside, he settled in and improved as it wore on. His ability to actually beat a man is in short supply in this United side and his physicality was something to marvel at at times.

Kobbie Mainoo actually looks to drive past players, a skill in short supply at United

Always has a buzz about him when he gets the ball and he was the only one to come back from Como with any crumb of credit. Here it was a more sobering affair where his influence was heavily restricted and it means his wait for a United goal goes on. Not managed one since December 2025.

A night of frustration for large spells but one that did eventually serve up a goal and assist for the United captain. All that aside, it was a poor look when he's berating team-mates when his own performance level is way below what he's capable of, mind you.

Could make a case for his best performance in a United shirt. It's up there.

Bryan Mbeumo will want his second half breakaway chance back after striking both posts

Muted in celebration at the end and given everything he's had to navigate this season that's perhaps understandable. But this was a shot in the arm, how big we need to wait and see. People have labelled him a dead man walking but he's not giving up yet.

Youri Tielemans (for Carlos Baleba, 51) - 5

Did OK, but didn't do a great deal to drive the play forward. Not exactly the perfect foil to Mainoo, who is stylistically similar.

Lifted the crowd and helped change the game. Should have won a penalty when he was hacked down and it was his assist to Cunha that sealed victory. Coudln't have made a stronger case to start on Sunday.

The fact he was far away from the eventual headlines was probably a good thing for all concerned after what transpired at Stamford Bridge.

#1381. Painful Coventry defeat will send shudder of fear through Newcastle

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

Matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”

The win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.

As for Newcastle, this raises uncomfortable questions about their summer recruitment, with so many expensive players on the bench or playing badly. It also means people will query whether Jaissle’s implementation of “vertical football” is working. The fact Lampard talked so openly about winning the duels to set up the win will anger the German.

Jaissle can point to two bad misses from one of the new arrivals, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m buy from Lille, in the first half. But his team are too easy to play through and the defence is an accident waiting to happen.

Even after Sven Botman’s stunning strike offered them a way back into the game, they capitulated at the back as Lewis Hall – who was off colour all evening – and Joelinton’s mistakes gift-wrapped a third for Ellis Simms. A fourth followed for Stephen Mfuni.

Ellis Simms off the bench with a big impact! 💥 https://t.co/XynFVxwERV

You can get a sense of what sort of mode a team are in within the first few passages of play and Newcastle were not sharp or precise. It was sloppy.

That was certainly true of goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who was off his line in no-man’s land trying to snuff out a through ball that he was not going to get. He stood up to deflect it away, but then rashly chased after it, diving at full stretch at the feet of Coventry’s Sidiki Cherif and failing to get the ball. Jack Rudoni coolly sent the Czech goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot.

Newcastle had been awful in their last away game at Leeds, another 4-1 thrashing, and there were many of the same faults on display.

It was not a good first half for Fernandez-Pardo up top. They are mystified in Belgium why he believes he is a centre-forward rather than a winger and he did not do himself any favours here. Newcastle’s best move of the game resulted in Lewis Miley playing in Jacob Murphy down the left. His cutback was perfect for Fernandez-Pardo to sweep home at the near post but instead of trying to make contact, he dummied it, thinking Harvey Barnes was better placed. He was not. It was a baffling piece of centre-forward play.

It had been the easiest 40 minutes Lampard’s side have had since they were promoted, but Newcastle still should have scored before the break.

Nico González spotted the run of Fernandez-Pardo through the middle. He wriggled clear of Bobby Thomas and sat down goalkeeper Carl Rushworth, but the Coventry centre-back got back to block his shot.

Newcastle pressed the self-destruct button early in the second half. A long throw into the box was half cleared. It should have been three. Again Wissa was partly to blame, losing the ball in midfield to set Coventry on the counter-attack. When Botman made a mess of a clearance it spun perfectly into the path of Cherif. The net should have bulged but the £20m summer signing from Fenerbahce scuffed wide.

Very, very satisfying. It’s so hard to win. We played like the team we want to be here. A team you look at and go there’s so much energy and spirit in the group. As the strains of We’ll Live and Die in These Towns dies down to segue into the Eton Boating Song, Newcastle kick off, attacking from right to left. When they lose the ball Wissa is penalised for tripping Rudoni 45 yards out.

Coventry are in blue and white stripes, harking back to the 1987 Cup final rather than the Mick Coop years. Newcastle are in vibrant lilac.

It was good to get a win. We worked very hard for it. It’s so hard to get wins, especially on the road. And now we’re back at home and we have to work on those attributes [that earned us the win] at Forest. We rotated pretty well, there are different aspects of the game we want to improve on regardless of shape.

A win for Newcastle United this evening will take Matthias Jaissle’s side up to fourth in the Premier League and vindicate the members of the club’s hierarchy who insisted they had appointed an elite manager to replace Eddie Howe.

It will also suggest they got their summer rebuild right and everything will point to an exciting future for a new look team.

Yet, should Newcastle lose against a Coventry City side – newly promoted to the top flight and yet to win at home this season – ripples of discontent will spread through the fanbase and everything about the summer, from managerial appointment to player recruitment will be called into question.

That may seem like an odd thing to write given how wildly different those reactions are but that is where Newcastle find themselves at the moment. We do not actually know if they are any good or what the expectations should be for a young team with a rookie Premier League head coach.

There remains an undercurrent of anxiety among supporters who have seen so many of their best players leave over the last 12 months and be replaced by young, emerging talent from across Europe.

The 4-1 thrashing at Leeds in their last away game was a painful reminder of the team’s vulnerability. They were bullied and outclassed.

Newcastle have not put together an impressive 90-minute performance since the opening day draw with Liverpool, yet that defeat to Leeds was also the only game they have lost. in all competitions. We will know a lot more about them after this. This is a game they are expected to win, so the ramifications of a defeat will be more severe.

When Brian Kilcline was at Notts County, the manager Jimmy Sirrel became a little perturbed by the nickname his young centre-back had carried since his school days. It might have been nice alliteration, but “Killer Kilcline” was not exactly the image he wanted his team to portray.

“Also the lads shouting, ‘get him Killer’ tended to alert referees,” Kilcline recalls.

So Sirrel decided he would put it to the County fans. He organised a competition to establish a better moniker for his foursquare defender.

“You know what they came up with?” Kilcline says. “Curly Wurly. Like the chocolate bar. It was to do with my hair, which was naturally curled. By the way, it was never a perm. But I mean, come on. I can’t imagine Curly Wurly would have intimidated anyone.”

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1380. Michael Carrick might STILL be one game from the sack. A one-night stand of epic proportions was up there with Man United's best but produced more questions than answers, writes CHRIS WHEELER

Published: 02:31 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 11:18 EDT, 4 November 2026

What a crazy, chaotic and, frankly, confusing night this was at Old Trafford. The grand old place has seen a few of them down the years, and Manchester United's incredible comeback win over Roma was right up there with the best.

By the end of it, the fans were loving United and hating the Glazers in keeping with their doctrine. Michael Carrick was savouring arguably his greatest moment as head coach, and yet might still be one game from the sack. Two-goal hero Matheus Cunha was being manhandled off the pitch and towards the tunnel, furious at not being able to celebrate with his teammates.

For Carrick, this felt like the equivalent of Erik ten Hag's win over Manchester City in the 2024 FA Cup final and Ruben Amorim's incredible 4-3 victory over Lyon in the Europa League quarter-final last year. The feelgood factor and sense of elation around Old Trafford was palpable.

Neither of those wins were enough to keep Ten Hag and Amorim in a job for much longer, and that is the conundrum for United bosses this morning.

If the feeling in the boardroom – and it remains an if – is to relieve Carrick of his duties, can they be swayed by a one-night stand, albeit one of epic proportions.

If United can follow this up with victory on Sunday over Aston Villa and Unai Emery – one of the candidates being touted as Carrick's replacement – can they really sack their head coach at the start of the international break?

Michael Carrick gave his players the half-time fire power needed to pull off a famous fightback

More than just pulling off the much-needed win against Roma, it felt as if his stars were playing for their manager

On another night when United fans turned on the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, director of football Jason Wilcox and even the players as boos greeted the half-time whistle and the 'play like you mean it' banner made a re-appearance for the first time in three years, it was a reminder that the most popular person at the club might be the man who is about to get the bullet.

The players certainly looked as though they are playing for Carrick, and afterwards Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans both gave him their backing.

Looking ahead to this game, Carrick had said: 'Whatever happens is going to happen after that in whatever direction it goes in, but we want to make it a big night tomorrow night first.'

Those words came true in spectacular fashion. For a while, it felt as though he wouldn't even survive until the Villa game as United's defence fell apart and Roma set a new record for a European opponent taking a two-goal lead at Old Trafford. It could have been worse.

Carrick got his players together at half-time and reminded them that it only takes one moment to light the touchpaper here. 'I don't like talking to the lads too much about the history of this place, but it's magical,' he said. 'There's something when we have these nights and we do it the hard way, and one moment can flip the whole feeling.'

Kobbie Mainoo put it more bluntly. 'We needed a bit of a kick,' said the United midfielder.

It worked. United roared back at Roma, showing a resolve and strength of character that has been missing for much of this season. Fernandes converted a retaken penalty, Cunha levelled and then smashed home the winner late on to give United their first victory in 10 games.

The Brazilian's sending-off for removing his shirt after scoring the third and then committing a silly foul on Leonardo Balerdi meant he wasn't allowed to go on the pitch at the end, much to his indignation. Carrick and his staff were there to reinforce the point.

Results clearly haven't been good enough this season, but one of the criticisms levelled at Carrick is that performances have been even worse. The combination of those two factors have left him fighting to save his job.

On the flip side, it felt like this win and the nature of it counted double. One that raised the roof at Old Trafford and lifted the soul.

Yet for so long on Tuesday night, the mood among the United faithful was one of mutiny. They revived the anti-Glazer campaign by bringing green and gold balloons into the Stretford End, and let them loose as the two teams walked out.

Rather like the protests against the absent owners who keep a safe distance thousands of miles away in America, they were never going to hit their target by reaching the pitch and floated harmlessly into the night air. A barrage of tennis balls had greater impact, but they too were soon cleared out of sight.

Chants against the Glazers, Ratcliffe and Wilcox rang out long before kick-off. 'You can stick your new stadium up your a***' chanted the fans. The game was seconds old when we heard the first rendition of 'sell United and f*** off home' followed by the tribute song to Carrick.

Even at a critical point in the game when VAR was studying Gianluca Mancini's challenge on Cunha to see if it warranted a penalty, the United fans broke into a chorus of 'we want Glazers out'. It was the same after Cunha fired the decisive goal as supporters turned on the Americans and voiced their support for Carrick once more. They were caught between wanting to vent their anger at the owners and back Carrick and the team.

Fervent and continuing protests against the ownership underscored Carrick's own popularity, despite being potentially days from getting the sack

Matheus Cunha might have been the late hero but he was unable to celebrate with his team-mates and manager after taking off his shirt

'The players one hundred per cent feed off the crowd, absolutely no doubt whatsoever,' said Carrick. 'I understand there's frustration and disappointment, I totally get that.

'Probably the time when it was easy for them not to be there, they were there. I felt that there was frustration, of course there was. I get it. But I know what they're like and we've got to give them something to go on.'

United managed to do that in the end, but it was a funny sort of night. One that produced more questions than answers. The biggest of them concerns Carrick. Is he doing enough to convince his employers that United can turn a corner? Victory in Europe doesn't alter the fact they are one place above the Premier League relegation zone.

There is one more game against Villa and then the choice is very simple: stick or twist?

#1379. Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome1. Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors2, which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR–Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal–fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases.

(a) Schematic diagram illustrating the preparation of subgenomic RNA-containing VLPs or empty VLPs with DogTag inserted into the envelope proteins. BHK-SGR-NL cells were transfected with a plasmid expressing the structural protein precursor CE2E1 to produce VLPs containing SGR (SGR-VLP). Plasmids encoding C-DTE2-E1, which contains an in-frame DogTag insertion between Gly1 and Leu2 of the E2 protein, and C-E2-DTE1, which contains an in-frame DogTag insertion between Asn213 and Gln214 of the E1 protein, were also expressed. Expi293F cells were utilized to produce large quantities of empty VLPs. (b) A series of SGR-VLPs encoding NanoLuc as a reporter were inoculated into Vero cells to assess infectivity. As a negative control, culture medium collected from BHK-SGR-NL cells expressing mCherry instead of CE2E1 was used. Infectivity was determined by measuring the relative activity of NanoLuc (n = 3 biologically independent cultures). (c) Western blot analysis to detect the E2 (left panel) or E1 (right panel) protein of SGR-VLPs. SGR-VLPs were incubated overnight at 4 °C in the presence or absence of DC-APEX2. SDS-PAGE samples were prepared by adding SGR-VLPs to SDS-PAGE sample buffer containing 2-mercaptoethanol and incubating at 95 °C for 5 min. Arrows indicate the original bands of viral proteins with an inserted DogTag, while arrowheads indicate those covalently bound to DC-APEX2. (d) Infectivity analysis of SGR-VLP mixed with PBS or DC-APEX2. SGR-VLPs were incubated overnight at 4 °C with PBS or DC-APEX2 and subsequently inoculated into Vero cells to analyze infectivity. As a negative control, culture medium collected from BHK-SGR-NL cells expressing mCherry instead of CE2E1 was used. Infectivity was determined by measuring the relative activity of NanoLuc (n = 4 biologically independent cultures). (e) Electron microscopic images of VLPs and APEX2-VLPs visualized by negative staining. (f) Following treatment of JAR4-SMS1KO22 cells under the indicated conditions, biotin-labeled proteins were detected by western blotting using HRP-conjugated streptavidin. (g) Fluorescence staining images of JAR4-SMS1KO22 cells treated with biotin labeling in the presence or absence of APEX2-VLP. RuV E1 protein, biotin, and nuclei are visualized in green, magenta, and blue, respectively. Images in left and upper right panels were obtained by confocal microscopy and are shown as z-stack projections. The boxed area in the left panel is magnified in the upper right panel. The cross-section obtained by cutting along the dotted line in the left panel is shown in the lower right panel. The plasma membranes stained with WGA are shown in gray in only the cross-section image. Data are mean ± s.d. Statistical analyses were performed using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc multiple comparison test (b) and two-way ANOVA with Šídák’s post hoc multiple comparison test (d). Statistical significance is indicated by asterisks: ****P < 0.0001; ***, P < 0.001; **, P < 0.01; ns, not significant. Exact P values are provided in Supplementary Table 5.

(a) Schematic diagram of the measurement of replication, transcription, and translation activity by the RuV subgenomic replicon (SGR). SGR-RNA, in which the structural protein gene of RuV was replaced by a fusion protein gene of puromycin-N-acetyltransferase (PAC), an FMDV 2 A protease cleavage site, and NanoLuc (NLuc), was generated by in vitro transcription. SGR-GND is an RNA replication-deficient mutant generated by substituting amino acids in the active center of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of p90 (GDD to GND). SGR-WT RNA or SGR-GND RNA was transfected into RajiSC-EV or RajiSC-hNectin-4 cells together with mRNA for RuV C protein and Firefly Luciferase (FLuc), and incubated at 35 °C. #1377. Unai Emery has closed gap between Aston Villa and Europe's elite - but rampant Barcelona proved there is still a way to go as Lamine Yamal dazzles, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 17:17 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 11:27 EDT, 4 November 2026

John McGinn heard the question. His eyes darted around Barcelona's packed media auditorium for a second or two on Monday night. What was it like to be about to play in the Nou Camp, the Aston Villa skipper had been asked, as if this were to be some sort of spin off from Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure.

McGinn was careful with his answer. He did not seek to downplay the nature of the occasion or the thrill that comes with lining up in such a majestic arena. But he was determined not to play the wide-eyed ingenu. 'What our club is trying to do now,' McGinn said, 'is make this normal, make this a yearly experience.'

So when he and his team-mates walked up the flight of steps from the dressing rooms into the vast bowl of the stadium on Tuesday evening, they were here to show that they were not arrivistes. Villa is a historic club. They won this competition in 1982, ten years before Barcelona ever did. They were not here for a treat or to get patted on the back just for turning up.

It is nearly 20 years since Liverpool became the last English club to win here and nobody gave Villa too much chance of ending that drought. They are being told constantly that the odds are stacked against them and that their much-admired manager, Unai Emery, may be tempted by the entreaties of struggling 'giants' elsewhere.

That was the reason why this game early in the league phase had attained so much importance. For Villa, it was a symbol of something they aspire to. They want to get used to belonging in this company, to walking up those steps, to emerging into the stadium in the pouring rain, and staring at players of the calibre of Lamine Yamal, Rodri and Pau Cubarsi staring back at them.

It still feels as if they stand on the cusp of something bigger but they blew their shot at proving that on Tuesday night. They needed to be at their best to have a chance of beating Hansi Flick's side, which sits atop LaLiga, and they were far too naïve in defence to get close to causing a shock. They are rising but this was a step too far at this stage of their evolution.

Lamine Yamal (centre) and Barcelona had plenty to smile about after beating Aston Villa 3-0

Yamal opened the scoring for Barcelona after just seven minutes with this left-footed finish

Raphinha (right) doubled Barca's lead after half-time with this strike at the Spotify Nou Camp

The Nou Camp, which is still in the midst of an extensive renovation and was only about two-thirds full, was ringed by towering yellow cranes, peering down at the floodlit patch of green. From their lofty vantage point, they saw Villa get off to the worst possible start.

Only seven minutes had gone when Emery's team gift-wrapped a present for the home side. Zion Suzuki played the ball out short to Joao Gomes but Gomes panicked under pressure from the Barcelona press and the close attention of Pedri. He played the ball square without looking, straight to Yamal.

Of all the players he could have found, Gomes had to find Yamal. The Spain superstar squared up Pau Torres and then curled the ball around him with a gentle caress of his left boot. Suzuki was helpless. The ball nestled in the corner of the net. Barcelona had scored 56 goals in 14 games before this match. Extending the hand of generosity to them must have felt particularly galling for Emery.

Villa almost hit back immediately. A stinging volley from Matty Cash was deflected wide and Barcelona looked jittery at the back. Nicolas Jackson played a square ball to Johan Manzambi, who should have equalised but scuffed his first-time effort wide of Joan Garcia. Barcelona were thankful for Garcia's intervention when he raced out of his goal to dispossess Jackson as he charged on to a through ball.

Yamal was rampant. His battle with Ian Maatsen was a mismatch and Maatsen was booked after 11 minutes for hacking him down. Villa were still intent on playing themselves into trouble. Suzuki repeated his mistake when he tried to play the ball out to Joao Gomes. This time, Pedri beat him to it and the loose ball fell to Gordon. Gordon hit his shot towards the corner but Suzuki redeemed himself by diving to push it away.

Barcelona had the better of the play. They looked like scoring every time they went forward. Time and again, either Raphinha or Yamal found space to run at the Villa defence, which was barely coping. Even in that context, though, it was an open game. Villa had chances, too. Manzambi forced a fine save out of Garcia. A Jackson breakaway was thwarted by a last-ditch block.

But seven minutes after the break, Barcelona doubled their lead. Fermin Lopez played a clever ball to Raphinha, who had found a yard of space in the box. Raphinha, LaLiga's leading scorer this season, drilled a left-foot shot goalwards and it deflected off the heel of Torres, wrong-footed Suzuki and rolled over the line.

Barcelona put the game out of reach midway through the half when Joao Cancelo forced his way past McGinn on the left flank and hit a sumptuous cross into the box with the outside of his right foot. Raphinha gambled on the path of the ball, darted behind his marker and tucked the ball away.

Raphinha completed the scoreline with this cute finish as Barcelona completed their victory

For Aston Villa, this will be a learning curve as they look to go far in the Champions League

Villa manager Unai Emery will have plenty to think about after another Nou Camp defeat

Substitute Leon Goretzka hit the face of a post for Villa late on but the game was already gone. There was no shame in losing to a team who are one of the favourites to win the competition this season but there was frustration in the way Villa had handed their opponents the advantage.

Emery looked bedraggled as he stood on the touchline in the rain, arms folded, shaking his head. This was his 15th defeat in 16 visits to the Nou Camp. As Villa's coach fights to edge his team closer to the elite of the game, this game will become just one more bad memory.

#1375. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

England thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

Lauren James with a SUMPTUOUS finish but unfortunately it's offside 🥹 Watch Greece v England on ITV1 📺 https://t.co/4s9neVKIaR

Ioanna Papatheodorou nearly gave Greece the lead when she dribbled past Esme Morgan and Leah Williamson with ease but her powerful strike hit the crossbar. It was a let-off for England, but they made it count by taking the lead just before half-time.

A fine team move ended with an excellent Stanway finish. It was her fifth goal in this qualifying campaign and she is England’s top scorer for 2025-26.

Le Tissier scored England’s second just past the hour mark before Alessia Russo made it 3-0 four minutes later. It appeared the floodgates may have opened but that proved to be a false dawn, with Greece scoring a deserved goal through Kallisti Brouksair after some poor England defending.

While this game will go down as largely forgettable, it will be remembered by 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson and Grace Fisk, 28, who came on for their senior debuts in the closing stages. It also means Parkinson, who could have played for Japan, Portugal or Singapore, is now tied to England.

She is an exciting player for the future but will feel she has a chance of making a World Cup squad, should England get there. For now, they are taking the slow route.

Maya le Tissier tells ITV: “I didn’t really know it went in to be honest because I thought the keeper saved it. I just smacked it so I’m very glad. It’s always good to get your first goal, so very happy.

“Not really [a moment she had dreamt about] to be honest because I’m a defender and I thought I’d just be stopping it but it’s always good to get up there. When I play that position, I find myself a little bit higher up, definitely something to work on but very happy to score my first goal.

“I do [like playing that position], I love defending as well. It’s obviously a bit different for me up there but I always try and give my best whatever position I play so I did enjoy it.”

Well, that was a warning sign for England! Ioanna Papatheodorou went past Esme Morgan and Leah Williamson with ease and is so unlucky not to have given Greece the lead. Hannah Hampton just watched as her strike hit the crossbar. A huge let off.

Papatheodorou sprints at goal, and two or three England defenders put in atrocious efforts to tackle her, and the striker smashes the ball goalwards, with it just touched wide.

England have averaged over 80% possession with half an hour gone. They’ve had 25 touches in Greece’s box. The hosts have had none in England’s. But it remains 0-0. It feels like a matter of time before the Lionesses score but they’re just missing a clinical touch at the minute.

James sends a free-kick wide of the near post, about 25 yards out, a couple of yards wide.

She has some of the best technique in the sport, and looks a constant threat.

England take a quick corner and earn another on the right wing.

Le Tissier stands a tempting cross up to the back post, but Giannaka heads away. The pressure is constant from England.

England are still in control, but search for the first goal once again.

Lauren James with a SUMPTUOUS finish but unfortunately it's offside 🥹 Watch Greece v England on ITV1 📺 https://t.co/4s9neVKIaR

That was a ridiculous chip from James but VAR correctly rules the goal out for offside. The forward was a good two yards beyond the last defender. A great finish but it remains 0-0.

An outstanding goal as she picks the ball up about 30 yards out, sees the keeper off her line, an expertly chips her.

THE #LIONESSES LEAD! 😍 A stunning strike! https://t.co/nydZnRYOxA

Le Tissier strikes at goal from distance.

It’s about 25 yards out, and the keeper does brilliantly to beat it away at full stretch for a corner.

Walsh tries to recreate Gary Neville’s chip against Juventus, and she nails it, in the sense that both of them missed.

Corner on the left wing for England, with James to take.

Greece fail to properly clear but they press England and eventually force them away from the box.

Stanway has room for a shot about a yard or two outside the box, but her low effort is dragged wide.

Hard to work out what exactly the England formation is here. It appears that Blindkilde Brown is playing more on the right, with James in the No 10. Le Tissier is also pushing up very high, almost like a wing-back at times.

Brookshire’s cross is cleared and England win the ball back.

Russo is released down the left wing, but England keep possession.

As expected, England have most of the early possession. They are keeping it in defence and midfield for now.

Reading between the lines - with big flashing guardrails - I think England believe this could be an easy game.

To qualify for the World Cup finals in Brazil, England must navigate a two-stage play-off system. Beating Greece over two legs is only step one; the winner will advance to face either Slovakia or Ukraine in a December decider.

The pundit was sure that Lauren Hemp deserved wider recognition.

The final preparations before the 5.30pm kick-off.

Tonight’s hosts are yet to qualify for a major tournament and are expected to set up in a defensive shape. England defender Esme Morgan believes the squad are ready for a long night of breaking down a stubborn opposition.

She told a pre-match press conference: “It’s just about persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. A really good example was the away game against Ukraine in qualifying. We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half - the keeper was making saves, we hit the woodwork - but the messaging at half-time was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities.

”Not to start snatching or taking shots from distance, just trusting in our style of play and our ability to find gaps. We came out for the second half and scored really quickly. It’s just about sticking to the plan and being patient.”

Erica Meg Parkinson, one of England’s new midfielders, was apparently named after Eric Cantona.

While Cantona still famously is proud of his kung fu kick, when he attacked an obnoxious Crystal Palace fan, Parkison is less enthused by football’s most famous case of breaking the fourth wall.

“My dad is a huge Man United fan so I was named after Eric Cantona,” Parkinson says. “It’s a pretty good player to be named after except for, you know, the karate kicks.

“My brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say in the name so she was dragged into it, but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.”

Hello from sunny Heraklion. It’s very calm here at the moment, with just under 50 minutes to go until kick-off.

Over 500 England fans have made the journey. There may in fact end up being more away fans than home supporters here. Tickets for all fans were free but as it stands, the locals are outnumbered.

It looks as though the Lionesses will set up in a 4-3-3 with Maya Le Tissier coming in at right back for the injured Lucy Bronze.

Our #Lionesses in Crete 🦁 🙌 https://t.co/qv4VnAgKiM

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1374. The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Animals learn about the external world in part through interoceptive signals1,2. For example, the nutrient content of food is first estimated in the mouth, in the form of flavour, and then it is measured again through slower signals from the gut. How these signals from the mouth and gut are integrated to drive learning is unclear. Here we identify a dopamine (DA) pathway that enables learning about the nutrient content of food. We show that DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area are necessary for associating nutrients with flavours, and that post-ingestive nutrients trigger DA release selectively in a small region of the anterior basolateral amygdala (BLA) but not in canonical DA targets in striatum. This nutrient-triggered DA release occurs preferentially in the left BLA in mice, and this same structure is preferentially activated by post-ingestive nutrients in humans. We identify the gut sensors that are responsible for nutrient-triggered DA release; show that they activate BLA-projecting DA neurons defined by expression of cholecystokinin; and demonstrate that stimulation of DA axon terminals in the anterior BLA drives flavour–nutrient learning but not other aspects of feeding behaviour. Two-photon imaging of neurons in the left anterior BLA reveals that they integrate gustatory and post-ingestive cues, and silencing these neurons prevents flavour–nutrient learning. These findings establish a neural basis for how animals learn about the nutrient content of their food.

Legends and additional references for Supplementary Tables 1–6.

Behaviour statistics. Summary information for all behavioural tests for each manipulation. Values are reported to 1 decimal place. Number of animals is reported as n. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). In cases in which a Benjamini–Hochberg correction was made for multiple comparisons, an adjusted P value (p′) is shown (where p′ = P × m/i, where i is rank and m is number of cohorts tested; Methods). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For self-stimulation, ‘presses’ means the number of inactive lever presses has been subtracted from the number of active lever presses. In flavour conditioning experiments in which mice began the test with >90% preference for one flavour, statistics are also provided (in parentheses) with these mice excluded. Permutation (perm.) tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n > 9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note: this means the lowest calculable P value is 1 × 10−5).

Dopamine imaging statistics. Summary information for all recordings of dopamine release in each brain region. Values are reported to 2 decimal places. Number of animals is reported as n. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For photometry traces, dF′/F′ means the dF/F values seen during sham infusion have been subtracted. For rise times, s′ means that the time is relative to approximate entry of liquid into the stomach. For fall times, s′ means that the time is relative to the end of the infusion. For peak times during licking, s′ means that the time is relative to the start of the first licking bout. The baseline is defined as the first 10 min of the recording for GI and post-GI measurements, or 0–20 s before the start of the first licking bout for oral measurements. Permutation tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n >9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note that this means the lowest calculable P value is 1 × 10−5).

Single-cell imaging statistics. Summary information for all 1- and 2-photon miniscope recordings. Values are reported to 2 decimal places. The number (n) of animals and number of cells are reported separately. P values are reported for all statistical tests, and are shown in bold if below standard significance level (α = 0.05). X′ corresponds to the normalized value of X. For rise times, s′ means that the time is relative to either the onset of the licking bout or to the approximate entry of liquid into the stomach. Population-weighted activity (pop-z) is calculated for a group of neurons (for example, activated or inhibited neurons) by multiplying activity by the fraction of neurons belonging to that group. Linear-mixed models (LME) treat mouse differences as both a fixed random effect and covariate (Methods). The relative contribution of mouse differences to total variance is reported by ICCs. Note that, for PCA, the number of PCs is equal to the number of cells. Permutation tests use an exact test (or 100,000 iterations if n > 9) and are unpaired, unless otherwise mentioned (note that this means that the lowest calculable P value for those tests is 1 × 10−5).

fMRI imaging statistics (n = 38). Activity from left and right BLA clusters binned every 2 min (20 min total), as shown in Extended Data Figs. 10f and 11n. For PET statistics, see ref. 56. Each of the ten time bins after glucose intake was contrasted against the baseline (2 min before glucose intake), representing the change in brain activity after glucose intake relative to the baseline. The contrast for the first effect was [ones(1,10)], and for the following contrasts [1], corresponding to the different time bins. The significance threshold was P < 0.05, FWE-corrected for multiple comparisons at the voxel level within the left or right BLA mask, respectively, with initial peak-level threshold set to P < 0.05 uncorrected.

Pseudorabies statistics. Regional labelling (load) was normalized to VTA load to control for injection efficiency. From the 1,328 annotated CCFv3 regions, only grey-matter areas were retained (372 total), with cortical layers collapsed into single structures. Regions smaller than 100 × 100 × 100 pixels were excluded to remove small nuclei with high variance from few labelled cells, yielding 131 analysed regions.

Brain connectivity tables. Connectivity matrices were generated manually, with each pair given a number indicating bidirectional projection strength from 0 (no known direct connection) to 5 (strongest projection known from this area). The connectivity strength between an area and itself was assigned a value of 5. For deciding what strength to assign a projection, large databases like the Allan Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas (ref. 1 of the Supplementary References) were preferred, supplemented by additional sources comprising reviews and anatomical tracing studies (refs. 2–32 of the Supplementary References).
