#1373. Newcastle Confidential: REVEALED - Players 'confused' by Matthias Jaissle's instructions, why formation tweak is a possibility, Joelinton injury worry and new transfer guru's methods explained

Published: 12:00 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 12:01 EDT, 4 November 2026

Newcastle’s players are ‘confused’ by what Matthias Jaissle wants from them, a source close to the dressing room has told me.

I've been told the squad remains supportive of Jaissle and there is a determination to get things right for the head coach – senior players accept there is a responsibility on them – but there is also a desire for clarity over what it is they are being asked to do on the field.

Jaissle said in the wake of Monday's 1-0 home defeat by Everton that he could not understand why the team had not followed his instructions and executed the tactics they had worked on in training. He said the plan was not to play ‘long balls’.

Sources also say Jaissle spoke to his players afterwards about their press not being what he wanted and their passing being too slow in the opposition half.

However, I have been told some players are unsure as to the playing style and strategy, and that has led to those in deep positions getting the ball forward as quickly as possible, invariably with a long pass. There are also some within the dressing room wondering why the team continues to play with a No 10 when they do not have a specialist in that position.

Another source close to a senior player says the logical solution is a return to the 4-3-3 of recent seasons. There was word from inside the training ground that Jaissle was considering such a change ahead of the trip to Crystal Palace last month, so it is not off the table.

The demand from supporters to find a place for teenager Sean Steur in the midfield could yet see a tweak to the system, especially as Jaissle believes he and Nico Gonzalez are not suited to playing together as a two.

Newcastle's players are understood to be 'confused' by what it is head coach Matthias Jaissle wants from them

The demand from supporters to find a place for teenager Sean Steur (left) in the midfield could yet see a tweak to the Newcastle system

Joelinton is a fresh injury concern and medical staff will know in the next 24 hours if he is set to miss Saturday’s trip to Fulham, I can reveal. The Brazilian was feeling some muscle discomfort post-match on Monday and there is hope that the issue is related to a severe case of cramp.

However, I understand that is yet to be confirmed and, given Joelinton’s history of muscle strains, including his hamstring, no chances will be taken. The 30-year-old only returned from a thigh injury three weeks ago having been sidelined since the summer.

In better news, Matias Fernandez-Pardo and Lewis Miley are set to return for the game at Craven Cottage.

I understand Fernandez-Pardo wanted to be included in the squad for the visit of Everton but was told by staff he needed more training. The Belgian had missed the previous two matches with what is being described as a ‘tricky virus’ and only returned to training over the weekend.

Fernandez-Pardo arrived on Tyneside insisting he wanted to be used as a central striker following his £51million move from Lille. However, Jaissle currently prefers William Osula in that position and Fernandez-Pardo will likely be competing for a place out wide at Craven Cottage.

Miley, meanwhile, was also pushing for involvement on Monday after recovering from a glute issue. The 20-year-old’s return is timely given the midfield struggles of late, as well as the fresh worry over Joelinton and Jacob Ramsey’s suspension following his red card against Everton.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo is available again for Newcastle after suffering with a ‘tricky virus’

One player who almost certainly won’t come in for a start is Aladji Bamba, although we are told he will NOT be going out on loan in January.

The 20-year-old has appeared for just 27 minutes since his £30m arrival from Monaco in the summer, and he has not featured at all since September 19.

But despite potential availability issues in midfield, Jaissle does not feel Bamba is ready to start Premier League matches. That has led to a suggestion among some that he could be loaned out in January, especially as he has made only 12 senior starts in his career.

However, I understand the plan is for Bamba to remain on Tyneside and there has been encouragement with his recent performances in training.

Aladji Bamba has impressed in training of late and won't leave on loan in January despite his lack of first-team minutes

It has been interesting speaking to those who know a little more about Newcastle's new head of recruitment Tomas Amaral, who was virtually unknown in the UK before his appointment last month.

The Portuguese, 35, has been described as a 'bookworm and laptop obsessive', a meticulous talent-spotter who works long into the night. Amaral, who spent four years scouting for Benfica and was most recently sporting director at Spartak Moscow, has also spoken previously of the dangers of clubs signing good players who do not fit the manager's system.

He believes recruitment should begin with a clear footballing identity, rather than collecting talented individuals and hoping they somehow fit together. He also argues that scouts should challenge managers over transfer targets, rather than simply indulge their wishes.

Interestingly, his recruitment strategy involves two lists – one identifying players good enough for the club, the other those specifically suited to the manager's demands. For him, character and adaptability are considered just as important as ability.

He was part of the Benfica scouting team who identified Enzo Fernandez when signing him from River Plate in 2022. The midfielder was sold to Chelsea for a near £100m profit the following year.

Amaral’s arrival at least gives clarity to the recruitment structure inside St James’ Park, and he would appear to have a busy 12 months ahead given what feel like obvious areas for improvement across the pitch. I understand there is scope to spend in January should the club feel it necessary.

Beneath first-team level, Newcastle have cast their scouting net a little wider this week with two promising teenagers from Gambia arriving on Tyneside.

We understand Omar Marong and Alieu Saine, both 16, will stay for a two-week trial and train with the academy. They are products of the Today Makes Tomorrow Academy and have been identified under the club’s new global talent drive.

The pair caught the eye during Gambia’s triumph at September’s West African Under-17 Championship. Central midfielder Marong captained the side, while winger Saine finished as joint-top scorer with four goals. Neither player can join permanently until turning 18 because of FIFA regulations, but Newcastle are keen to assess their potential.

Meanwhile, the club are also set to appoint a specialist scout in Africa.

Finally, Newcastle prospect Matheos Ferreira could soon be at the centre of an international tug of war.

The 18-year-old, born in Ashington and raised in Berwick, has been called up by Brazil Under 20s for friendlies against Japan and Singapore this month. He is the only English-based player in the squad.

Newcastle prospect Matheos Ferreira could play for England, Italy or Brazil

But Ferreira, whose father is Brazilian and mother Italian, also qualifies for England and Italy. He has previously represented England at youth level and recently obtained an Italian passport.

I have seen him play a handful of times and there is certainly plenty of talent and potential. Interestingly, he has been operating as a No 10 at times this season, having come through the ranks as a winger.

Maybe there is a No 10 inside the club after all…

#1372. My Everton #178: What Makes It The People's Club

It all started with my dad who used to go to both Everton and Liverpool games well before my time.

Over the years, he started a family and, thankfully, his allegiances started to move towards Everton.

Jimmy, my eldest brother, came along years later and he started following the Blues straight away, going to the games as soon as he was allowed to.

I came along in 1984 and soon became the newest Blue in the house.

From the age of around 10, Jimmy took me to my first game at Goodison and I fell in love with Everton from that day. Me and Jimmy went to every home game and a few of the local away fixtures as well.

Our dad didn’t really go to many games with us. He did start coming again around 1999 but had a heart attack after one of the games. He never went again – but followed from the couch at home.

Moving forward some years Jimmy met his future wife, Christine, who at the time was a Leeds fan... not for long, though! It took only three games watching the Blues to convert her and extend our home seats by another.

We loved the tradition of a home game day: the meet-up at my mum and dad's house and the drive listening to Radio City’s football talk.

We had season tickets for many years until Christine became ill and needed constant treatment. We all decided to give them up and buy each game separately if and when we could around her treatment.

Unfortunately, after a year, Christine lost her battle and left us. Jimmy needed to get back to Goodison as soon as possible, so again, we all started going to every game together.

Skip through to 2024 and our dad passed away. Another blue light gone out.

Me and Jimmy made sure to remember him at the new stadium with a stone and photo inside.

Jimmy was obsessed with the new stadium build, watching drone progress daily. He waited so long for a new stadium. Unfortunately, Jimmy also passed away just two months after our dad, not getting to step inside the new stadium he always dreamed of.

Again, with losing my dad and Jimmy, who I always went the game with, I decided that I would also stop going.

For the past two seasons I've supported from home, but all while still singing the Blues!

Family is what makes Everton the People's Club.

Its love is passed down through each family member. All those years ago my dad could have chosen the red side but didn’t.

Since then, at least 15 family members have supported and followed the Blues.

I still haven't been a game at our new stadium, but Jimmy and Christine's grandkids do, singing in his name.

My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present.

#1371. Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision with Spanish footballer speaks out to reveal his 'enormous pain' and says he will 'face whatever comes' after police opened homicide investigation and fans called him 'murderer'

Published: 11:22 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 13:47 EDT, 4 November 2026

Jesus Owono, the goalkeeper involved in the fatal collision with the late Jesus de Miguel, has spoken for the first time since the tragic incident.

FC Andorra goalkeeper Owono collided with opposing striker de Miguel in the latter stages of a hotly contested 2-2 draw with Tenerife in Spain's second division on Monday.

De Miguel immediately collapsed following the devastating blow in which Owono's knee appeared to strike the forward in the chest. He passed away in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

Owono has since shut down his Instagram account amid the significant backlash he has received – which saw him subjected to chants of 'murderer' by the Tenerife fans as he left the pitch – but he has now issued a statement alongside his club.

'FC Andorra continues to be deeply affected by the death of Jesús de Miguel,' they wrote. 'In these very difficult moments, our player Jesús Owono wishes to personally share a few words.'

Owono said: 'These are being the most difficult days of my life. I am struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to assimilate anything that has happened.

Jesus Owono has broken his silence after being involved in a fatal collision with Jesus de Miguel

Tenerife striker de Miguel died on Tuesday morning following the horrifying clash with Owono

'I feel an enormous pain for the loss of Jesús. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address; I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesús.'

The club added: 'FC Andorra asks for the utmost sensitivity and respect.'

Andorra held a minute's silence at the club's training ground today, and the collision has opened the debate surrounding challenges involving goalkeepers and outfield players in football.

Former Real Madrid and Spain international goalkeeper Santiago Canizares, speaking on El Partidazo de COPE, conceded he believed Owono used ‘excessive force’ when going for the challenge.

Canizares, however, offered a defence of Owono by explaining the goalkeeper’s likely thought process and explained that they typically use their knees as protection and to help avoid collisions.

‘It's a goal-scoring opportunity, and what Owono has in his head is “I have to contest that ball,” ball or player,' Canizares said.

‘For me, the problem is that Owono uses excessive force, and he lacks the physical dexterity to pull himself back when he sees he's won the duel.

‘He goes all out and goes all out until the end. That physical dexterity is key when only one of the two is contesting.

‘What happens in this case is that I think the momentum causes the knee to rise due to the force and excessive speed it brings.’

The striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line

Owono said he could not 'think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing' (Source: Instagram/Jesus Owono)

FC Andorra defender Lautaro Spatz has also defended his team-mate, writing that the goalkeeper has been 'deeply affected' by the tragedy.

'There are moments when football loses its meaning. Moments that mark you forever and make you realise how fragile life can be,' Spatz wrote in a statement shared on social media.

'What we went through is something none of us will ever forget. A tragedy that has left us completely broken, speechless, and with a sadness that is difficult to explain.

'First and foremost, I want to express my deepest condolences and all my love to Jesús’s family, friends, and loved ones, as well as to the entire Tenerife community and the entire football family. Since yesterday, the entire FC Andorra squad has been shocked, devastated, and deeply affected by what has happened. It is a tragedy we never imagined we would experience on a football pitch.'

Spatz continued: 'I also want to say a few words to my teammate, goalkeeper, and friend, who is deeply affected by what happened. Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is. We know how much he is suffering right now and that he would never intend to hurt anyone.

'In football, unforeseen events occur, but no one can imagine that one of them could end with such tragic consequences. Today, football doesn't matter. All that remains is to offer our condolences, show the utmost respect, and send all our strength to the family and to all those suffering this terrible loss. Rest in peace, Demi.'

Police investigating de Miguel's death are now probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged yesterday homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Police are investigating the death of de Miguel due to protocol, and they are also now probing the emergency medical response

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

But overnight it emerged the police probe will also review the medical response to Monday's emergency and seek to address questions about whether de Miguel was given oxygen on the pitch and whether a defibrillator was used from the outset as well as issues around the assistance he received during his ambulance transfer.

The 30-year-old father-of-one died on Tuesday morning at Nuestra Senora Candelaria University Hospital after his club revealed his neurological condition had worsened.

Medical personnel involved in the footballer's care are expected to be questioned and detectives will sift through medical reports as part of the probe.

#1370. Everton's Remembrance Day Plans

Everton and Coventry City will come together ahead of Friday’s Premier League fixture at Hill Dickinson Stadium to remember the fallen and honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women during conflict.

The pre-match Remembrance ceremony will involve players and staff from both clubs, as well as representatives of the Royal Navy, British Army, Royal Air Force and Merchant Navy.

Those taking part in the tribute will include serving personnel from the Tri-Service Toffees Supporters’ Club and former servicemen and women supported by Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme.

Supporters are requested to arrive to their seats from 7.50pm, ahead of the ceremony, which will follow the walk-out by the teams and match officials.

As part of the Remembrance ceremony, the captains of Everton and Coventry City will lay commemorative poppy wreaths on the pitch ahead of kick-off, along with representatives from the Armed Forces, the Tri-Service Toffees and Everton in the Community.

Players from both sides will wear shirts bearing the poppy emblem, in memory of the fallen.

We will proudly welcome the following service personnel to take part in our pre-match tribute:

The following former service personnel will also participate in the tribute through Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme:

Following the laying of the wreaths, The Last Post will be performed by bugler Andrew Manning.

As a mark of respect, the traditional pre-match siren will not sound before the teams enter the pitch, though Z-Cars will play as normal.

As part of the Club’s recognition of serving personnel, Steve McCann and Danny Jackson, both members of Tri-Service Toffees, will take part in the half-time Hit the Bar competition.

The Tri-Service Toffees is an affiliated Everton supporters’ club for those serving in the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force, whether regular or reservist. Evertonians interested in joining or finding out more about the supporters’ club should email triservicetoffees@gmail.com.

Shirts worn by Everton’s Men’s and Women’s players during the Remembrance period will be auctioned to raise vital funds to support the work of the Royal British Legion. To find out more – or to bid for a shirt – click here.

What Remembrance Means to Me – A Message From The Tri-Service Toffees

Remembrance is about remembering. It really is that simple.

Remembering the sacrifices made by so many, from the First World War through every conflict since. Not just those who served in uniform, but the families, friends, colleagues and civilians whose lives were forever changed.

It is about taking a moment to acknowledge those sacrifices, both great and small, and the individuals who made them.

Having served for over 37 years, including numerous operational tours in conflict, I don’t reflect on my own sacrifices. Those will be for others to remember when I am gone.

Instead, I remember my mum, who served in the Royal Navy, and my uncles Tony and Frank (her brothers). All three have now passed away, but each played a significant part in inspiring my own military career. I also remember the friends and colleagues who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the hope of making a difference.

But perhaps the person foremost in my thoughts is my wife, Shirley.

Throughout my military career, she has made countless sacrifices of her own, often quietly and without recognition. Like so many military spouses and families, she has carried burdens that others rarely see, whilst asking for little in return.

Their sacrifices deserve our remembrance, too.

So, when you pause to remember, think not only of those who gave their lives in service to our nation, but also of those closest to you, whose sacrifices may never have been publicly acknowledged.

At the going down of the sun and in the morning, we will remember them.

Major Anthony John Sandle RLC, Second-in-Command, 156 Regiment, The Royal Logistic Corps(pictured above with Everton Ambassador Graham Stuart)

Arsenal haven't scored a first-half goal in any of their last five games in the Premier League or Champions League. Their last goal before the break was against Chelsea on 6 September. https://t.co/ZfScceDs6u

The XI on the pitch are trusted to find the opening goal, and that also suggests Arteta is keen to manage minutes.

Barcelona are drawing at Galatasaray and Bayern Munich are 2-0 down against Viking. With Man City playing PSG tomorrow night, these are an important three points for Arsenal to win, relative to the other teams we expect to fill the top spots of the league phase.

Absolute SCENES as Viking double their lead over Bayern Munich 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/rYqhAgwqyx

It has not been much of a spectacle so far, with Arsenal’s rotated attack stuttering but probably mustering enough chances to have scored by now. Lille managed one moment of danger with the offside goal, but are yet to have a shot on target. A half-time change by Arteta cannot be ruled out.

Great double save from Ozer in the Lille goal after Guimaraes’s shot from distance took a deflection, and he did well to get up and push the ball away from Gyokeres to deny the striker a tap-in.

Lille goalkeeper Berke Özer saves Bruno Guimarães' effort, then stops Viktor Gyökeres from tapping the ball in ⚡️ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/UYCmuevG22

Andre heads Madueke’s corner behind for another one as half-time approaches. Good delivery to the near post this time but the Lille defence stands firm.

Eze with a loose square ball in midfield, but Arsenal are spared by an offside flag going up against Lille. Arsenal fans wanted the officials to play advantage with a break on.

Corner now for Arsenal. Lovely backheel from Madueke to Timber but his low cross towards Gyokeres is turned behind.

Arsenal yet to score from a corner this season.

Things look like happening for Arsenal when Guimaraes or Eze get on the ball around the top of the penalty area, accessing those areas has been the problem against a well-structured Lille team so far. Arsenal do not look unduly troubled but the home crowd would have expected more so far.

Mikel Arteta is becoming increasingly frustrated on the touchline, primarily with the officiating but one suspects he is also irritated by the wastefulness of his team. The Arsenal manager has, er, expressed some of these emotions to the fourth official, Richard Hempel. But Hempel, who appears to be an absolute German giant of a man, was having none of it. He really towers over Arteta and he wasn’t afraid to play that card.

Big chance for Eze! But he shoots straight at the goalkeeper. The opportunity was created by a lovely defence-splitting pass from Guimaraes through the Lewis-Skelly, who dragged the ball back for Eze. The flag went up for offside, but Lewis-Skelly would have been onside.

Merino with a volley on the turn in the Lille box, but he slices over the bar. Snappy football from Arsenal and Rice to tee up Madueke for the initial cross.

Then Arsenal work the ball patiently from right to left and Eze feeds Lewis-Skelly on the overlap, but his cross is too high and into the goalkeeper’s gloves. That needed to go along the six-yard line.

Eze caught offside after Lewis-Skelly did well to fizz a pass down the line into his feet. Arsenal’s first-choice attackers Odegaard, Saka and Havertz will not be fearing for their places at Forest on the basis of this first half.

Arsenal could do with a little more precision from their front three. Madueke, Eze and Gyokeres have had a few opportunities to hurt Lille but they haven’t done so yet. This is a big night for Eze and Gyokeres, especially, as they largely been marooned on the bench this season.  With Tzolis out, Eze could lock down that left wing slot. But he needs to do more.

Another wasted Arsenal counter-attack, this time Merino turned the wrong way and misplaced a pass before making a frustrated challenge at the expense of a yellow card.

Arsenal probing, without really pulling Lille apart or unduly stressing their defence. Chance on a transition from a midfield giveaway, but Bentaleb did well to show Gyokeres wide and win the ball without conceding a free-kick.

Lille have the ball in Arsenal’s net but the flag goes up for offside! There was a double deflection from a Bentaleb shot, and the ball bounced off Haraldsson straight to Ueda, who finished past Raya from close range. The striker was onside when Bentaleb took his shot, but the second deflection did for him. There was a stoppage for a VAR check, but the decision stands.

Lille thought they'd taken the lead at the Emirates, but it's ruled out for offside ❌ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/c0k49kH5sn

As Sam said, the chances are starting to come for Arsenal now, with Timber lifting a cross straight on to the head of Merino but he failed to generate enough power and his effort was straight at the goalkeeper.

Madueke drops a shoulder to make room for a right-footed cross, but his delivery is over hit. Mikel Merino is playing in the Odegaard role tonight, but is not as nimble footed as the Arsenal captain.

That is Arsenal’s best chance so far though! Loose ball picked up and Timber released on the overlap, and it was a good pull-back to pick out Bruno Guimaraes but he fired wide.

There’s a goal coming here, and it’s going to be scored by Arsenal. They are finding gaps between the Lille lines and getting into some extremely dangerous positions in the inside channels. It feels like a matter of time.

David Raya gathers a cross after good defending from Timber, but then the Arsenal goalkeeper almost does a Shay Given against Dion Dublin at the edge of the box, but Rice put his foot in to get Raya out of bother. There was a frantic cry of “man on!” from the Arsenal crowd.

Lewis-Skelly and Madueke both deliver crosses into the Lille penalty area but they are repelled. Arsenal lacking some familiarity with their combinations off the flanks so far, but Eze does well to burst past his man to tee up Guimaraes but the shot is blocked.

Arsenal fail to make the most of a wide free-kick, before Bruno G elicits a cheer from the crowd when he slides into a tackle at the expense of a throw in. With Lewis-Skelly at left-back and Eze in front of him, there is not much natural width on the Arsenal left.

Bentaleb, the former Spurs midfielder, puts his head up to pick out the stretching run of Ueda, but the Lille forward lacked support and the moved fizzled out. It’s been quite a tidy start from the French side.

From Czechia sub at Wembley last week, Ondrej Zmrzly, a man with no vowels in his surname, to tonight and Lille sub Soriba Diaoune who has the full set in his.

End-to-end football for a couple of minutes. Madueke with a cute reverse pass into Merino inside the box but it broke down for Arsenal, before Lille launched a dangerous counter-attack through on-loan Forest attacker Bakwa, who cut inside and let fly. Great block from Gabriel.

Madueke did some encouraging things against Leeds but has been a bit untidy so far, slipping and handling the ball before miscuing an attempted pass towards Timber on the overlap.

Then Lille do well to play out from deep and work the ball into midfield but Andre gives away a sloppy pass.

Both teams enjoying a feel of the ball in the opening exchanges, and there is some good work in a tight space down the right from Konsa and Timber but Madueke could not take the ball with him.

Arsenal then start to establish some dominance in the Lille half, moving the ball from side to side.

Lille get the game under way at the Emirates.

Declan Rice captains Arsenal. Were it not for Martin Zubimendi sustaining a knock in the post-Leeds warm down, Rice may well have been on the bench with Saka, Odegaard and Havertz.

Arsenal’s right-back has looked quite rusty on his fleeting appearances so far this season, searching for rhythm after a pretty serious groin problem. He pushed himself to appear in the Champions League final and subsequently missed the World Cup.

I would expect him to play like a third centre-back at times, allowing Lewis-Skelly to drift into midfield from left-back. That role might also help Timber preserve his legs.

It had escaped my attention that Arsenal defender Gabriel is facing his former club tonight. At £27m, signed in 2020, he has to go down as one of Arteta’s best signings, and one of the best value signings any Premier League club has made this decade.

It’s very difficult. You come across very special people in life and Ken was certainly one of them. He’s an absolute legend of this football club. I think he’s the soul of this football club and someone that has given his life to this club.

This stadium wouldn’t be built if not for him. So, very sad news. The legacy he’s leaving is immense and our thoughts are with his family and we want to pay a proper tribute when we can.

Our players will be wearing black armbands this evening in memory of Ken Friar OBE. Rest in peace, Ken ❤️ https://t.co/xf91JABjrD

Lille’s manager is Davide Ancelotti, the son of Carlo, and you would assume he has picked up a few tips and tricks from his dad about success in this competition. Carlo, after all, has won the European Cup on five separate occasions. This is Davide’s second job as a manager, following a spell at Brazilian side Botafogo.

Some of Bukayo Saka’s finishing has been wayward so far this season, but the volume of chances coming his way bodes well. At this fledgling stage of the season, only Erling Haaland is averaging more non-penalty expected goals per 90 minutes in the Premier League.

As Sam Dean explores in this piece, Arteta seems to be encouraging Saka to take up more central positions inside the box.

Sam writes: “Is Saka becoming a proper penalty-box predator? It is too early to say for certain but it is absolutely clear that he is taking up different positions, closer to the opponents’ goal, this season. Not only when the ball is on the left flank, but also when Arsenal are attacking through midfield.”

Saka starts among the substitutes this evening, but will play his part towards the end of the game.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

The artist Northbanksy has plumped for another Oasis-inspired dig at Manchester City, this time with Rui Pinto taking centre stage, the man whose leaked emails kicked off the Premier League investigation into City’s financial affairs.

A consequence of Piero Hincapie’s injury on Saturday (he hurt his ankle in a cool-down session after the game, embarrassingly) is that Myles Lewis-Skelly is seemingly now the backup left-back. Arsenal can’t trust Riccardo Calafiori’s body to play two games in a week and are clearly saving him for Premier League action on the weekend. Lewis-Skelly has been so impressive in midfield that it must be frustrating to change position now.

Bakwa is on loan from Nottingham Forest, while those at the Emirates with long memories will remember that Nabil Bentaleb played for Spurs. Only the knowledgeable shall boo.

Lille XI: Özer; Perraud, Alexsandro, Ngoy, Goffi; Bentaleb, André; Mukau, Haraldsson, Bakwa; Ueda

Subs: Gill, Srdanovic, Giroud, Sahraoui, Kjaergaard, Onal, Kouassi, Verdonk, Cossier, Perrin, Diaoune, Sajous

Bukayo Saka, Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard drop to the bench, so some rotation from Arteta with a weekend trip to Nottingham Forest in mind, a venue where Arsenal have drawn 0-0 on their last two visits.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Lewis-Skelly; Bruno, Rice; Madueke, Merino, Eze; Gyokeres

Subs: Meslier, Kepa, White, Mosquera, Salmon, O’Neill, Hashi, Saka, Odegaard, Havertz, Dowman

Will Olivier Giroud receive a warm welcome back to the Emirates Stadium? The Frenchman spent six years as an Arsenal player but burned a few bridges when he left the club for Chelsea, and then celebrated wildly when Chelsea beat Arsenal in the Europa League final of 2019. Now 40, Giroud has shown remarkable longevity and is unquestionably one of the best strikers of his generation. But can he hurt this formidable Arsenal defence? It’s a tough ask.

Olivier Giroud back at the Emirates ❤️ https://t.co/TPBgcNDsVW

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

#1368. Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

VEGF is frequently targeted in clinical settings to suppress tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and retina disease6. However, resistance to VEGF-blocking antibodies arises over time, which limits the effectiveness of such treatments4,5,7,8. By contrast, resistance to loss of VEGF signalling has not been reported during physiological vascular development.

Embryos or postnatal tissues lacking activity of the VEGF signalling pathway in all cells fail to develop vessels3. VEGFR2 (encoded by the Kdr (also known as Vegfr2) gene in mice) is the most important VEGF receptor and has been shown to be essential for angiogenesis in all vascular development contexts studied so far1,9. Germline mutants for this gene completely lack blood vessels and die very early during embryonic development2, and mouse embryos chimeras formed by wild-type and Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) progenitor cells cannot form endothelial cells (ECs)10. Conditional deletion of Vegfr2 with Tie2–Cre after endothelial differentiation11, or in postnatal tissues with Cdh5–CreERT2, also strongly impairs angiogenesis12, without any evidence of genetic compensation or resistance.

Despite a large body of literature showing that VEGFR2 is essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, migration and survival, previous studies involving deletion of Vegfr2 in all ECs (Vegfr2iDEC) during embryonic or postnatal organ development could only analyse its effect on angiogenesis for a relatively short period of time. Its essential role in vascular development and hence in tissue development and organ function causes severe impairment of angiogenesis and premature lethality of Vegfr2iDEC embryos and postnatal animals; thus, such studies have been unable to determine whether ECs can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 over time or make certain organ vascular beds in the complete absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling.

Here we used iFlpMosaics13 and iSuRe–HadCre14 to mosaically induce and longitudinally track Vegfr2KO ECs, enabling us to assess the role of this gene during the entire embryonic and postnatal vascular development of different organs. We found that despite its essential role during the initial wave of embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is dispensable for many subsequent angiogenic processes originating from veins. Vegfr2KO ECs expand and out-compete wild-type ECs in venous vessels, which serve as a continuous source of these mutant cells for angiogenesis in most organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time through upregulation of ligands for other VEGF receptors and through increased expression of venous-specific genes, particularly Nr2f2. Targeting these adaptive and resistance-associated molecular mechanisms prevents expansion of ECs following prolonged loss of VEGFR2 signalling.

Given the essential role of VEGFR2 in early angiogenesis and embryonic development, we induced mosaic loss of VEGFR2 with iFlpMosaics13 to investigate whether mutant cells could adapt and form new vessels over time. This technology enables FlpO-dependent ratiometric induction and tracking over long periods of time of cells expressing MTomato-2A-Cre (knockout for any floxed gene) or MYFP (wild type). To induce these mosaics, we used the Apln-FlpO allele, which is expressed in the first angiogenic and sprouting ECs at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) and throughout vascular development. In female embryos, the X-chromosome-located Apln–FlpO allele is mosaically silenced15 and expressed only in a fraction (23–50%) of ECs, generating relatively few mutant and wild-type cells, which we found to be compatible with embryonic development (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Analysis of major organs of Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic mice showed that ECs with full loss of VEGFR2 (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) were able to survive and proliferate during embryonic development and until postnatal day 7 (P7), with only a relatively minor competitive disadvantage (2–7-fold) compared with wild-type cells (Fig. 1b). This competitive disadvantage was more pronounced in the lung and kidney endothelium and less so in brain ECs (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). As Apln-FlpO is constitutively active and can drive recombination at later stages of embryonic development, we also induced Vegfr2 deletion using 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at E10.5 and E12.5 in embryos carrying Cdh5-CreERT2, iSuRe-HadCre and an iMb2-Mosaic16 control reporter that recombines independently of Vegfr2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). This resulted in a maximum of 1–6% recombined ECs, as opposed to 23–50% with Apln-FlpO. However, this recapitulated the trend in which brain ECs were least affected by VEGFR2 loss, followed by those in the heart, liver, lung and kidney (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

a, Schematic of iFlpMosaics induced by Apln-FlpO from E8.5 to P7. b, log2 ratio of MTomato+/MYFP+ within CD31+CD45− cells detected by FACS for the indicated organs. The absolute fold change of the ratio of Vegfr2KO ECs versus the ratio of control Tomato+ cells is indicated in red. c, Representative gating scheme for the ratiometric analysis (see also Extended Data Fig. 1a). d, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 retinas immunostained for Tomato, YFP and ERG (which labels EC nuclei). Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing the zonal distribution and percentage of Tomato+Cre+ cells when equal numbers of randomly selected YFP+ and Tomato+ cells were plotted (see method in Extended Data Fig. 3a). Right, log2 ratio of Tomato+/YFP+ cells detected in whole-mount retina immunostainings, showing an overall competitive disadvantage of Vegfr2KO cells in the mapped retinas. e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for ERG at P7, from pups injected with 4-OHT at P1. Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing distribution of MTomato+ERG+ (wild-type, Vegfr2HET or Vegfr2KO) cells in space in relation to MTomato−ERG+ (wild-type) cells. f, Bar plot contrasting the relative frequency of the indicated cells in the indicated areas and genotypes. g, log2 fold change of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 cells relative to the respective control wild-type cells. Numbers indicate fold change (×) between the two groups. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm. A, arteries; AF, angiogenic front; dist., distance; freq., frequency; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; LE, leading edge; MA, mature area; V, veins; WT, wild type.

VEGFR2 activity is essential for NOTCH activation and the development of arteries17,18,19. Arteries are formed by tip ECs20, which have the highest level of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling and guide vascular growth. Our high-resolution spatial zonation data with long-term iFlpMosaics showed that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were significantly enriched in veins and surrounding capillaries, and avoided angiogenic front capillaries or tip ECs, but were able to form arteries (Fig. 1d; see also Extended Data Fig. 3a for the heatmapping method).

To complement these results, we intercrossed the Vegfr2 floxed allele with Cdh5-CreERT2 and iSuRe-HadCre14 alleles to ensure fast (24 h; Extended Data Fig. 3b,c) and effective mosaic genetic deletion and full loss of VEGFR2 protein and downstream targets in ECs (Cdh5 expressing), after a single injection of 4-OHT. Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs were located mainly in veins and surrounding capillaries, as well as in the more proximal and mature segments of retina arteries (Fig. 1e). This indicates that when Vegfr2KO ECs are induced in the initial retina sprouting plexus at P1, they can make arteries forming from P1 to P3. However, owing to their inability to continue to sprout and form tip cells at the leading edge, they cannot participate in the subsequent arterial development process occurring from P3 to P7, which in the retina is dependent on incorporation of new tip cells21.

Notably, compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1−P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front capillaries (Fig. 1f,g) and were still able to make arteries. This suggests that embryonic Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs can adapt to long-term loss of VEGFR2 and contribute to venous vascular growth, tip cells and arteries at postnatal stages.

We next investigated how Vegfr2KO ECs could compete with wild-type cells and contribute to growing vascular networks over long periods of time, given the proposed important role of this pathway in EC proliferation1,22. During angiogenesis, there are two main locations for EC proliferation: the capillary angiogenic front and veins (Fig. 2a). We found that the surviving Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs proliferated (as determined by Ki-67 detection) as well as wild-type cells in postnatal brain, heart and lung vessels (Fig. 2b).

a, Representative confocal micrograph of a control P7 retina immunostained for the proliferation marker Ki-67 and the EC nuclear marker ERG. The chart shows the frequency of Ki-67+ERG+ (pink pseudocolored) nuclei in different vascular zones. b, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 mice at P7, immunostained for YFP, Tomato, ERG and Ki-67. Yellow arrows indicate YFP+Ki-67+ cells and magenta arrows Tomato+Ki-67+ ECs. c, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 retinas induced at P1 and analysed at P20. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing that Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 ECs grow in veins and surrounding capillaries. d,e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 and respective quantification charts, showing increased apoptosis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 but not Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs. f, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice induced at P4 and analysed at P7. Arrows indicate recombined ECs (Tomato+) that are Ki-67+ (yellow) and Ki-67− (white), respectively. Chart shows the percentage of Tomato+ ECs positive for Ki-67. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm (a,c–e), 50 μm (b,f). Cap., capillaries; CC3, cleaved caspase 3; Ctrl, control; DCap, distal capillaries; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; PCap, proximal capillaries. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

Venous ECs provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis and these migrate against the blood flow to capillaries and then towards arterial vessels20,23,24. When we induced Vegfr2KO ECs for longer periods of time, from P1 to P20 (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20), we observed that mutant cells stayed in the vein stem, where they proliferated and gradually outcompeted wild-type cells, which moved outwards towards the VEGF-rich leading edge and adjacent capillaries (Fig. 2c). This preferential occupation of the venous stem niche by Vegfr2KO ECs allowed them to continue proliferating for longer periods of time and later to form most of the perivenous capillary vessels and the deeper vascular plexus that developed during a second wave of VEGF-independent angiogenesis from P7 to P20 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). This was consistent with previous findings showing that the tip cells that dive to form the deeper vascular plexus in the retina lack expression of the VEGFR2 signalling target gene Esm1; instead, their migration is dependent on other pathways such as Alk or TGFβ and WNT signalling25,26,27.

Together, these data show that VEGFR2 function is essential for the initial sprouting angiogenesis driven by high VEGF levels in hypoxic embryos and organs but not for the development of veins and perivenous capillaries or the subsequent steps of capillary angiogenesis and remodelling that occur after the first vascular plexus is formed in various organs. Thus, by forming veins, which are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis23, Vegfr2KO ECs can continue to proliferate and participate in subsequent steps of vascular development for long periods of time.

We previously observed that the distribution of Vegfr2KO ECs in the retina plexus at P7 differed between animals with long-term (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) and short-term (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7) mosaic deletion of Vegfr2. Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front than Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs (Fig. 1f,g). Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs also proliferated normally (Fig. 2b). Therefore, we hypothesized that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs might be genetically rewired and adapt over time to loss of the most important receptor for VEGF.

To assess the early response of ECs to loss of VEGFR2, we first analysed apoptosis markers in growing retina vessels, as VEGFR2 has been shown to regulate EC survival. Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice showed a very significant increase in the number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase 3 positive) ECs (Fig. 2d). This apoptosis was a reaction to the acute loss of VEGFR2, as Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 or even Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 mice did not show any apoptotic ECs (Fig. 2e), suggesting adaptation of the surviving cells over time. When the acute loss of Vegfr2 was induced in all ECs, we observed an immediate depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs from the VEGF-high angiogenic front, but not from veins or more mature vessels (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Therefore, even though many ECs in the retina plexus showed upregulation of the apoptosis marker in the first days after Vegfr2 loss (Fig. 2d), only the angiogenic ECs that were exposed to high VEGF levels at the time of Vegfr2 deletion died (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

We also found that Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs were significantly less proliferative than control cells only in the heart and kidney (Fig. 2f), whereas the proliferation of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was similar to that of controls (Fig. 2b). This suggests that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time and are later able to proliferate in these organs. In the newborn retina, deletion of Vegfr2 did not affect the proliferation of surviving ECs in any segment (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that in this organ VEGFR2 mainly controls EC migration and survival, not proliferation.

Together, our data suggest that ECs lacking VEGF signalling during active angiogenesis suffer an acute VEGFR2 withdrawal effect, followed by a period of adaptation to the loss, after which they can form new vessels. ECs that are more distant from the VEGF source, and therefore have less VEGF signalling, adapt better to the loss and can expand over time, particularly in veins and perivenous vessels.

To further confirm the insensitivity of more mature ECs to loss of VEGFR2 signalling, we deleted Vegfr2 in several adult quiescent vascular beds for 2 weeks. Only the quiescent sinusoidal liver endothelium showed a strong sensitivity and loss of Vegfr2KO ECs, whereas only the kidney endothelium showed significantly lower proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting that only fenestrated or discontinuous mature endothelial vessels present in these organs remain sensitive to VEGFR2 loss.

Given the observed differences in the biology of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of these cells and respective control Tomato+ cells to identify possible differences in their transcriptional profiles and potential mechanisms of adaptation to loss of VEGFR2 signalling in distinct organ vascular beds.

Although VEGFR2 is a central regulator of angiogenesis and widely regarded as essential for EC biology, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs showed only modest changes in their transcriptome (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6), even though VEGFR2 protein and downstream signalling were lost already within the first 24 h following 4-OHT administration (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). In general, the expression of genes related to sprouting or tip cell biology was decreased, whereas that of genes related to apoptosis and vascular permeability was increased in all organs analysed (Fig. 3a,b). However, considerable differences were observed among organs.

In the brain, clusters of proliferating (S–G2–M) ECs expressing venous capillaries markers were increased after Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days (Fig. 3c–f). This was consistent with higher clonal expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs from P1 to P20 in this organ (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Clusters comprising capillary and activated or angiogenic ECs (with high expression of Apln, Adm, Mcam, Lamb1 and Angpt2) were decreased (Fig. 3d–f). In total, only 569 genes were significantly deregulated (Fig. 3g). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an increase in the expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as G2M, DNA repair and mitotic spindle genes, confirming the increase in EC proliferation (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a). The expression of most tip cell marker genes was decreased in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 6a–f).

In contrast to those in the brain, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 capillary ECs in the heart were significantly less proliferative (Fig. 3j–m and Extended Data Fig. 7b), matching the 54% decrease in Ki-67 percentage observed in sections (Fig. 2f). The proportion of mutant ECs found in bigger vessels (arteries and veins) was increased 2- to 4-fold (Fig. 3k–m), suggesting a proportional fast depletion of Vegfr2KO capillary ECs in only 3 days. Unlike in the brain, GSEA of Vegfr2KO heart ECs showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as decreases in expression of G2M, mitotic spindle and tip cell genes (Fig. 3n–p), in accordance with the decrease in proliferation and sprouting of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 heart ECs. Vegfr2KO heart ECs also showed upregulation of genes related to apoptosis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Fig. 3n–p), as has been shown previously for ECs losing ERK signalling28.

In contrast to the results for brain and heart, we found no significant difference in the proportions of proliferating cells among control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in lung (Extended Data Fig. 6g–j), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 and clonal analysis (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7c). The proportion of the vein cluster was only slightly increased, and the capillary cluster was slightly decreased. Despite the lack of significant changes in cluster proportions, GSEA showed increased TNF signalling through NF-κB, hypoxia and reactive oxygen species signalling and a decrease in the interferon response (Extended Data Fig. 6k,l). In lung, there was only a small trend of decreased expression of tip cell marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 6m), and several genes related to apoptosis were upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 6l,m).

In the kidney, similar to the heart, Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days led to an increase in the relative proportion of ECs of bigger vessels (arteries and veins), suggesting fast depletion of a fraction of capillary ECs in only 3 days (Extended Data Fig. 6n–q). Proliferation and clonal expansion of kidney capillary ECs were also reduced (Extended Data Figs. 6o,q and 7d), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 (Fig. 2f). GSEA showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F, G2M and mitotic spindle genes and an increase in the expression of genes related to p53, xenobiotic metabolism and apoptosis (Extended Data Fig. 6r,s), indicative of cellular stress in kidney ECs after short-term Vegfr2 deletion from P4 to P7. Similar to brain and heart ECs, the expression of tip cell marker genes was also decreased in kidney Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 6t).

Following our analysis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs of distinct organs to identify potential differences in gene expression related to long-term adaptation of cells to loss of VEGFR2 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). In contrast to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs exhibited predominantly upregulation rather than downregulation of genes, including marked upregulation of several venous-enriched genes (compare Figs. 3a,b and 4a).

In contrast to brain Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had increased frequencies of venous capillaries (Extended Data Fig. 8b–d) and marked upregulation of the key regulator of vein specification Nr2f2 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Similarly to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had decreased frequencies of activated and sprouting ECs and lower expression levels of several tip cell genes (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). The number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), particularly upregulated genes, was much higher (1,621 versus 569 DEGs) in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs; this is likely to represent a long-term adaptation response to loss of VEGFR2 function (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e with Fig. 3g). Whereas in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs, genetic pathways related to EC proliferation and cellular activity (E2F targets, MYC, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis) were paradoxically increased, in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs they were decreased (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e,f with Fig. 3g,h). This suggests that brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs adapt to the long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling through a decrease in cellular activity and upregulation of Nr2f2, which probably decreases their dependence on VEGF signalling for growth and survival.

In the heart, we confirmed previous histological analysis showing that heart Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs proliferated at levels similar to those of control cells and markedly higher than those of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (compare Fig. 3k,m with Fig. 4b–d). They also had many more DEGs (1,750 DEGs versus 242 DEGs), particularly upregulated genes (compare Fig. 3n with Fig. 4e). GSEA showed increased epithelial–mesenchymal transition, KRAS signalling and angiogenesis, and less expression of metabolic-pathway-related genes (Fig. 4e,f), as seen in the brain. Expression of tip or activated EC genes was not as compromised in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Fig. 4g), suggesting some adaptation over time to the loss of VEGFR2. Notably, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4c,d), similar to our observations in the retina (Fig. 1d–f), confirming that mosaic loss of Vegfr2 causes mutant ECs to expand more in veins. In comparison with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed strong upregulation of most venous-specific genes, including Nr2f2, Fbln2, Igf1 and Vwf (Fig. 4e). This was not caused only by the increased proportion of venous ECs in these mutants; capillary and angiogenic ECs also showed much higher expression of these venous marker genes, indicating venousization of mutant Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 capillary ECs over time (Fig. 4h,p).

In the lung, the same adaptation and venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was observed. Mutant cells were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4i–k), and even capillary or CAR4+ ECs showed significantly upregulated expression of lung venous genes including Vegfc, Nr2f2, Vwf and Fbln2 (Fig. 4l,m and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Similar to findings in the other organs, lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had significantly more DEGs than lung Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (3,116 vs 502), particularly upregulated genes (compare Extended Data Fig. 6k with Fig. 4m). Volcano plots and GSEA revealed upregulation of many venous-enriched and epithelial–mesenchymal transition genes, as well as oestrogen response genes. Lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had lower expression of E2F targets and metabolism genes, as seen in the other organs (Fig. 4m,n).

Notably, deletion of Vegfr2 for 2 weeks in adult organ blood vessels did not induce venousization of adult Vegfr2KO ECs; instead, it decreased expression of venous genes (Extended Data Fig. 8g–u), indicating that upregulation of Nr2f2 and venousization may represent a long-term adaptative response to VEGFR2 loss that occurs only during active angiogenesis.

The scRNA-seq data indicating venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs over time were confirmed by immunostaining for the master regulator of venous development NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII) (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). To understand the venousization requirement for long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs, we also analysed Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic Vegfr2Flox/Flox, Nr2f2Flox/Flox mice. When ECs lacked both VEGFR2 and NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), their capacity to expand was significantly reduced, particularly in veins (Fig. 4q,r and Extended Data Fig. 9e). This suggests that endothelial venousization is a key mechanism of adaptation to long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis that enables mutant cells to expand in veins and derived vessels over time.

In addition to analysing embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, we tested the capacity of Vegfr2KO ECs to form tumour vessels over a period of 2 weeks. When Vegfr2 deletion was induced a few days before tumour implantation, Vegfr2IECKO-day-3–adult ECs formed tumour vessels mainly at the tumour border and failed to penetrate deeper into the tumour, where they were 5.2-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10a). By contrast, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–adult ECs, which had undergone venousization throughout embryonic and postnatal development, could better reach inside the tumour and were only 2.6-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). These data show that although VEGFR2 signalling promotes tumour angiogenesis, ECs can progressively adapt to its absence and sustain tumour angiogenesis.

In addition to our findings with respect to venousization, we observed significant upregulation of expression of other VEGF receptor ligands in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11a), including PGF and VEGFC, which bind and activate VEGFR1 and VEGFR3, respectively1. In the absence of VEGFR2, VEGFR1 is the only other receptor that can bind VEGFA. However, all studies so far have shown that VEGFR1 kinase activity is too weak29,30, whereas its extracellular soluble form (sVEGFR1 or sFLT1) acts as a strong VEGF decoy receptor31. Therefore, when VEGFR2 is present, VEGFR1 is considered to mainly antagonize VEGFA–VEGFR2 signalling and angiogenesis. However, we found that Vegfr1 expression was much higher in ECs in the brain, the organ least sensitive to VEGFR2 loss (Extended Data Fig. 11b). We also found that during postnatal angiogenesis, sVegfr1 showed 2–5-fold lower expression than the membrane full-length Vegfr1 (flVegfr1) mRNA form, except in brain ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11c), suggesting a potential signalling role for flVEGFR1.

To evaluate whether VEGFR1 could compensate for loss of VEGFR2, we induced mosaic codeletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 in ECs with iSuRe-HadCre from P1 to P7 (Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1–P7). Compared with Vegfr2KO ECs, Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed a further decrease in ability to migrate and form retina capillaries, but not veins or arteries (Fig. 5a). In veins, Vegfr1/2KO ECs could clonally expand (Extended Data Fig. 11d). Brain and heart Vegfr1/2KO ECs proliferated less than Vegfr2KO ECs at P7 (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Deletion of both Vegfr2 and Vegfr1 had a stronger effect on endothelial and pup survival (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i), confirming the requirement for VEGFR1 signalling when VEGFR2 is absent in capillaries. Mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 alone also led to a decrease in EC migration towards the VEGF-rich front (Extended Data Fig. 11j). In contrast to deletion of Vegfr1 in all ECs, mosaic loss of Vegfr1 in single ECs did not increase VEGF signalling (as assessed by ESM1 expression), probably owing to normal levels of sFLT1 present in the mostly wild-type microenvironment (Extended Data Fig. 11k).
