Base maps in a were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

Sampling is now relatively dense across the region of interest during much of the Bronze and Iron Age, with the exception of the cremation-dominated Urnfield Culture (3200–2800 bp). We therefore first focus on the well-sampled peripheries: England and the Czech Republic, where dense sampling continues throughout the Bronze and Iron Ages, and France, where Iron Age sampling has been greatly improved32. To visualize the changes through time, we plot the IBD mixture modelling proportions as timelines for England, France and the Czech Republic (Figs. 3b and 4b).

In England, the prominent Farmer ancestries change through time (Fig. 3b). Before 4000 bp, individuals tend to have a slightly higher proportion of local British–Irish Neo.-related ancestry relative to the other Neolithic-related ancestries. From 3800 bp to 3200 bp, Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry exceeds the local Neolithic ancestry (Fig. 3b), consistent with a “large-scale migration” from the mainland34,42. Between 3200 bp and 2800 bp, we see a shift, in which the proportion of Italy Neo.-related ancestry has increased to similar proportions to that of Iberia–France Neo.-related, coinciding with the appearance of Anatolia BA-related ancestry. Bronze Age sources (Fig. 4b) show S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry appearing in England between 4000 bp and 3200 bp, consistent with the appearance of Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry. Between 3200 bp and 2800 bp, we see Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry increasing, becoming widespread by at least 2600 bp (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 6).

In France, we see a similar transition (Fig. 3b). Before 3500 bp, more local Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry than Italy Neo.-related ancestry tends to be present. After 2800 bp, the relative proportions have reversed, so Italy Neo.-related ancestry is the highest, accompanied by Anatolia BA-related ancestry. When using the Bronze Age sources (Fig. 4b), we see an increase in the Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry and a decrease in the local S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry at corresponding times. However, because of the lack of samples from the Late Bronze Age, the time of this transition cannot be directly measured. Nevertheless, the increased proportions of Italy Neo.-related (set C3) and Hungary–Serbia BA-related (set C4) ancestry between 3200 bp and 2800 bp in Britain (Figs. 3, 4) and Iberia (Supplementary Fig. 1.35) suggests that this ancestry was present in France by this time. We also observe in France a subtle increase in East North Sea (ENS)-related ancestry between 2800–2470 bp and 2470–2000 bp, corresponding to the transition from Hallstatt to La Tène in France (Supplementary Fig. 1.46). ENS-related ancestry is found throughout the Bell Beaker region and is found in the highest proportions in the Netherlands throughout the Bronze and Iron Ages (Supplementary Fig. 1.10). Although limited sampling between the Netherlands, western Germany and northern France means that a more precise source region for this ancestry cannot be assessed, it should be noted that the transition occurs after the spread of Celtic under all models. Nevertheless, the subtle increase in ENS-related ancestry in France is consistent with the integration of more northern ancestry by the La Tène period, as suggested by previous studies35.

Further east, in the Czech Republic, an increase in Italy Neo.-related and Anatolia BA-related ancestry is observed by roughly 3300 bp in Tumulus-associated and Knovíz-associated individuals (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 3). Because Italy Neo.-related ancestry is also present east of the Adriatic Sea (Fig. 3a), this population movement need not originate in Italy. Consistent with the influence from the southeast inferred from the Neolithic ancestries, we detect an increase in Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry between 3600 bp and 3300 bp when including the Bronze Age sources (Fig. 4b). Unlike England, the Czech Republic shows no increase in Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry between 4000 bp and 2600 bp that would reflect a movement from western Europe (Fig. 3b). We do, however, note an increase in S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry from roughly 3300 bp (Fig. 4b). Combined, these results allow France and Iberia to be excluded as potential source regions from which the influx of ancestry came into the Czech Republic, and instead point to a movement from a region in which S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry is present yet Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry is absent, for example Italy (Supplementary Figs. 1.10 and 1.11) or central Europe (sets C3 and C4, Supplementary Fig. 1.37).

We interpret the persistent northwestern Bell Beaker-related ancestry together with shifts in local ancestry as resulting from several admixture processes between Bell Beaker-related populations and local Farmers across Europe, who subsequently moved within the region. Relative to the Celtic source regions proposed under linguistic models, we see movements to Britain from within the Celtic-from-the-West and Celtic-from-the-Centre source regions from 3800 bp, and from within the Celtic-from-the-East source regions from roughly 3200 bp.

The timing and distribution of the westward spread of Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry corresponds closely to the expansion of the Urnfield Culture (Supplementary Note 6). However, few genomes between 3200 bp and 2800 bp exist due to the Urnfield-associated practice of cremation. Including Urnfield context individuals from Iberia43 as IBD mixture modelling targets reveals an influx of Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry by 3150 bp (set C4, Supplementary Fig. 1.35), consistent with previous suggestions of an influx of ancestry from central Europe43,44. In the Czech Republic, individuals associated with the Urnfield subgroup of the Knovíz Culture are also represented in the dataset. Consistent with the results from the Urnfield context in Iberia, we find that the Knovíz individuals are modelled with high Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry (Extended Data Fig. 3). To test whether the Knovíz individuals represent Urnfield ancestry more broadly, we included Knovíz individuals as a source (set C5). By 2800 bp, when sampling improves, Knovíz-related ancestry is modelled in high proportions across western, southern and eastern central Europe in former Urnfield regions, complemented by more local sources (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8). We note that in this study, ‘Knovíz-related ancestry’ is used as a proxy for a broader group rather than representing people specifically of the Knovíz Culture.

In Iron Age England, the highest ancestry proportion tends to be modelled as Bell Beaker-related, followed by Knovíz-related and S. France–N. Iberia BA-related (Extended Data Fig. 7). By contrast, on the mainland, the proportion of ancestry modelled as Bell Beaker-related tends to be low or absent, with the Steppe ancestry in these individuals better modelled by the other Bronze Age sources, that is, Knovíz-related, S. France–N. Iberia BA-related and Hungary–Serbia BA-related. When including more Bronze Age sources from England (set C6) and France (set C7), the increase in Knovíz-related ancestry by roughly 2800 bp remains apparent (Supplementary Figs. 1.19 and 1.20). Thus, compared with England, the effect of Knovíz-related ancestry is particularly high in France, Germany and the Czech Republic (Extended Data Fig. 7). In Austria, we note considerable diversity at the eponymous Hallstatt archaeological site, with individuals modelled with particularly high proportions of either Knovíz-related or Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry, more similar to Hungary, Slovenia and Slovakia, where the Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry is modelled in high proportions (Extended Data Fig. 7). In Iberia, we see Knovíz-related ancestry becoming present in almost all individuals after 3200 bp (set C5, Supplementary Fig. 1.35). Although a number of individuals before this point are modelled with small proportions of Knovíz-related ancestry in set C5, they lack Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry (set C4, Supplementary Fig. 1.35) expected for movements from central Europe. The results here indicate gene flow from eastern central Europe occurring between 3200 bp and 2800 bp, coinciding with the expansion of the Urnfield Culture. We note that the genetic effects diminish the further west they spread. Finally, we note in the Czech Republic a subtle increase of S. France–N. Iberia BA-related ancestry roughly 2400 bp, aligning with small proportions of Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry in set C3 (Supplementary Fig. 1.54), corresponding to the beginning of the La Tène period.

Identifying which populations were involved in the formation of the Knovíz-related ancestry profile remains difficult due to the lack of samples between 3700 bp and 3300 bp. Compared with the earlier Únětice individuals of the Czech Republic, we see that Knovíz-related individuals have experienced an influx of Italy Neo.-related ancestry (found around the Adriatic Sea roughly 4000 bp) and Hungary–Serbia BA-related ancestry (found in the Balkans roughly 4000 bp) (Extended Data Fig. 3), suggestive of an influence from the southeast. We also see a subtle increase in ENS-related ancestry, which is found across the entire Bell Beaker range but occurs in the highest proportions in the Netherlands, suggestive of influence from central or northwest Europe. As a result, the specific populations and time of formation remain unclear, as does the possibility of some degree of local genetic continuity. However, two signals are clear and relevant to this study. First, we do not see evidence of Iberia–France Neo.-related ancestry in the Czech Republic from roughly 3300 bp to 2800 bp (Fig. 3b). The absence of this ancestry excludes western Europe as a potential source in the formation of Knovíz-related ancestry, which is of relevance to the evaluation of the Celtic-from-the-West and Celtic-from-the-Centre models. Second, we find that the Steppe ancestry in Knovíz individuals, as well as those across the entire Iron Age Celtic-speaking range, is modelled primarily as Bell Beaker-related rather than Corded Ware-related or extra Yamnaya-related ancestry (Fig. 2). In this historical period, Corded Ware-related ancestry is associated with Germanic-speaking populations in northern Europe32, and further Yamnaya-related ancestry (Supplementary Fig. 1.31b) with Greek-speaking populations in the Aegean33. Thus, regardless of the precise timing and populations involved in the formation of the Knovíz-related ancestry, its Steppe ancestry derives from Bell Beaker populations, suggesting that the dialect ancestral to Celtic, too, can ultimately be traced back to Bell Beaker groups. Improved sampling from Bronze Age northern Italy and central Europe will probably provide further insight into the formation of Knovíz-related ancestry (Supplementary Note 1), potentially also explaining the linguistic ties between the Celtic and Italic branches of the Indo-European language family (Supplementary Note 5).

We tested the robustness of these results using qpAdm, chromopainter and Y haplogroups. Full qpAdm results are provided in Supplementary Note 2, Supplementary Figs. 2.1 and 2.2 and Supplementary Tables 2.1–2.4, and full chromopainting results in Supplementary Note 3, Supplementary Figs. 3.1–3.7 and Supplementary Tables 3.1 and 3.2. Y chromosome analyses are provided in Supplementary Note 4. These independent analyses supported the main demographic events inferred through IBD mixture modelling: gene flow into Britain after the Bell Beaker period, and into western Europe from further east at the end of the Bronze Age.

Past population genetics is increasingly invoked to evaluate competing hypotheses in historical linguistics when language change is assumed to result from population movements and resulting admixtures11,12,16,17,32,33,34,35. Extending approaches from traditional archaeolinguistic syntheses45,46,47, the present study uses genetic evidence to assess which linguistic models require the fewest extra assumptions about population movement, timing and language persistence (Methods). We stress, however, that linguistic change is not exclusively driven by demographic factors and therefore does not necessarily leave behind a population genetic signature48,49.

With the above in mind, we set out to evaluate the four main linguistic models, based on different interpretations of historical-linguistic and archaeological data, for how Celtic could have acquired its historically documented range across the European continent. These are the Bell Beaker model; the Celtic-from-the-West model; the Celtic-from-the-Centre model and the Celtic-from-the-East model. Across the dataset, we identify three demographic processes that intersect differently with these four linguistic models (Fig. 5a,b): movement 1, the initial transmission of Steppe ancestry through the Bell Beaker region (4400–4000 bp); movement 2, population movements to Britain (3800–3200 bp) and movement 3, the westward spread of Knovíz-related ancestry from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp). We note that movements 1–3 are extended processes, not discrete single events.

Base maps in a were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).

Movement 1 aligns with the linguistic Bell Beaker model, which attributes the formation and spread of Celtic to Bronze Age Bell Beaker populations (roughly 4750–4500 to 4000–3800 bp). Under this model, movement 1 would represent the arrival of Celtic to the regions from which movements 2 and 3 occurred, with the later movements potentially reflecting the spread of a branch of Celtic. In the time following movement 1, we do not see an influx of Corded Ware-related or Yamnaya-related ancestry in the Bell Beaker region, suggesting Indo-European dialects in the region are Bell Beaker-mediated. If Celtic or its ancestral dialect arrived later, it probably did so with limited demographic movement.

Movement 2 is consistent with the view that maritime connectivity of the Atlantic Bronze Age drove the formation of Celtic, as proposed by the Celtic-from-the-West model. It is furthermore geographically consistent with a hypothetical spread of Celtic from France (and possibly northern Italy), as claimed by the Celtic-from-the-Centre model. However, the latter specifically claims a spread after 3000 bp, whereas this movement occurred during the previous millennium, resulting in a chronological mismatch.

Movement 3 aligns with the Celtic-from-the-East model. This model draws on archaeological evidence indicating a westward expansion of populations deriving from the Urnfield Culture from eastern central Europe into France and northeastern Spain50,51. We also note that, like movement 1, this movement affects all known Celtic-speaking areas of Europe. Archaeologically, the persistence of Knovíz-related ancestry into the Iron Age is consistent with the transition from the Late Urnfield to the Hallstatt Culture being seen as a reorganization of settlements rather than the arrival of a new population52 (Supplementary Note 6). In addition, under the Celtic-from-the-East model, the westward expansion of Hallstatt C (2750–2600 bp), from the Rhine into England and Ireland53,54, then provides an extra potential vector for the spread of Celtic varieties, that is, Brittonic and Goidelic, to Britain.

Finally, all linguistic models converge on a Late Iron Age eastward spread of Gaulish-related dialects during the La Tène period (2400–2200 bp)55, ultimately extending from France to northern Italy, central Europe and the Balkans. Consistent with previous studies35, we indeed detect subtle genetic shifts (Supplementary Figs. 1.10 and 1.54) suggestive of a movement from the west during this period. It should be noted, however, that this genetic signal is more subtle than that of movements 1–3, and thus needs further confirmation.

For the four linguistic models, we identify relevant movements based on overlapping geographical ranges and assess their compatibility with the linguistic date estimates (Extended Data Table 1). When evaluated against the demographic movements identified here, the Bell Beaker model and the Celtic-from-the-East model require the fewest independent population dispersals and the least reliance on auxiliary assumptions to account for the historically attested distribution of Celtic. Whereas the Celtic-from-the-West model can be aligned with movement 2, it also requires the prolonged maintenance of Celtic linguistic identity across regions undergoing substantial subsequent admixture (movement 3).

To further assess the feasibility of these movements as vectors for the spread of Celtic, linguistic dating provides an extra constraint. The underlying linguistic date estimates and associated literature are summarized in Supplementary Note 5, Supplementary Fig. 5.1 and Supplementary Table 5.1. A plausible population vector for the spread of Celtic must fall after the initial Pre-Celtic linguistic divergence from other Indo-European branches, allowing time for the shared innovations that define Proto-Celtic to accumulate and before the subsequent diversification into the attested Celtic branches (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Most estimates for the divergence of Pre-Celtic overlap at 5000–3500 bp, with the highest density between 4500 bp and 3800 bp (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Estimates for the subsequent formation and fragmentation of Proto-Celtic fall mostly between 3600 bp and 2800 bp, with the highest overlap between 3200 bp and 3000 bp (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Finally, the divergence time of the Goidelic and Brittonic Celtic branches from each other has most estimates overlapping between 3500 bp and 2000 bp, with the highest overlap at 2800–2500 bp (Extended Data Fig. 1d).

Only movement 3 falls within the bounds provided by most quantitative estimates (the divergence of Pre-Celtic and the divergence into Goidelic and Brittonic), while also coinciding with the highest overlap of the qualitative estimates for the formation and fragmentation of Proto-Celtic (Fig. 5 and Extended Data Table 1), supporting the Celtic-from-the-East model. By contrast, movement 1 overlaps with many estimates for the divergence of Pre-Celtic, and both movements 1 and 2 predate most estimates for the formation and fragmentation of Proto-Celtic (Fig. 5 and Extended Data Table 1).

Given the present sampling density and available linguistic date estimates, we find the Celtic-from-the-East model to be the most parsimonious of the four predefined scenarios evaluated here (Methods). This preference does not rest on an assumption that linguistic spread must mirror demographic processes, but reflects that alternative models require further, at-present untested mechanisms such as prolonged linguistic continuity across major demographic turnover. At the same time, we note that human history does not necessarily follow the most parsimonious trajectory9, and the partial support for other models may result from a more complex divergence and spread, which cannot be excluded based on genomic data. If Bell Beaker groups with Steppe ancestry indeed transmitted Indo-European language varieties, it is likely that a continuum of related dialects, including those ancestral to Celtic, Italic and Lusitanian, were spoken across the region after 4400 bp. With this view, it is plausible that the people of movements 2 and 3 retained a degree of mutual intelligibility with the local population of Britain. Thus, the spread of Celtic may have involved the diffusion of Celtic linguistic features rather than a complete replacement of local languages: a complexity invisible to parsimony approaches. Although our findings do not definitively establish the homeland of the Celtic languages, they do constrain the demographic processes through which their formation and diffusion may be modelled. As a result, any revised or newly proposed models for the spread of the Celtic languages will need to reconcile with the demographic patterns identified in this study.

The 578 new ancient individuals included in the analyses here are part of a larger dataset of 712 ancient shotgun-sequenced genomes32. Details on the sampling, data generation, quality checks, site description and detailed metadata can be found in that study32. In brief, ancient samples were visually identified as suitable for processing. Samples were drilled, predigested56, extracted17, built into libraries57,58 and sequenced on Illumina HiSeq 4000 and NovaSeq 6000 platforms. Sequenced reads were mapped against the human reference genome build 37 (hs37d5) and authenticated based on the length of reads, damage patterns, endogenous rates and presence of contamination. All samples with a genomic coverage greater than 0.1× were imputed, and close relatives identified using ngsRelate (v.2)59 were excluded for IBD-based analyses.

Genomes were imputed using Glimpse (v.1.1.1)60 against the 1000 Genomes v.5 phase 3 dataset61. Shared IBD segments were called using IBDseq (v.r1206)62 with default parameters. Segments with a logarithm-of-the-odds (LOD) score less than three and hotspot regions39 with excess sharing were excluded. A detailed description can be found in the accompanying paper32.

To identify fine-scale structure, we applied IBD mixture modelling39. The use of non-negative least squares modelling has been routinely applied using chromopainter chunks shared between ancient source and target sets63. However, recent studies have shown that using shared IBD segments between ancient individuals is effective at recovering fine-scale detail32,39. We relied on the dataset and IBD clustering from the accompanying paper32. The cluster IDs for all individuals included can be found in Supplementary Table 1.1. The 4,587 ancient individuals in the dataset were determined to be suitable for IBD mixture modelling on the basis of a series of filtering steps for genomic coverage (0.1× for shotgun-sequenced data, 1× for 1,240,000 capture data), average genotype probability for the 1,240,000 capture sites (0.9) and the removal of close relatives. The final dataset included 690,211 sites that intersected with the 1000 Genomes panel and the 1,240 K sites, pass the 1000 Genomes mappability mask and had an imputation INFO score greater than 0.5.

For each of the 4,587 ancient individuals in the dataset, a palette was created representing the proportion of sharing with all other clusters, and with the other individuals in their own cluster. The proportions were normalized by the number of individuals in each cluster. To account for the fact that the sharing within the individual’s own cluster has n − 1 individuals, sharing with all other clusters excludes one individual at random. As a result, clusters with a single individual do not contribute to other individuals’ palettes. All segments greater than 1 cM, with a LOD score greater than 3, that did not originate from a hotspot of IBD sharing39 were included in the palettes. IBD mixture modelling was then undertaken using these palettes, by modelling the target individual using non-negative least squares38, as described in ref. 39. Standard errors of the ancestry proportions were calculated using a weighted block jackknife, leaving out each chromosome.

A strength of this method is that target palettes are modelled as combinations of potential source palettes, meaning information from all other individuals in the dataset is incorporated into the modelling, rather than relying solely on the sharing of segments between the source and target individuals. When applied to densely sampled regions such as Holocene western Eurasia, sources and targets separated by 10,000 years continue to be modelled reliably32.

To understand the trends in ancestry through time, we performed spatiotemporal kriging (STAdmix, v.c72d845)64 to interpolate IBD mixture modelling results for points in time and space where genetic data are not available. For the ancestry of particular relevance for set C2 (Corded Ware-related, Bell Beaker-related and European Farmer-related), set C3 (British–Irish Neo.-related, Iberia–France Neo.-related, Italy Neo.-related and Anatolia BA-related) and set C4 (S. France–N. Iberia BA-related and Hungary–Serbia BA-related), we fit spatiotemporal variograms by means of a metric covariance model65.

qpAdm analyses were undertaken on the 690,211 sites of the dataset described above, using admixtools2 (ref. 66). Populations were placed into three sets: left_fixed, right_fixed or rotational (Supplementary Table 2.4). The ‘left_fixed’ population was included as a potential source in all qpAdm analyses. The ‘right_fixed’ population was included as outgroups in all analyses. In one population model, all ‘rotational’ populations were included as outgroups. For two population models, one ‘rotational’ population was placed together with the ‘left_fixed’ population as potential sources, and all others as outgroups, in all possible combinations. For three population models, two ‘rotational’ populations were placed together with the ‘left_fixed’ population as potential sources, and all others as outgroups, in all possible combinations.

In the present context, parsimony is understood as the minimization of independent population dispersals, chronological mismatches and auxiliary explanatory mechanisms (such as prolonged language persistence under repeated large-scale admixture) required to reconcile linguistic, archaeological and genomic evidence. Parsimony here functions as a comparative constraint on explanatory models rather than as an assumption about how prehistoric language spread must have occurred. Accordingly, parsimony is used here as a heuristic for model comparison rather than as a criterion of historical likelihood.

To evaluate whether a linguistic model is parsimonious with the genetic data, we assess whether a movement occurred in a direction and to a geographical extent consistent with the spread proposed by the linguistic model. In addition, we test whether the time of the movement is consistent with expectations based on linguistic dating. A plausible population vector for the spread of Celtic must fall after the initial Pre-Celtic linguistic divergence from other Indo-European branches, allowing time for the shared innovations that define Proto-Celtic to accumulate, and before the subsequent diversification into the attested Celtic branches.

The extent to which each model is consistent with the most relevant movement and further assumptions required to fit the model to the movement are detailed in Supplementary Table 1. The model that requires the fewest independent population movements, chronological mismatches and auxiliary assumptions is evaluated as most parsimonious.

Kriging results are shown for 4822 bp: the approximate time of arrival of Steppe ancestry into northern Europe; 4370 bp: the approximate time of arrival of Steppe ancestry into western Europe; 3314 bp: the Middle to Late Bronze Age; and 2560 bp: the Iron Age (left to right). Kriging was performed on the IBD mixture modelling Set C3 results. The raw mixture modelling results for these ancestries can be visualised in Supplementary Fig. 1.32. Base maps in a–d from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).

The raw mixture modelling results for these ancestries can be visualised in Supplementary Fig. 1.33. Base maps in a–c from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com).

For each target individual (n = 709), point estimates of the proportions of ancestry modelled from these ancestry sources are plotted. For each point estimate, standard errors were calculated using a weighted block jackknife with n = 22 chromosomes, sequentially leaving out one chromosome at a time. The trendline shows the rolling median of the point estimates, using a window of 5. This plot includes Italian and Spanish samples from the auxiliary dataset (Supplementary Note 1).

For each country, the ancestry proportions for all individuals are shown as violin plots, coloured by source. The range of values within a violin thus represents the proportion of ancestry modelled by that source in all individuals at that time. The full set of IBD mixture modelling results, including jackknife error bars, are plotted in Supplementary Fig. 1.6.

For each target individual (n = 702), point estimates of the proportions of ancestry modelled from these ancestry sources are plotted. #1361. Matchday Guide: Everton v Coventry

Fans are strongly advised to arrive early as Everton host Coventry City in the Premier League at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday 6 November (8pm kick-off).

This game marks Everton’s annual Remembrance fixture, which will see a tribute take place ahead of kick-off involving representatives from the Armed Forces, the laying of commemorative poppy wreaths in memory of the fallen and a rendition of The Last Post. More details on the Remembrance ceremony can be found HERE.

Supporters are advised to plan their journey in advance due to ongoing engineering works taking place on the Merseyrail network, which will entail replacement bus services operating between Hunts Cross and Moorfields (NB: there is no rail replacement bus stop by Liverpool Central).

Train services will be running as usual between Southport, Ormskirk and Headbolt Lane & Liverpool Central, and return journeys. For the latest updates Merseyrail, click HERE

On the approach to the stadium, Boundary Street is currently down to one lane due to emergency gas works.  Boundary Street will continue to operate as a one-way street in the direction of Hill Dickinson Stadium in the three hours prior to kick-off, minimising disruption for matchday traffic and bus services. However, supporters are advised to leave more time for their journey in case of delays in and around this route.

Some key information follows, and for everything else you need ahead of your visit - including general travel information, food and drink options, digital ticketing support, accessibility guidance and more on what’s happening around the stadium - visit evertonfc.com/matchday.

9am - The Ticket Office opens until half-time. The away ticket office, located outside the North Stand, will open at 5pm.

5pm - Access to the stadium site opens via the Regent Road wall, with food and drink outlets on the Budweiser Plaza. All available gates (A–E) in the Regent Road wall will be open and supporters are encouraged to use the full range of entrances to help avoid unnecessary congestion.

6pm - Stadium turnstiles open, with food and drink available across all concourses, including Early Bird offers until 6pm. Please ensure your digital match ticket has been downloaded to your mobile device before arriving at the stadium. A step-by-step digital ticketing guide and stadium map can be found HERE.

7.50pm – Remembrance service sees service armed forces personnel, standard bearers and veterans escorted pitchside ready for commencement, upon team walk-outs.

9.50pm - Following the end of the game, the South Stand Bar will remain open for one hour for supporters, with Level 0 open for 30 minutes (see below for more).

NB: Following the game, supporters should leave Hill Dickinson Stadium using the designated exit gates (A–E) on the Regent Road wall. The Nelson Dock exit, accessed from the Budweiser Plaza, is reserved exclusively for supporters with allocated parking in this area, including supporters using accessible parking. Please note, there will be no pedestrian access from Nelson Dock onto Regent Road after the game.

Please be advised that a short period of flashing lights will take place ahead of the teams taking to the pitch. Fans with photosensitive disorders, sensitivity to strobing lights, or who may react to flashing lights, may wish to remain in the concourse until this activation has concluded. Lighting will return to normal as the players emerge on the pitch.

Early bird deals, available inside the stadium for the first 60 minutes following turnstiles opening, are as follows:

Salt and Pepper Chicken Sharebox & 2 pints of & San Miguel for £30 (Flight Birds)

Salt and Pepper Chicken Sharebox & 2 pints of Budweiser - £28 (Flight Birds).

The Upper South Stand bar will remain open for one hour after the final whistle.

All supporters on Level 2 can access this bar after the game and, subject to capacity and operational requirements, home supporters from lower areas will also be able to access the bar post-match. This will be via the Lower South escalators for fans on Level 0, or via pass gates at Entrance 7a if coming from other areas of the stadium.

Please note, supporters on Level 0 will not be allowed to access Level 2 until it is safe to do so. A bar on Level 0 will be open for supporters for 30 minutes while they wait for the Upper Tier crowd to disperse and for access to be granted.

Everton has introduced a new digital service that will allow supporters to access Audio Description Commentary through their own mobile devices when attending matches at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The technology – accessed via a web link - enables blind and partially-sighted supporters to listen to live Audio Description Commentary (ADC) through the flexibility of their own smartphone and headphones, removing the need to collect and return a separate receiver and offering a more seamless and independent matchday experience.

Fans wishing to access the new service should visit the Accessibility Ticket Office on matchday, where members of the Club's accessibility team will help them download the app and get connected.

NB: Supporters will need to bring their own headphones compatible with their mobile device to use the service.

For further information on Hill Dickinson Stadium’s accessible provision, click here or contact accessibility@evertonfc.com

We hope you enjoy your visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

If you see or hear anything that does not feel right, please report it to a steward or police officer. In an emergency, call 999.

#1360. Hearts dealt ANOTHER injury blow as winger Calvin Miller is ruled out for two months with knee injury

Published: 15:47 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 16:07 EDT, 4 November 2026

Hearts boss Wouter Vrancken has revealed star winger Calvin Miller will require surgery on a knee injury that will keep him out for two months.

Both Tomas Magnusson and Miller came off during the first half of Hearts’ Premier Sports Cup semi-final defeat to Edinburgh rivals Hibernian at Hampden on Sunday.

Icelandic midfielder Magnusson was taken to hospital with concussion, while former Celtic, Morton and Falkirk attacker Miller left the national stadium on crutches with his knee in a brace.

Vrancken, who will be without ten first-team players for Thursday’s Conference League game against FC Thun in Switzerland, was asked about Miller and said: ‘It will be two months, let’s say, depending on what the surgery says because it’s a meniscus injury. It’s a pity, but it is what it is.

‘Tomas is doing good. The day after was already a lot better. There is a protocol, of course, with concussions. He will be for sure back after the (international) break.’

Vrancken will attempt to put together a side capable of getting a first win in the competition, following a 1-1 home draw against Nordsjaelland and a 2-0 defeat away to Trabzonspor. He added: ‘Yes, it’s a puzzle. I’m always happy to see that the players we work with and play out of position are always motivated to do it. They know how much they help the team by doing it.

Calvin Miller holds his injured leg before being taken off in Hearts' League Cup defeat to Hibs

‘It’s good to see because they take responsibility and they don’t live by excuses. They have already done it for weeks. That’s how we also get good results and good performances.

‘Now we have to try to do it two more times before the break. I’m confident in the players that they are mentally ready to play the game.

‘They (Thun) have a good team, they have a lot of energy, a lot of intensity. We will have to be spot on, we have to be on our level to make the result. But the aim is to try to get a win here.’

Meanwhile, the Tynecastle club yesterday announced a loss of £2.4million after investing heavily to return to European football this season. However, the club reported they are also in ‘positive’ discussions about further investment in the January transfer window and are confident of a ‘significantly improved financial result’ in a year’s time.

#1359. Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

“I’m really happy for Bradley, because you were asking me yesterday about him, not making the numbers,” Iraola smiled. “Also Florian [Wirtz], and I think both of them played really, really well. They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

We can look at the late switch off in due course but the only place to begin is with Barcola, who looked ready for business as early as the eighth minute when his first touch was a cushioned back heel, taking possession by crossing one leg behind the other, and how he seized his moment.

Liverpool had already taken the lead when Ronald Araújo rose powerfully to head in a Kostas Tsimikas corner but, two minutes after, the Barcola show began, a confident right-footed shot being swept past Lukas Jungwirth from 10 yards after some good build-up play from Rio Ngumoha and Lewis Koumas.

Araujo rises to score his first goal for Liverpool 🔴 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/W1C4iYd89m

Bradley Barcola gets off the mark for Liverpool with an instinctive finish 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/5K7YBB7UyG

He put his fingers in his ears as he celebrated, with every outfield player running to engulf him, and it was clear how much Barcola was aware of the requirement to get up and running, especially with Cody Gakpo, Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai injured.

Liverpool needed Barcola to deliver as much as the player himself needed to prove a little point and there is absolutely nothing wrong with having a cause to light a fire. Like a batsman who has been waiting nervously to get off the mark, soon the France international began playing his shots.

There were cushioned touches, changes of gear and even a stunned pass to Ryan Gravenberch, using his heel, that showed confidence had started surging through him and how obvious that was when Wirtz sent him scampering away in the 37th minute to finish with his left foot.

Partnership building... 👀 Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola link up for Liverpool's third 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UJC9VW82Q8

That effectively ended the game as a contest, so it was bizarre how it ended up 6-3. Jeremie Frimpong had made it 4-0 and Robert Ljubicic’s reply in the 65th minute looked nothing more than a consolation before Barcola completed his hat-trick.

A brilliant night should have been glossed by Koumas’s first European goal – he matched Steven Gerrard in becoming just the second player aged 21 and under to assist and score for Liverpool in a Champions League game – but LASK kept pushing and exploited spaces to halve the deficit with a double from Florian Flecker, much to Alisson Becker’s obvious disgust.

Look how much it means to Lewis Koumas to score Liverpool's sixth of the night 🥹 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fLYhslbFGq

But some lapses of concentration won’t detract from this being Barcola’s night. The ambition, however, must now be to do it in the Premier League. Liverpool have invested all that money for him to do it over and over again and it would be quite the thing to repeat the trick at Brentford.

“You never know how he is going to play the next day,” Iraola said. “But it wasn’t a big surprise because we were feeling he was in a good place going into the game. He has to enjoy this.”

21 - Lewis Koumas is the second player aged 21 or younger to both score and assist a goal in a UEFA Champions League match for Liverpool, after Steven Gerrard against Dynamo Kyiv in October 2001 (also 21). Emulating. https://t.co/vmfSEaotQ9

A very entertaining way for Liverpool to make it six points from six in the Champions League. The hardest game they have left is Inter away – a fixture they won last season when badly out of form – so they have a real chance to push for a top-two finish that would mean home second legs in the knockout-stages.

This was a good night for Iraola, who was able to rotate before a tough game at Brentford. A hat-trick for Barcola and a much-improved performance from Wirtz were most welcome, but now they need to show some consistency.

Mac Allister and Gravenberch make hard work of clearing a low LASK cross, but they eventually do so. The home team have finished with a flourish and the scoreline looks more respectable for them.

Liverpool’s substitutes have not had the desired effect. Munoz is now on for Barcola, and Ngumoha has gone down with some cramp. The young wingers is substituted, as well as Nyoni, replaced by Mac Allister and Chambers.

Ngumoha too quick for LASK to handle once again, and he is hacked down at the expense of a free-kick. From there, Liverpool win a corner, which they take short and keep possession. Just trying to restore some order in the game.

The score is now LASK 3 Liverpool 6 if you are struggling to keep score. Liverpool have conceded three since Van Dijk was introduced. This was a very tidy finish from Flecker, guiding a bouncing ball beyond Alisson with the inside of his foot.

With the exception of fixtures against a select band of eight or 10 teams, these Champions League nights are becoming like League Cup ties for the Premier League teams: loads of goals, youngsters impressing and senior players in second gear.

The player who scored against Liverpool in December 2023 in the Europa League has done it again, finding an empty net with a diving header after some more loose Liverpool defending.

Denied twice by the offisde flag, Koumas has now scored his first Champions League goal. LASK were caught in possession in their left-back area, and Frimpong delivered to the unmarked Koumas who swept the ball beneath the goalkeeper Jungwirth.

Look how much it means to Lewis Koumas to score Liverpool's sixth of the night 🥹 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fLYhslbFGq

Ngumoha has been a livewire throughout the game, and another shot on the LASK goal is blocked.

Then Barcola is in behind again, showing his pace to reach a Tsimikas through ball, but the winger’s dink over the goalkeeper is cleared.

That is a really well-worked Liverpool goal, with Ngumoha slipping a pass between wing-back and centre-back for the run of Frimpong and his low cross picks out Barcola at the back post for a tap-in.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

Ljubicic had only been on the pitch for 30 seconds or so, but he has just beaten Alisson with a composed finish after the Austrian side found a way in behind down Liverpool’s right. That gives the home fans something to take home with them.

An unnecessary blot for Liverpool, Joe Gomez  – who had only been introduced 60 seconds earlier  – played LASK onside and the home side now have a goal. Gomez found himself being chided by both Alisson and Trey Nyoni.

Here come the Liverpool changes, and they come at centre-back: Araujo and Jacquet off, replaced by Van Dijk and Gomez.

Iraola opting to keep his centre-back options fresh, perhaps with an eye on the aerial bombardment that a trip to Brentford can involve. Araujo has been played at right-back domestically.

Alisson called into action for the first time tonight, and it was a sharp save down at his near post after Flecker cut inside from the right and let fly with his left foot.

The one thing that will put a gloss on the evening for Andoni Iraola is if Lewis Koumas can get himself a goal. The whole squad will be willing him to hit the target, having had two efforts ruled out for offside already. He’s provided a real lift to the atmosphere, an academy product showing you can still make the grade with hard work and a refusal to give up.

For the second time tonight, Lewis Koumas thought he had his goal only for the offside flag to be raised. Correctly, once again. Just a little too eager for his chance, but if he keeps going there is a goal in this for Koumas.

I doubt any Liverpool fans had a Frimpong headed goal on their bingo card, but that is a much-needed positive contribution from the right-back. Barcola dangerous down the left again, Tsimikas chips a cross into the box, and it was an impressive leap from Frimpong to score.

Jeremie Frimpong rises to head home and put Liverpool four goals clear ⚽️ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/0KbDZvWowz

The home team moving the ball around with some confidence, but they look so vulnerable to Liverpool’s counter-attacks whenever they lose possession.

That LASK attack carried more punch though: there was an important defensive touch from Nyoni, before Lang fires just wide of the post at the edge of the box.

How many more goals will Liverpool add to their tally in the second half?

Flecker replaces Jorgensen. Iraola has decided against making any subs.

19 - Liverpool have recorded the most shots by an away team on record in the first half of a UEFA Champions League away match (since 2003-04). Volume. https://t.co/AFlsqZlKFh

Liverpool well on their way to consecutive wins in the Champions League league phase, and the big positive is the threat offered by Barcola, Wirtz as well as Ngumoha. Barcola and Wirtz also offered signs of a promising partnership. The gulf in class is stark, and Iraola can now make changes with Brentford in mind.

Wirtz looking a far more confident player, not that this is the most exacting test, and he tests the goalkeeper with a curling shot towards the far corner. There will be just one minute of added time to play.

Liverpool’s wingers Barcola and Ngumoha have just been far to sharp for their markers, LASK cannot cope with the pace on offer. The home team keep pushing numbers forward which could be a dangerous straregy.

That’s a very nifty assist from Florian Wirtz, played through legs into Barcola’s feet in the box, and the French winger’s touch teed him up for a left-footed finish across the goalkeeper. Game over, which was already the case.

What a difference a goal makes. Barcola’s touches and feints and skills are getting a full airing now and rightly so. He looks like he is relaxing and he should be aiming to score himself a hat-trick. Liverpool are miles clear of this team.

Writing Partnership building... 👀 Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola link up for Liverpool's third 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/AffQ8kSy2C

This game is a non-contest. Gravenberch lines up another shot from the edge of the box, before Barcola shows some quick feet in the box and his side-footed attempt loops over. The question for Iraola is the extent to which these performances and chances created will translate to Premier League standard.

Ryan Gravenberch so unlucky not to score with a shot across Jungwirth, which struck the inside of the far post and bounced away to safety, before a Wirtz shot deflects behind. Liverpool waltzing through the LASK defence with ease now.

Lewis Koumas thought he had scored a third for Liverpool, but the flag was raised for offside. He was a yard or two off, but it was still a very accomplished finish.

Liverpool just need a goal or two from Wirtz now and the night would be complete. LASK actually made a confident start in the first 20 minutes but conceding from a corner has deflated them.

Barcola is the scorer, but the initial danger was instigated by Ngumoha, dribbling around the outside of the LASK defence and into the box where he is tackled. The ball breaks free to Koumas, and he sets it back for Barcola to find the far corner. Liverpool now in command.

The goals have been coming from Liverpool and, really, it should be a night for them to plunder a hatful. LASK have loud supporters and the atmosphere being created is typically of one of these smaller European stadiums but Liverpool are miles better than LASK and should rip them apart. Bradley Barcola looked like a weight had been lifted as he got his first goal and you would now like to see him get a couple more – it’s certainly possible for him to do so.

Bradley Barcola gets off the mark for Liverpool with an instinctive finish 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/5K7YBB7UyG

A Van Dijk-esque header you could say, and Liverpool have punished LASK’s jittery set-piece defending. Good delivery from Tsimikas, and Araujo rose highest around seven yards out to plant a header byone Jungwirth.

Araujo rises to score his first goal for Liverpool 🔴 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/W1C4iYd89m

Some harrying from Gravenberch is enough to win Liverpool another corner, their fifth of the game so far. The goalkeeper was shaky again, but the ball glances off a LASK head and out for another corner.

LASK are targetting Liverpool’s left flank with direct balls forward, and the big centre-forward Adeniran caused Jacquet all manner of problems near the touchline but his touch ran away from him in the box.

The another good Barcola run is found, but his shot is screwed just wide of the near post. Barcola and Wirtz certainly more involved so far.

Diligent defending from Jorgenson to halt the progress of Barcola after a burst into the penalty area from the left. From the Liverpool corner, LASK goalkeeper Jungwirth was uncertain but Araujo could not not get enough on the header.

There really is something incongruous about seeing Kostas Tsimikas wearing the Liverpool captain’s armband. He should never have been given it again after throwing it on the floor after a pre-season friendly in the United States when he, Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai bickered with each other. The reason Alisson doesn’t wear it is because if there is a decision that requires him to talk to the referee in the opposition area, he would be miles from his own goal and potentially vulnerable. Alisson is the real leader on this pitch for this team.

Liverpool starting to turn their screw now. First, Wirtz skipped through a couple of challenges and fired a low shot straight at the goalkeeper before Ngumoha, playing on the right, drops a shoulder and drives to the byline, standing up a dangerous cross.

Then Wirtz tries another dribble through the middle, but his shot is charged down.

Liverpool struggling to clear their lines from the corner, and Schopf scoops a shot over the bar from the edge of the area.

Nyoni then tries a difficult reverse pass back towards Barcola but overcooks it. Moments before, there was a nice touch from Barcola to bring down a switch of play.

Lewis Koumas looking dangerous again, peeling behind LASK’s defence and rounding the goalkeeper Jungwirth on the corner of the penalty area, but he was forced wide and had to settle for a corner which the goalkeeper claims.

Then LASK pour forward again after a cheap giveaway by Araujo, and the home team win a corner of their own. Lively enough start.

Tsimikas scrambling rather to deal with a cross towards Jorgensen, before Alisson puts Liverpool under pressure with a stray pass, and LASK have a corner. Taken short, and then stood up to the back post but Liverpool clear.

Kostas Tsimikas captains Liverpool tonight, not words I ever expected to type but it is a team short of experience. Liverpool enjoying all of the possession so far, LASK are defending in a 5-2-3 shape, so Liverpool’s full-backs should have some time and space. Gravenberch does well to win a foul in midfield.

The home team play in all red, so Liverpool are in their white away strip. It looks like there is some Liverpool support among the locals/neutrals in the home end.

LASK XI: Jungwirth, Jorgensen, Mbuyamba, Alemao, Andrade, Dibango, Danek, Bogarde, Schopf, Lang, Adeniran

Subs: Schutzenauer, Schillinger, Freckleton, Ljubicic, Kalajdzic, Verhaeghe, Elfadli, Flecker, Kane.

A young Liverpool team has been selected to face Linz – the third youngest, according to Opta, that the club have fielded in the Champions League – and Andoni Iraola is being mindful of players such as Virgil van Dijk and Alexis Mac Allister being overburdened ahead of Saturday’s trip to Brentford.

One novice who certainly deserves his starting spot is Trey Nyoni, the England Under-21 international has impressed in the opportunities he has been given so far this year. Watch out for his calmness on the ball and the efficiency with which he uses it.

He should get more chances in the next 10 days, as it is difficult to see Dominik Szoboszlai being ready at least until the home match against Brighton on Sunday week.

Asked about Liverpool’s youthful team, Iraola said: “For me Trey [Nyoni], [Lewis] Koumas and Rio [Ngumoha] are young players coming in from the academy but they are first team players.

“They are first team players because we trust them, and in our situation, where we have some injuries, and we come from playing three days ago. I think they can play well, and I hope they do well.”

24 - Liverpool's starting XI against LASK has an average age of 24 years and 186 days, their third-youngest ever for a UEFA Champions League game, older only than September 2001 v Borussia Dortmund (24y 136d) and December 2020 v Midtjylland (24y 26d). Knocks. https://t.co/4JeW73N87k

Iraola makes four changes from the defeat by City so in come Frimpong, Tsimikas, Nyoni and Ngumoha.

Liverpool XI: Alisson, Frimpong, Araujo, Jacquet, Tsimikas, Nyoni, Gravenberch, Wirtz, Barcola, Koumas, Ngumoha

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Munoz, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Sonni-Lambie, Lucky

Our team to take on LASK ✊ #UCL https://t.co/8vObg7mgLF

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

#1358. Moyes' Pride At Reaching Incredible Everton Record

David Moyes will equal Harry Catterick's record of most games managing Everton when he takes charge of the Blues' clash with Coventry City at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday night.

To mark the occasion, the Official Matchday Programme will be centred around Moyes – including a special cover and an in-depth interview, where he reflects on his time with the Toffees and plots his future hopes.

“Yes I am proud,” he explains in his exclusive interview with the Official Matchday Programme. “The thought of being the Everton manager who has managed the most games is something I’m very proud of.

“I’m sure Harry Catterick, Howard Kendall and Joe Royle were also incredibly proud [to do this job]. The Club gets you, and if you get the Club – then it’s so big."

Discussing if anything took him by surprise when he first joined Everton as manager in March 2002, he says: "Nothing really took me by surprise.I was well versed in football, in watching football so I knew exactly what I was coming to.

“But probably the big thing which struck me was when I was driving in, and I’ve told this story before, but it’s absolutely true.

“I was coming in on a nice Spring evening. I can remember it was quite bright and looking out the windows all I could see was Everton strips everywhere.

“That was my over-riding memory. I was relatively young and inexperienced in some ways, but I’d been around the leagues and I just remember thinking, ‘My goodness, everybody in the streets in Liverpool are Everton supporters.’

“That was where I came up with ‘the People’s Club’ line. I think in a way that might have helped me be accepted.

“A lot of people said, ‘Ah, you must have thought that up beforehand’ but I didn’t. It was genuinely just driving in when I thought it."

With Moyes poised to set a new Club-record for most games managed when Everton travel to Brentford after the international break, he continues: “Everton has been huge for me and my family. My son David has gone everywhere and my father has lived it with us as well, watching it all.

“That’s so important. What is also so important is that I’ll always try to do the right thing for Everton Football Club.”

#1357. Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Ribosomal frameshifting, an uncommon translational recoding event, is best known for its regulatory roles in viral gene expression1,2, whereas its physiological relevance in mammals remains poorly understood. Here we show that specific codon pairs trigger efficient −1 frameshifting preferentially in cancer cells. Mechanistically, this recoding arises from ribosomal pausing associated with tRNA and amino acid availability, and is amplified by impaired ribosome quality control and sustained phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6. We found that this codon-pair-specific frameshifting represents an intrinsic state of translational dysregulation, which is prevalent across cancer cells and reshapes protein synthesis. Taking advantage of this frameshifting-permissive state in cancer cells, we engineered a frameshifting-activated synthetic therapeutic circuit (FAST) that conditionally expresses the pyroptotic effector gasdermin D. FAST is activated across diverse cancer cell types, inducing potent and selective pyroptosis, while sparing normal tissues from detectable toxicity. As a proof of concept, systemic AAV9-mediated delivery of FAST in mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer elicited pronounced tumour regression, robust immune activation and synergistic effects with immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, these findings reveal codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting as a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells and establish translation-coupled gene circuits as a strategy for cancer-selective therapy.

a, Schematic of the dual-luciferase reporters used to quantify +1 and −1 ribosomal frameshifting activity, together with the corresponding control constructs. b, Histogram showing the distribution of read counts for the +1 and −1 frame reporter libraries. c, Nucleotide frequency across the randomized 10-nt insert sequences in the reporter library. d, Quantification of +1 frameshifting activity across multiple cancer cell lines using 10-nt randomized dual-luciferase reporters. “Ctrl” denotes a control reporter lacking an inserted sequence. e, Quantification of −1 frameshifting activity across multiple cancer cell lines using 6-nt randomized dual-luciferase reporters. “Ctrl” denotes a control reporter lacking an inserted sequence. f, Quantification of frameshifting activity for positive-control constructs transfected into HEK293T cells using dual-luciferase reporters containing known frameshifting elements. g, Correlation between out-of-frame rates estimated from Ribo-seq and mean frameshifting activities measured by dual-luciferase reporters in f. h, Heatmap showing in-frame rates for codon pairs across the Ribo-seq dataset. i, Aggregation plots displaying in-frame rates and −1 frame rates before and after codon pairs. “Low” indicates the bottom 10% of codon pairs (n = 372 pairs). “Low-Rev”: codon pairs identical to those in the “Low” group, but with the order of the two codons reversed. j, Scatter plot showing the correlation between Fluc/Rluc ratios and Ribo-seq-derived −1-frame rates. 29 codon pairs were randomly selected, inserted into dual-luciferase reporters and quantified for frameshifting activity. In d–e, data are mean ± s.d.; n = 3 biologically independent samples. In f–g, data are mean ± SEM; n = 4 biologically independent samples. In g and j, Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated and two-sided P values are shown.

a, Frame analysis of Ribo-seq, with the majority of datasets showing in-frame rate higher than 70%. b, Frameshifting activity of individual codon pairs in HCT116 cells. A single codon pair was inserted between Rluc and Fluc in the dual-luciferase reporter, with Fluc placed in the −1 frame relative to Rluc. Numbers on the bars refer to average values (%) of the three replicates. Although a single codon pair is sufficient to induce significant frameshifting signals in HCT116 cells, to increase the detectable frameshifting signal in other cells and thereby facilitate analysis of both regulatory mechanisms and anti-tumour effects, we used 5× tandem repeats of the frameshifting motif in this study. c, Comparison of frameshifting activity using different repeat numbers of the frameshifting motif. For the 3×, 5× and 10× constructs, adjacent motifs were separated by a CCC codon. CCC was selected because cytosine-rich spacer sequences are less likely than A-, T- or G-rich spacers to generate premature stop codons (TAA, TAG or TGA) with adjacent sequences, thereby minimizing unintended effects on reporter expression. Numbers on the bars refer to average values (%) of the three replicates. d, Comparison of frameshifting activity when repeated frameshifting motifs were separated by different synonymous proline codons. CCC produced the lowest frameshifting activity, whereas CCG produced the highest. Because CCG is a relatively rare proline codon (RSCU = 0.46) compared with CCC (RSCU = 1.3), these results suggest that spacer codon usage can influence motif activity. In the AGAACG construct separated by CCT, the spacer introduces a − 1 frame stop codon (TAG), thereby terminating −1 frame translation. e, Frameshifting activity in HEK293T and HCT116 cells stably expressing the indicated 5× motif reporter constructs. f, Box plot comparing out-of-frame translation in the +1 and −1 frames between codon pairs with high in-frame rates (top 10%, n = 372 pairs) and low in-frame rates (bottom 10%, n = 372 pairs). Out-of-frame rates are shown relative to the high in-frame group to correct for basal differences in footprint counts across reading frames. g, Comparison of +1 and −1 frameshifting activity in HCT116, PANC-1 and A549 cells. In HCT116 and PANC-1 cells, the frameshifting-prone codon pairs AGAACG and ACGAGA exhibited significantly higher −1 frameshifting activity than the frameshifting-negative control pair CCAAGT, whereas +1 frameshifting at these pairs was low and comparable to CCAAGT. By contrast, in A549 cells, −1 frameshifting was lower than in HCT116 and PANC-1 cells, whereas +1 frameshifting was higher, reaching 2.7% for AGAACG and 1.1% for ACGAGA. h, Analysis as in g using a reporter containing codon pair GGATCC, which showed minimal −1 frameshifting but higher +1 frameshifting. If Fluc expression were driven by alternative initiation or a cryptic promoter, Fluc activity in the control reporter would be comparable to that in reporters containing the insert. In this study, control reporters showed minimal Fluc activity, suggesting that the observed out-of-frame translation is unlikely to be attributable to spurious initiation or cryptic promoter activity. c, Schematic illustrating potential alternative splicing in the dual-luciferase reporter and the corresponding expected Fluc/Rluc ratios. #1356. O'Neill reiterates support for Trusty as Celtic boss slams McAvennie's comments about defender's absence

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 17:48 EDT, 4 November 2026

Martin O'Neill has stressed that Auston Trusty has the full backing of everyone at Celtic — after describing Frank McAvennie’s comments about the defender’s ongoing absence as being ‘in poor taste’.

Trusty remains with his family in the US on compassionate grounds following the recent passing of his father Walt.

Speaking on his Let me be Frank podcast this week, former Parkhead striker McAvennie questioned why Trusty wasn’t back playing — describing it as ‘nonsense’ perpetuated by ‘the woke brigade’.

‘I’ve got every respect for that, but how long do you want off?’ McAvennie said. ‘Martin (O’Neill) says he’s away to celebrate the life of his dad.

‘Celebrate the life? You’ve got football. You’re getting paid and we’re in trouble. How long is it going to be?

‘It’s the woke brigade now, isn’t it? It’s nonsense. My dad was the best man, the only man I looked up to when he died, but you’ve got to get on with it.’

Trusty has missed Celtic's last four games after returning home following his father's passing

Those remarks brought a huge backlash with McAvennie later forced into a public apology, claiming he meant no disrespect to Trusty or his family.

‘I should have chosen my words more carefully,’ said McAvennie, who scored 37 goals in 85 games across two spells with Celtic. ‘I can understand why people feel my comments were insensitive. Everyone deals with grief differently and I certainly meant no disrespect.

‘Celtic need the big man back and that’s what I was clumsily trying to say. I wish him and his family all the very best.’

Evidently unimpressed with that attempt to backtrack, O’Neill made it clear that his player, who’s been absent for four matches — against Celta Vigo, Hibernian, Dundee United and Falkirk — should take all the time he needs before returning to Glasgow.

‘That’s really poor taste. That’s really poor,’ said the Celtic boss. ‘I know I’ve said some things and ended up backtracking. But that’s a family bereavement.

‘And that’s making someone’s mind up about how long they should be grieving and stuff like this here. That’s not on.

‘Trusty asked me for some time (off). Even if it’s a celebration (of his late father’s life) it doesn’t matter.

McAvennie has been widely criticised for comments he made on his podcast

‘The father’s been in poor health for quite some considerable time. And I know there was a stage where he thought that he wasn’t going to see it through.

‘But I’m with Trusty the whole way there. Because I wouldn’t want anybody to tell me that I had to grieve over a brother or sister dying. And I’ve had that.

‘He’s 28 years of age. And he’s taken it badly. He has taken it badly. Honestly.

‘I’ve afforded him all the time he wants.

‘At some stage, obviously, he’ll come back. But, at the end of the day, I’ve given that time because I know that we might be talking about different eras or whatever the case may be. That’s nothing to do with it.

‘This is a family thing. And that’s not right.

‘So, Trusty has got the time and he’s got the backing of myself and he’s got the backing of the club.’

#1355. Branthwaite Fitness Update & Team News For Coventry Test

David Moyes hopes to have Jarrad Branthwaite fit and available for Everton's Friday night clash with Coventry City at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The Toffees head into the fixture on the back of two wins in quick succession over Newcastle United – in the Carabao Cup and Premier League respectively – and currently sit seventh in the league table.

Branthwaite was withdrawn after 82 minutes of the 1-0 victory at St James' Park on Monday with cramp but, speaking in Thursday's pre-match press conference at Finch Farm, Blues boss Moyes said he is hopeful the defender will be ready to feature against Coventry.

Moyes said: "Yeah, we're just nursing [Branthwaite] along a wee bit, just checking to see he's okay, so we need to see how he is, yes."

When asked about the availability of Jack Grealish for Friday's game, Moyes added: "Jack is not available. I wouldn't give you the plan, but we will be working with Jack again soon."

Discussing a potential maiden England call-up for Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, with Three Lions head coach Thomas Tuchel set to announce his squad for the upcoming international break on Friday, Moyes said: "I say this every time I get asked but thank goodness I don't have to pick the England team, because I think England have got so many good players to choose from.

"Kiernan's form is getting back to his levels of last year. Recently, in the past couple of games, he's been very good. So, I hope he does. He certainly must be around it, knocking on the door – but, again, the position he plays in, there are so many good players who could also claim those roles.

"As long as he keeps doing well for Everton, we'll be pleased, but if he gets recognised for England, then that would be great as well."

Frank Lampard is set to be in the opposing team's dugout for the first time since leaving his role as Everton manager in January 2023.

Coventry City will be without Aurele Amenda and Haji Wright for the game, while Josh Eccles and Luke Woolfenden are also expected to remain sidelined.

Bobby Thomas and Frank Onyeka face late fitness checks.

#1354. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.
