#1344. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

9 - Florian Wirtz's nine chances created from open play against Brentford is the most by a player in a Premier League game since Sadio Mané v Burnley in January 2021 (9) and the most by a player in an away game since Samir Nasri v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Progress. https://t.co/xyMIQP9y5p

A huge moment for Alvaro Arbeloa and Fulham 💪 A 1-0 win over Hull takes them out of the relegation zone for now ⬆️ #FFC #BBCFootball https://t.co/cQaDybcESl

𝐌𝐚𝐧 𝐂𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝟑-𝟐 𝐈𝐩𝐬𝐰𝐢𝐜𝐡 City make it seven Premier League wins from seven but were made to sweat by Ipswich in the end. Erling Haaland has now scored 100 non-penalty goals in the PL, reaching the milestone in fewer appearances than any other player (139). #MCIIPS https://t.co/uHahqEW3NU

Erling Haaland straight down the tunnel at full-time here. He was limping for the last minute of the match after a block from Jack Clarke caught his ankle/shin area.

Liverpool turn things around, but you wonder whether this match would have ended differently had Yarmoliuk kept his head on the stroke of half-time.

Haaland’s double is enough for City today, but the Norwegian hobbles down the tunnel immediately having taken a knock in the dying minutes of the game. It is to be seen if that’s anything to be worried about... City maintain their perfect record, anyhow.

FULL-TIME: Erling Haaland grabs a brace as Man City beat Ipswich at the Etihad 🔵 https://t.co/WGp2lzpFjs

Brentford have not given up, but Liverpool are hanging on. Barcola the latest player to make a meaningful defensive intervention.

Fatawu is presented with an opening but the Ghana winger loses his footing and the chance passes Ipswich by.

A second Brentford red card! Janelt pushes Ngumoha with the youngster bearing down on goal and is given his marching orders. The hosts will finish this match with nine men.

Could have been 4-2. Ndiaye tries to shape an effort around Walton instead of squaring to Haaland and the chance to put the game to bed goes begging.

Twelve minutes of time added on have been indicated.

Fulham have won a Premier League football match! Arbeloa will breathe a sigh of relief after that. The hosts were by far the better side but almost undid their own good work at the end.

Sessegnon is off deep into stoppage time for a poor challenge on Hull’s Vaz.

Fulham are making themselves work for what would be their first three points of the season. All self-inflicted, of course.

Manchester City 3 Ipswich Town 2 (Flemming) It could have been 4-1 moments ago, but instead City are in for a nervy finish. Flemming goes straight down the middle.

The referee goes to the monitor after Guehi fells Fatawu inside the City box... and the penalty is awarded!

Barcola hits the woodwork! The Frenchman attempts to lob Kelleher off the second phase of a corner but his effort comes off the crossbar.

Manchester City 4 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Ndiaye’s effort crashes off the crossbar and the ball falls to the feet of Enzo, who picks out Haaland and the Norwegian does the rest. What a finish. That’s his 13th City hat-trick.

Huge chance for Brentford! Anthony flashes a threatening ball across the face of goal and there Thiago is waiting and surely should score! He cannot arrange his feet quickly enough and Alisson is able to gather the ball with ease.

Liverpool’s front four have taken some criticism this season, and rightly so, but they have turned up in this second half. Wirtz assisted Munoz for the equaliser, and now Barcola has assisted Isak for the second.

The red card was the turning point in this game but the £400m frontline have delivered what was expected of them since the break.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 2 (Isak) The Swede is only just back from injury, and in all fairness has not looked great for much of this afternoon, but he’s put Liverpool infront here. Mac Allister plays a one-two with Wirtz down the right and the ball is worked to Barcola at the far post. The France winger nods it into the path of Isak who composes himself before spearing the ball beyond Kelleher.

Hull haven’t given up the ghost at Craven Cottage, knowing how easily Fulham crumbled last time out. Belloumi tries his luck from distance but cannot find the target.

Superb finish by Victor Munoz to level the scores here. Brentford were caught upfield and they were in trouble from the moment Florian Wirtz was able to slide the ball in behind for the Spanish winger. It comes as Liverpool were just starting to make their numerical advantage count.

Manchester City 3 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Ndiaye does well to play in Haaland who breezes past Outtara before lacing the ball into the bottom corner.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 1 (Munoz) Ngumoha plays the ball infield to Wirtz on the half-way line, and the German threads a ball in behind for the rapid Munoz to gallop on to, he cuts inside Lewis-Potter and fires the ball beyond Kelleher with his left foot.

Iwobi goes close. His curled effort has Tzolakis scrambling but zips just wide of the mark.

Fernandez, on as a second-half substitute, tries his luck with a free-kick from 25 yards out, but he cannot get the requisite dip on the ball to bring it down and it flies over.

Fulham are still dominating the ball and have been by far the better side. Their possession share remains in the high seventies. They’ve completed 476 passes to Hull’s 94.

A second goal would surely put this one to bed.

Liverpool brought on Jeremie Frimpong as a half-time substitute but he’s already limped off. That’s the second injury they have picked up today, after Dominik Szoboszlai.

This is a proper test of Liverpool’s creative ability now. Ten-man Brentford are going to sit deep for most of this second half, I am sure. Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola... time to deliver some game-changing quality.

Jacquet goes into the book. A loose pass out from the back is picked off my Brentford substitute Schade and Jacquet snaps in too enthusiastically and receives a yellow.

Chance! Will Fulham rue all these missed chances? King is involved once more, standing up a cross to the back post where Garcia nods down for Iwobi to stroke goalwards near the penalty spot, but Tzolakis does well to get down low to his left and keep Fulham’s advantage to just one goal.

Mateo Kovacic comes off injured for City. It is probably just a knock as he’s sat on the bench rather than heading down the tunnel. Was a standout player in the first half.

Close! Ajayi’s clearance comes straight back and Charles works the ball to King on the right, but with just the keeper to beat, the midfielder’s effort is saved by Tzolakis with his feet. King really should be scoring there.

Still some time before the Liverpool game resumes given the time added on at the end of the first half.

Following his clash of heads with Jarrad Branthwaite in the lunchtime kick-off at the Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Chelsea goalkeeper has now been taken to hospital to undergo precautionary tests.

Brentford lead Liverpool thanks to Keane Lewis-Potter's header, but the second half could be tricky for the Bees after Yehor Yarmoliuk was sent off just before half-time. Liverpool are yet to have a shot on target despite having seven shots in the first half. #BRELIV https://t.co/o9HE2Fh8qb

Andrews will be furious with how that first half ended. His side had done brilliantly to establish a lead, but will have their work cut out keeping Liverpool out after the break with the visitors a man to the good.

With half-time fast approaching and Brentford in front, this is absolute madness. Yarmoliuk looks to have butted Jacquet in an incident that reminds of Bentacur’s red card at Old Trafford last weekend.

The referee is sent to the pitchside monitor after a lengthy delay and Yarmoliuk is off!

We’ve had the second VAR review in just a few minutes here, and this one has resulted in a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk for a “headbutting action”. I have to say, this feels harsh. It’s pretty tame. There is a tiny movement towards Jacquet, who collapsed to the turf in dramatic fashion, but he’s hardly caused the Liverpool defender any damage. That will change the dynamic of this game.

Haaland restores City’s lead after Maeda had cancelled out Foden’s opener.

Arbeloa’s side are in front and could have been ahead by a wider margin, but we’ve been here before...

Gary Neville is a w-----, is a w-----.....is quite a loud chant here at City. Fans in a good mood here after Erling Haaland scored in his eighth game in a row.

Brentford 1 Liverpool 0 (Lewis-Potter) Outtara curls in a wonderful cross and Lewis-Potter steals in to head the ball beyond Alisson from 10 yards out.

Brentford take the lead, and it’s a lead they probably just about deserve on the run of play. It’s an absolutely superb header by Keane Lewis-Potter, up from left-back, as he thumps Igor Thiago’s cross into the top corner of Liverpool’s net. Textbook technique.

Just after Wirtz was denied a penalty of his own, Mac Allister looks to have won a spot-kick for real off a challenge from Outtara. The referee gives it, but is then sent to the monitor and the decision is reversed. Correct decision. Outtara clearly got a piece of the ball first.

Liverpool have been awarded a penalty but I don’t think this will stand. It shouldn’t stand. Dango Ouattara got a touch on the ball when he lunged in on Alexis Mac Allister.

Yep, the penalty has been overturned. Referee John Brooks missed Outtara’s touch on first viewing but the replays were pretty conclusive.

Manchester City 2 Ipswich Town 1 (Haaland) Kovacic wriggles free of his markers and darts to the by-line. He’s able to stand up a cross and Haaland heads the ball forcefully downwards - just as your grassroots football coach always told you to - and Walton is unable to keep it out. Probably should have done better.

Fulham 1 Hull City 0 (Iwobi) A big, big goal for Fulham and Arbeloa. They are finally able to convert their overwhelming dominance with the ball into something material. This goal comes at the end of a sweeping move, with Iwobi stroking the ball beyond Tzolakis, who probably should have done better.

Bradley Barcola may not be justifying his fee at Liverpool yet but another Frenchman, Jeremy Jacquet, certainly is. The centre-back has been excellent all season and he has just produced a goal-saving challenge on Brentford’s Igor Thiago. A sliding tackle, perfectly timed, just as Thiago was about to score.

Brentford are getting the ball forward quickly, and Kelleher is the one to initiate the latest move. He finds Thiago on the halfway line, who gets the ball back off Outtara, but the Brazilian’s effort is well blocked by Van Dijk.

Some bad news for Liverpool, though, as Szoboszlai sits on the turf. It looks like his afternoon might already be over.

Daizen Maeda showed good strength to hold off Marc Guehi’s challenge before scoring his first goal for Ipswich since signing from Celtic. City will be disappointed with the defending there - it was a straightforward ball down the channel from Abdoul Ouattara.

Before that Phil Foden sent a message to Thomas Tuchel with the opening goal. Foden, playing in central midfield, was left out of the last England squad and has seen Alex Scott climb above him in the pecking order. But Scott is injured for next month’s international which may give Foden a chance.

Was Bradley Barcola’s midweek hat-trick the start of a great run of form for the £123m forward? Not on this evidence. A defensive mix-up allowed the Frenchman a clear run at goal, one-on-one with Brentford’s Caoimhin Kelleher, but his finish was woeful. An attempted dink that bobbled harmlessly wide. “What a waste of money,” comes the cry from the Brentford fans.

Manchester City 1 Ipswich Town 1 (Maeda) Woah, barely a minute between these two goals at the Etihad. Guehi relinquishes possession to Maeda and, left alone in the box, he stears the ball into the far bottom corner.

Manchester City 1 Ipswich Town 0 (Foden) While Foden has scored, huge credit must go to Doku, who did brilliantly down the left, working the ball on to his right foot before squaring to Foden who gets a shot away - Walton does well to get a hand on the ball, but he cannot keep it out.

Liverpool are looking bright, with Barcola and Wirtz combining well - just as they did in midweek - to force a corner. The ball is worked to Mac Allister on the edge of the box but his effort sails well over.

“You’re going down with the City,” sing the home fans at the Ipswich travelling support.

Arbeloa’s side have dominated the ball thus far, claiming an 87 per cent share of the ball. Hull have completed a grand total of 14 passes. But this has been the story of their season so far, lots of the ball but very little incision. Let’s see if they can be more productive this afternoon.

Bright start by Brentford here, although Liverpool have just created their first chance of the game as Szoboszlai shoots over from the edge of the box.

Thiago is putting himself about in Liverpool’s box, winning a corner which is headed behind for another by Van Dijk, but it comes to nothing.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1342. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

“Our decision-making in the final third was lacking today,” Jaissle said. “I am frustrated, I understand the supporters’ reaction, that is their right [to boo after a defeat at home].”

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

On another day, Newcastle could also have had centre-back Sven Botman sent off for a lunge on Jackson. Then it really would have become ugly, but the Dutchman survived a VAR check.

Villa were always the better side. There was no fluency in Newcastle’s game, no structure, no patterns of play. Every time they turned over the ball, they looked stretched. Every time they got a set-piece, it was defended easily. Every time they went forward in the first half, the ball was sent aimlessly long and came straight back at them. In the second, they huffed and puffed but did not sustain any pressure on the Villa goal. The missed chances late on were not clear opportunities and they were snatched at by the hapless Yoane Wissa.

Yoane Wissa fails to hit the target after an inspiring run! ❌ https://t.co/ohabzLZBRv

It was largely poor and so was the manner in which Villa took the lead. João Gomes was given the time and space to loft a cross to the far post for Manzambi, who had drifted away from Lewis Miley, to head home.

Newcastle were in disarray and it should have been 2-0 almost immediately when Emiliano Buendía received the ball in the middle of the area and crashed a shot against a post.

The home crowd tried to remain patient and supportive, but the sight of yet another long, aimless ball being punted forward straight to a Villa defender tipped some over the edge. There were boos and jeers in the stands while Jaissle screamed at Joe Willock and Wissa. There were more boos at half-time; things felt combustible.

Newcastle needed a big second half. They were better, but it was hardly anything to get excited about. A shot on the turn from Botman, superbly saved by Suzuki. Then a few half-chances were squandered, the occasional flash of a threat and that was it.

#1341. Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8, suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear9,10,11,12,13. Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

The capacity of cancer cells to switch phenotypic states, also called cellular plasticity, is a hallmark of cancer and is involved in tumour initiation and progression, including therapeutic resistance1. Glioblastoma (GB), the most common primary brain tumour in adults, is characterized by profound cellular heterogeneity and a dismal prognosis2,3. Although the genomic landscape of GB has been catalogued extensively, actionable genetic drivers remain scarce, and clinical responses to targeted therapies have been minimal4,5,6. Longitudinal studies have underscored the limited contribution of therapy-induced genetic evolution in GB and revealed remarkable clonal stability despite treatment7,8, suggesting that non-genetic mechanisms, such as epigenetic plasticity and transcriptional reprogramming, are central to adaptation and treatment resistance in GB. Seminal single-cell transcriptomic studies have shown that malignant GB cells occupy a continuum of cellular states resembling developmental progenitors (for example, oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC)-like and neural progenitor cell (NPC)-like), as well as astrocytic and mesenchymal-like phenotypes9,10. Patient-derived xenograft models have demonstrated that individual GB cells can give rise to multiple states, implying substantial plasticity10,11. However, whether these state transitions follow stereotyped routes or variable trajectories12,13, and how gene-regulatory mechanisms promote or constrain them, remain poorly understood.

Here, and in a companion study14, we address these questions by integrating single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing; snATAC-seq) profiles from more than one million cells from isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wild-type primary GBs. Using a computational approach (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference; scDORI) and systematic transcription factor (TF) perturbations, we decode enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks (eGRNs) at single-cell resolution and map the regulatory landscape that underlies the identity and plasticity of GB cells. Specifically, we model the gene-regulatory processes that govern GB cell states, identify key transcriptional regulators for each state, elucidate their roles in driving cell-state conversions and reconstruct a hierarchical roadmap of GB transitions. Our analyses reveal a structured landscape of GB state transitions shaped by epigenetic ‘highways’ and ‘barriers’. Neuronal-like cells emerge as a constrained, low-plasticity state stabilized by a network of transcriptional repressors that actively silences alternative malignant fates. We identify MYT1L as the key repressor in this network: gain-of-function of MYT1L restricts plasticity and induces a neuronal-like identity in patient-derived GB cells, and reduces tumour growth after transplantation in mice; by contrast, removal of MYT1L enhances plasticity and malignant features. These findings suggest that enforcing repressive barriers could lock GB cells into less adaptive states, and identify plasticity restriction as a potential therapeutic strategy.

Together with our companion study mapping spatio-temporal trajectories in GB tumours14, our findings reveal a conserved, epigenetically controlled hierarchy of cell states and transition routes in GB. Our work establishes transcriptional repressors as key suppressors of plasticity and underscores the potential of targeting the epigenetic foundations of state switching in brain cancer.

To characterize the regulatory landscape of GB, we generated a multiome snRNA–snATAC-seq atlas (see the companion study14), spanning parallel gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiles of more than one million cells collected across multiple sites (4–15) from 12 IDH-wild-type primary GB tumours, including peritumoral regions. In line with previous studies10, malignant GB cells exhibited vastly heterogeneous transcriptional profiles, ranging from developmental-like (OPC-NPC-like, OPC-like, OPC-neuronal-like, NPC-neuronal-like and astrocyte (AC)-progenitor-like) to glial injury response and hypoxia-associated (AC-gliosis-like, gliosis-like and hypoxia) phenotypes, as well as cycling signatures (proliferative) (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a).

a, Experimental set-up, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot and annotation of the RNA modality of 368,054 TME and 657,275 GB cells from 12 patients with IDH-wild-type GB profiled by snRNA–snATAC-seq. Colours and labels denote states of the indicated malignant GB and TME cells. b, Schematic of computation of the epigenetic plasticity score. A linear classifier trained on gene expression to predict transcriptional states is applied to gene accessibility profiles, with ambiguity of predictions indicating epigenetic plasticity. c, Epigenetic plasticity score determined using the approach in b, visualized for all cells on the UMAP plot in a. High scores denote high epigenetic plasticity. d, Confusion matrix for the accessibility-based predictions from the classifier in b: state prediction probability on the basis of gene accessibility profiles (rows), averaged across cells from each transcriptionally defined state (columns). Off-diagonal mass reflects accessibility compatible with several transcriptional states, the ambiguity that drives the epigenetic plasticity score in b. Malignant states (yellow box) show the lowest accuracy, indicating increased epigenetic plasticity. e, Average epigenetic plasticity score for the indicated cell states across n = 12 patients. Malignant states differ in plasticity, with NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like states showing the lowest levels (P = 5.0 × 10−6, two-sided t-test). Box plots show the median and interquartile range (IQR); whiskers are 1.5× IQR. f, Variance component analysis of epigenetic plasticity, assessing the contribution of patient, cell type and other sources of variation (residuals). Illustrations in a,b created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

First, we investigated the epigenetic plasticity of GB cells, assuming that accessible gene regions without active transcription indicate epigenetic plasticity. Inspired by a previous study15, we quantified how well accessibility profiles of cell-state markers predict transcriptionally defined cell states (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1b,c, Supplementary Table 1 and Methods). Cells whose chromatin profiles yield uncertain predictions are scored as more epigenetically plastic. Our analysis revealed that malignant cells exhibit greater epigenetic plasticity than non-malignant tumour microenvironment (TME) cells and analogous neurodevelopmental cell types (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1d–f), with chromatin accessibility in malignant cells often being compatible with multiple cell states (Fig. 1d). However, the extent of this plasticity varied significantly across GB cell states (Fig. 1e), and NPC-neuronal-like and OPC-neuronal-like cells stood out as the least plastic states. The variations in epigenetic plasticity could not be explained by differences in global coupling between gene expression and accessibility, were robust to differences in cell numbers per state and were consistently observed across patients (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). These data suggest that specific regulatory mechanisms underlie GB plasticity and govern cell-state heterogeneity.

To determine the specific gene-regulatory processes that underlie the observed differences in epigenetic plasticity, we aimed to identify relevant TFs, cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their interplay across GB states using eGRNs. Established eGRN inference methods are not designed for the heterogeneity of a single-cell tumour atlas like ours16,17,18,19,20,21,22. Specifically, existing methods assume discrete, predefined cell-types and therefore cannot capture the continuous, cell-state-specific variation in eGRNs that defines malignant heterogeneity. Many also scale poorly to datasets of this size23. Moreover, previous methods focus mainly on signatures of transcriptional activation, despite the growing recognition of gene repression as a key regulator of cell identity and plasticity in cancer24,25.

To address these limitations, we developed scDORI, a computational approach for inferring continuous eGRNs and their relationships across cell populations using single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and scATAC-seq multiome data (Fig. 2a and Methods). Building on autoencoders26, scDORI performs joint dimensionality reduction of gene expression and chromatin accessibility profiles, decomposing both into gene-regulatory modules16,27,28,29,30,31,32 that are hereafter referred to as ‘Topics’. Each scDORI Topic encodes an eGRN in which TFs bind to CREs to control target gene expression, so the factors carry regulatory meaning rather than describing co-variation alone (Fig. 2a). Coupled decoders enforce this structure through established eGRN signatures: peak co-accessibility, TF chromatin binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that distinguish activation from repression16,17,18,19,20,21,22 (Extended Data Fig. 2a). By modelling each cell as a mixture of Topics, scDORI can capture continuous variations in eGRNs across cell states, without relying on predefined annotations. Conversely, a single Topic can be active across multiple cell states, enabling the identification of shared aspects of gene regulation. scDORI scales to datasets comprising millions of cells, and performs favourably, compared with existing eGRN inference methods, on benchmarks such as the prediction of enhancer–gene links33 (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

a, Overview of the scDORI model, inferring continuous eGRNs from scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq multiome data. scDORI models each cell as a linear combination of co-active Topics, with each Topic encoding an eGRN that links TFs, CREs and target genes. Auxiliary decoders impose mechanistic constraints from peak co-accessibility, TF binding, CRE–gene linkages and TF–target expression correlations that separate activation from repression. b, Activity of selected Topics in malignant cells, visualized on the UMAP representation from Fig. 1a. c, Heat map with hierarchical clustering of selected Topic activation patterns across GB states, revealing an activation continuum. Colour denotes average Topic activation, scaled across states. For complete Topic scores, see Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2. d, Chromatin accessibility of Topic-associated ATAC peaks (blue) and expression of their predicted cis-linked genes (orange) across cell states. Rows correspond to peak and cis-linked gene pairs, grouped by the Topic with the highest peak association. e, Annotation of scDORI Topics by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), using genes ranked by Topic-association score. The normalized enrichment score (NES) is shown for two representative pathways per Topic (P < 0.05). Expanded analysis in Supplementary Table 2. ChS, chondroitin sulfate; ECM, extracellular matrix; EMT, epithelial–mesenchymal transition; PCP, planar cell polarity. f, GB TRs: TFs with the highest cumulative activation of genes in each Topic-specific eGRN. Topic activation scores are shown for selected TRs and Topics. TFs previously reported as GB cell-state markers or as being highly expressed in developmental (dev.) cell types are indicated in the top panels. g, TSs: TFs that repress Topic programs of at least two alternative states. Rows show the predicted repression of alternative Topics exerted by each TF. The source Topic is labelled at the bottom. TFs previously reported as GB or developmental markers are indicated in the top panels. Neftel states10: NPC1-like; NPC2-like; AC-like; OPC-like; MES, mesenchymal; Verhaak states4: CL, classical; PN, proneural; MS, mesenchymal. NSC, neural stem cell. Illustrations in a,d created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

Applied to our GB atlas, scDORI identified 31 active Topics with distinct patterns of activity across cells and patients (Fig. 2b,c, Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 2), each capturing co-accessible chromatin regions that were cis-linked to co-expressed genes (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Notably, the mechanistic constraints came at no cost to descriptive power: scDORI Topics explained transcriptional variation in tumour cells as well as or better than conventional dimensionality reduction methods did18,29 (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Clustering transcriptional GB states according to Topic activity patterns revealed four major regulatory states alongside a distinct proliferative (cycling) population, including developmental states (neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like) and AC–gliosis–hypoxia states (AC-like and gliosis–hypoxia) (Fig. 2c). Topics specific to individual states reflected gene programs that are characteristic of their developmental counterparts, such as neurotransmitter release in neuronal-like cells (Topic 37), PDGF signalling in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 34) and calcium ion homeostasis in AC-like cells (Topic 20)34,35,36 (Fig. 2e, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Table 2). These programs were also active in corresponding TME cell types, consistent with tumour cells co-opting developmental pathways.

As well as explaining differences between GB states, scDORI resolved functional heterogeneity within individual malignant states. For instance, in gliosis–hypoxia cells, distinct Topics captured hallmark features such as hypoxic stress (Topic 11), cytokine signalling (Topic 19) and vascular wound healing (Topic 12)37,38,39 (Fig. 2e). scDORI also identified ‘inter-state’ Topics (7, 9, 25, 29, 33, 36 and 49) that span several GB states. Most of these were enriched for programs linked to fate commitment and differentiation, indicating a potential role in mediating state transitions (Fig. 2c,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Finally, scDORI identified Topics that were broadly active across most tumour cells, reflecting tumour-wide programs, such as inflammatory response (Topic 31) and cell adhesion (Topic 18)40 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). The inferred Topics were reproducible across model restarts, consistently represented across patients with GB and transferable to independent single-cell GB atlases10 (Extended Data Figs. 3c and 4d–f). Notably, scDORI Topic-specific eGRNs accurately captured differential expression between GB cell states of these independent atlases (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h).

The eGRN encoded by each Topic directly yielded Topic regulators (TRs), defined as the TFs with the strongest predicted activation of the Topic-specific gene program. On average, scDORI identified about nine TRs per Topic (Fig. 2f, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). These included known GB cell-state markers, such as ASCL1 in OPC-NPC-like cells (Topic 36), SOX11 in neuronal-like cells (Topic 24) and FOSL1 in gliosis–hypoxia cells (Topic 19), as well as TFs associated with the respective Topic programs, such as hypoxia (NFKB1, Topic 19) and stress response (JUND, Topic 11)10,41,42,43,44. State-specific TRs included lineage-specific TFs, such as SOX6 (Topic 34, OPCs) and TRPS1 (Topic 9, ACs), further supporting the idea that GB cells reuse developmental TFs and gene programs45,46,47. Besides positive regulation, scDORI-inferred repressive links and identified Topic safeguards (TSs): TFs that regulate an identity by silencing gene programs of states distinct from their state of activity; that is, alternative states (Fig. 2g, Supplementary Table 2 and Methods). For instance, ST18 and SOX10 emerged as putative repressors of alternative state programs in neuronal-like and OPC-NPC-like programs, respectively. Several TSs also act as TRs of their own Topic, revealing factors that both activate their own identity program and repress those of alternative states. Collectively, scDORI redefines GB heterogeneity from a gene-regulation standpoint and reveals state-specific activators and repressors, many of which have not yet been described in GB.

The extent to which GB state transitions follow defined regulatory rules, and which TFs drive them, remain central questions in GB biology9,10. We reasoned that if scDORI faithfully captures these processes, then activating the predicted regulators should induce the associated cell states. To test this, we performed a pooled single-cell lentiviral overexpression (OE) screen of 55 TR and TS candidates across three patient-derived GB cell (PDGC) lines, co-cultured with primary cortical cells to provide a neural microenvironment (Fig. 3a, Extended Data Fig. 5, Supplementary Table 3 and Methods).

a, Pooled gain-of-function screen of 55 TFs across three PDGCs (S24, P3XX and BG5). Barcoded TFs were lentivirally delivered using doxycycline (Dox)-inducible (Tet-ON) vectors. Transduced cells were co-cultured with primary cortical cells, induced with Dox, sorted by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and profiled by scRNA-seq. b, Effects of TF OE on GB state identity. From left to right: log2-transformed fold change (log2FC) of TF expression (OE versus control averages); number of captured OE cells per TF after quality control; average change in state probability (Δstate score, OE versus control) across GB states; and consistency with scDORI predictions together with the predicted type of regulation (TR or TS). Dot size in the Δstate score panel denotes significance (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05, pooled and single-line analysis, permutation test, Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment), and black boxes mark significant effects with an odds ratio greater than 1.5 (FDR < 0.05). n = 3 (BG5) and n = 6 (S24 and P3XX). c, Consistency of scDORI predictions with the functional evidence from the screen. Shown is the proportion of regulators whose overexpression induced the predicted identity shift, evaluated at the state and Topic level (from b and Extended Data Fig. 5g). d, Agreement of high-confidence state drivers from the screen in b with scDORI predictions. Waterfall plots order drivers in each state by state induction activity (Δstate score, normalized (norm.) to TF fold change), with colour denoting significance. Shown are: Pearson correlation between TF level and state probability (dose–response); NES (P < 0.05) of state marker genes among OE-induced differentially expressed genes (DEGs); scDORI state regulation score; and the predicted regulatory mechanism, shown as a bivariate heat map of activation (red) versus repression (blue) strength on state marker genes. Top drivers on the basis of strength of state induction, dose–response and enrichment of state signature are highlighted (box). Illustration in a created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

After quality control, we recovered 261,566 cells, with 54 of 55 candidate regulators showing robust and balanced induction (at least 100 cells captured with more than 1.5-fold change) across all three lines (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Fig. 5a–d and Supplementary Table 3). We used logistic regression models trained on the patient atlas to assign cell state and Topic identity to each screened cell, revealing perturbation-induced shifts (Supplementary Table 3 and Methods). Two-thirds of candidates induced state changes consistent with scDORI predictions, spanning both TRs (for example, SOX4, ASCL1, MEOX2 and EPAS1) and TSs (for example, ST18, RBPJ, ETV1 and FOSL1) (Fig. 3b). Perturbation effects were also mostly concordant across all three patient lines, despite their distinct baseline cell-state compositions (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 5e). Top-ranked regulators as predicted by scDORI induced their target states most strongly, particularly those of neuronal-like and AC-like states (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Performing the same analysis at the more granular Topic level, we confirmed that regulators from nearly all Topics induced their respective Topic programs, even when their gain of function was not sufficient to induce a full state conversion (for example, ESR2, BCL6 and NR3C2) (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). A notable exception was regulators of hypoxia-response Topics 11 and 12, which are likely to require extrinsic hypoxic signals for complete activation. Overall, 76% of tested regulators showed identity shifts consistent with our predictions at either the Topic or the state level (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5h).

We defined high-confidence drivers for each of the four core GB states, combining three experimental lines of evidence: the strength of state change; the enrichment of the state gene signature after TF gain of function; and the dependence of state conversion on TF dose (Fig. 3d, Extended Data Fig. 5i,j and Supplementary Table 3). We then asked whether these regulators were also among the top-ranking scDORI predictions. We found that 81% (25 out of 31) ranked among the top predicted regulators of the corresponding state-associated Topics (Fig. 3d). Notably, scDORI also resolved distinct mechanisms of action among these drivers: some mainly activated state marker genes (MEOX2, PRRX1 and JUN), others repressed alternative-state marker genes (MYT1L, ST18 and SOX10), and a subset combined both modes (SOX4, FOXO1 and CEBPD) (Fig. 3d). Together, these results show that scDORI accurately nominates functional regulators of GB identity, and that their activation is sufficient to trigger corresponding state-specific transcriptional programs.

Having established that individual scDORI-predicted regulators can drive GB state transitions, we asked whether their endogenous expression and accessibility could explain how these transitions arise in patients. Examining each state’s TRs in cells of alternative states, we found that 39% (34 out of 87) were already expressed in at least one alternative state, whereas 68% (59 out of 87) were chromatin-accessible but transcriptionally silent, suggesting epigenetic priming for specific state transitions (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b).

To quantify primed transitions systematically, we computed a Topic activation potential (TAP) for each pair of Topics—an estimate of how readily cells in a source Topic can activate the TRs of a target Topic and mediate an identity shift. TAP scores integrate three components: the regulatory links from source-Topic TFs onto target-Topic TRs; the accessibility of those target TRs in source-Topic cells; and the importance of each TR in the target Topic (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 6c–f, Supplementary Table 4 and Methods). TAP scores revealed a structured and markedly asymmetrical landscape of transitions between GB states (Fig. 4b). Inter-state Topics (33, 36 and 49) acted as connectivity hubs linking multiple states, consistent with their enrichment for fate-change signatures (Fig. 2e). By contrast, state-specific Topics differed sharply: OPC-NPC-like (34) and AC-like (9, 20 and 44) Topics showed strong TAP connections to multiple alternative states, whereas connections from neuronal-like (24, 37 and 41) and gliosis–hypoxia (11, 12 and 19) Topics were mainly confined within their own state (Fig. 4b,e). Together, these results highlight how the regulatory architecture and epigenetic priming of each state jointly determine its permissiveness to transition (Extended Data Fig. 6d–f).

a, Schematic of TAP, quantifying how cells in a source Topic A activate TRs of a target Topic B, integrating regulatory (reg.) links from TFs in A to TRs in B, TR accessibility in source-Topic cells and TR strength in the target Topic. b, TAP network linking the indicated Topics of core GB states, overlaid on the UMAP from Fig. 1a. Nodes are Topics; edge colour denotes the source Topic and width denotes the TAP strength. Significant TAP links are shown (>95th percentile of 1,000 randomized TAP distributions; TAP score > 0.25). c, Schematic of TRS, the repressive analogue of TAP. d, TRS network, as in b. e, Number of TAP and TRS outgoing links in b,d from source Topics towards Topics in the same state (yellow) or alternative states (orange; state transitions). f, Pearson correlation between epigenetic plasticity per Topic (as in Fig. 1c, averaged over the top 5,000 cells per Topic) and (i) cumulative net transition potential towards alternative state Topics (Topic-driven plasticity; P = 0.0017) or (ii) total repression exerted by those Topics (P = 0.036). g,h, Transition-promoting (red) and repressive (blue) interactions (g) and net transition potential (h) between core GB states. State-level scores aggregate the corresponding Topic-level scores, weighting each Topic by its relative activity within the state. Arrow colour and thickness denote direction and strength. i, Spatial co-activity of cross-state Topic pairs across matched Visium sections (n = 97) (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Left, representative sections showing the dominant Topic per GB state. Right, spatial co-activity of cross-state Topic pairs stratified by net transition potential. Colour bars indicate Topic abundances (derived from cell2location mapping of Topic-associated gene programs onto Visium spots). j, Temporal co-activity of cross-state Topic pairs across clonal cell populations ordered by pseudotime (n = 57), quantified as the cosine similarity of their temporal activation (Extended Data Fig. 8d), binned by net transition potential. Box plots in i,j show median and IQR; whiskers are 1.5× IQR. Illustrations in a–e,g–j created in BioRender; Mall, M. https://biorender.com/51tfsoq (2026).

The overall low transition potential of neuronal-like and gliosis–hypoxia Topics raised the question of whether these states are deprived of activating cues or actively constrained by repression. We therefore defined an analogous Topic repression score (TRS), mirroring TAP but built from the inverse signals: the repressive links from source-Topic TFs onto target-Topic TRs and epigenetic inaccessibility of those TRs in source-Topic cells (Fig. 4c, Extended Data Fig. 6g, Supplementary Table 4 and Methods). Neuronal-like Topics (24 and 37) showed the most widespread repression of alternative state Topics and marker genes, attributable to the aggregated activity of several neuronal-like TFs (Fig. 4d,e, Extended Data Fig. 6h,i and Supplementary Table 4). By contrast, other Topics showed either state-restricted repression (2, 20 and 36) or minimal repression overall (9 and 44) (Fig. 4d,e and Supplementary Table 4). Total Topic-level repression negatively correlated with the epigenetic plasticity of associated cells (Figs. 1e and 4f), further supporting a role for repression as an active barrier to state transitions.

To assess how activation and repression jointly shape transitions, we defined a net transition potential as the difference between TAP and TRS (Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). Aggregation at the state level revealed a hierarchy of transition potentials and barriers, consistent with the epigenetic plasticity of the respective states (Fig. 4f–h and Supplementary Table 4). OPC-NPC-like and AC-like states showed predominantly activating interactions towards other states, reflecting broad permissiveness to transitions, whereas neuronal-like and gliosis–hypoxia cells showed limited activation and, in the case of neuronal-like cells, predominant repression towards alternative states (Fig. 4g,h and Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). These interactions were often asymmetrical, pointing to preferential, directional routes of state change.

We next asked how this landscape compares with normal development, applying the same analysis to the developing human dorsal telencephalon48. There, transitions remained confined within neurogenic and gliogenic lineages, confirming that the model recovers established lineage relationships49,50,51,52 (Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 5). GB, by contrast, permits transitions across these lineage boundaries, identifying its expanded transition potential as an aberrant feature of malignancy rather than a rewiring of normal developmental hierarchies. Together, these results define a structured, asymmetrical transition landscape, jointly shaped by activation and repression, that qualitatively diverges from normal lineage programs.

Because we derived the transition landscape from profiles of dissociated cells, we wanted to find out to what extent this intrinsic logic could explain tumour organization in space and time. We therefore investigated the relationship between transition potentials and the spatial and temporal co-activity of Topic pairs in orthogonally derived data. In 97 matched spatial transcriptomics tumour sections (338,481 Visium spots)14, cross-state Topic pairs with a high transition potential (for example, Topics 9–25, 44–34 and 9–19) were more frequently co-active in the same regions than were pairs with weak or repressive links (for example, Topics 24–12, 24–2 and 37–44) (Pearson r = 0.488, P = 2 × 10−6, n = 84 pairs; Fig. 4i, Extended Data Fig. 8a–c and Supplementary Table 6). Across 57 pseudotemporally ordered clonal populations14, pairs with a high transition potential likewise showed stronger temporal co-activity (Pearson r = 0.466, P = 8 × 10−6, n = 84 pairs; Fig. 4j, Extended Data Fig. 8d–f and Supplementary Table 7). Transition potentials derived from Topic-specific scDORI eGRNs aligned more closely with both spatio-temporal patterns and epigenetic plasticity than did those from a single network averaged across Topics or eGRNs from alternative methods, showing the advantages of continuous, Topic-resolved modelling (Extended Data Fig. 8g–i). Although spatial and temporal co-activity alone cannot establish direct transitions, their convergence with the regulatory predictions supports the inferred GB transition roadmap. Together, these findings support a revised model of GB plasticity in which structured regulatory relationships both enable and restrict cell-state transitions, revealing potentially targetable effectors of malignant state change.

Increased cellular plasticity is likely to contribute to tumour progression and therapy resistance in GB53,54. Our transition analysis identified neuronal-like cells as the least plastic GB state, stabilized by transcriptional repression. We therefore asked whether neuronal-like regulators could be harnessed to restrict GB plasticity.

To this end, we profiled chromatin accessibility and transcriptional changes after gain of function of ten candidate TFs in PDGCs, comprising both predicted safeguard repressors (BCL11B, NR3C2, MYT1L, ST18, POU2F2 and BACH2) and activators of neuronal-like programs (SOX11, SOX4, ASCL1 and PBX1) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). All candidate TFs induced specific regulatory changes consistent with scDORI predictions (Fig. 5a–c), and the predictions of differentially regulated genes were more accurate than were those of other eGRN methods (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Notably, all repressors silenced non-neuronal-like state programs at both the chromatin and the transcriptional level, whereas activators predominantly induced neuronal-like gene expression (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9e). Although activator-driven identity induction modestly suppressed alternative states, repressor-driven chromatin closure was substantially better at constraining other cell fates, indicating that repression restricts plasticity more effectively.
