#1303. Official: Latest Italy U21 squad includes Inacio, Mane, Lulli and Bartesaghi

Silvio Baldini has named a squad of 26 Italy U21 players including the likes of Samuele Inacio, Filippo Mane, Emanuele Lulli and Davide Bartesaghi for a pair of international friendlies against France and Belgium in November, as the Azzurrini prepare for the European Championships coming up this summer.

Like the senior Italy squad, the U21s will also be in action against France and Belgium in November, although the Azzurrini will face France away and Belgium at home: The opposite of the senior Azzurri squad.

These will both be friendly matches, following the completion of U21 European Championship qualifying last month.

The Italy U21s beat Armenia 1-0 last month, before an important 6-2 victory over Poland, which saw the Azzurrini leapfrog their opponents into first place in their qualifying group, earning them a guaranteed spot at the final tournament in the process.

The latest Italy U21 squad features several players who have returned after being named in the senior squad last month: Massimo Pessina, Eddy Kouadio and Inacio.

The squad also features a handful of players who had been considered for the senior squad this time around, but have been left with the U21s for another camp, including Milan’s Bartesaghi and Roma’s Lulli. Cher Ndour has also stayed with the U21s.

Regular centre-forward Antonio Raimondo is unavailable through injury. There are still several other Frosinone representatives, though, namely Lorenzo Palmisani, Gabriele Calvani, Matteo Cichella and Seydou Fini.

Luca Koleosho, a regular fixture of the U21 side during their European Championship qualifying campaign, has been promoted to the senior squad for November.

Goalkeepers: Giovanni Daffara (Parma), Diego Mascardi (Torino), Lorenzo Palmisani (Frosinone), Massimo Pessina (Bologna);

Defenders: Davide Bartesaghi (Milan), Gabriele Calvani (Frosinone), Fabio Chiarodia (Borussia M’Gladbach), Pietro Comuzzo (Torino), Eddy Kouadio (Monza), Emanuele Lulli (Roma), Filippo Mane (Borussia Dortmund), Brando Moruzzi (Avellino);

Midfielders: Lorenzo Amatucci (Deportivo La Coruna), Tommaso Berti (Cremonese), Matteo Cichella (Frosinone), Matteo Dagasso (Venezia), Giacomo Faticanti (Avellino), Luca Lipani (Sassuolo), Cher Ndour (Fiorentina);

Forwards: Alessio Cacciamani (Torino), Francesco Camarda (Milan), Luigi Cherubini (Benevento), Jeff Ekhator (Juventus), Seydou Fini (Frosinone), Samuele Inacio (Borussia Dortmund), Dominic Vavassori (Palermo).

#1302. Newcastle Star Causes Chaos After Bow and Arrow Incident

A current player on the books of Newcastle United has caused chaos in England after being spotted with a bow and arrow. The Premier League star in question is defender Amar Dedic.

The Bosnian international signed for the Magpies in the summer from Benfica in a deal worth just under £30m. The right-back was consequently reunited with Matthias Jaissle, his former coach at both FC Liefering and RB Salzburg.

Dedic has been a key player for his new side as well, with six starts in the league to his name from the opening nine games, producing two assists in that time. Newcastle, however, will be concerned to learn the defender's car was recently at the centre of a major police operation this week.

Scholes specifically chose one Arsenal player ahead of Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane.

As reported by the Daily Mail, Dedic sparked police alarm on Wednesday after being spotted carrying a bow and arrows in Northumberland. A concerned member of the public reported the Newcastle defender and a friend after they were seen with the weapon near a reservoir in the countryside outside Newcastle.

It's said that 'at least six patrol cars' were then involved in the search for the footballer, as they were dispatched to the area in Harlow Hill. Not all the police cars were marked, but it's understood that some were armed response units.

Dedic and his companion were finally intercepted around seven miles away in the exclusive Darras Hall estate. Sources described a dramatic swoop on Dedic's vehicle before officers searched the car and seized a bow and arrows, with the 24-year-old questioned about his activities.

Adding to the drama, Newcastle goalkeeper Mark Gillespie and former defender Paul Dummett arrived at the scene while police were speaking to Dedic. It is said that the pair were simply in the area by chance and stopped to offer assistance.

After speaking to the two men, officers were satisfied there was no threat to the public, with police subsequently stating that the equipment was believed to have been intended for recreational use. Dedic is said to have fired some arrows while in the countryside, although it remains unclear what he was aiming at. Hunting any animal or bird with a bow and arrow or crossbow is illegal in the UK.

A Northumbria Police spokesperson has now shared a statement on the matter. It explained that enquiries remain ongoing into the incident:

"Shortly after 1.55pm on Wednesday, we received a report of two men carrying a bow and arrows while walking along a track by the reservoir on Military Road in the Harlow Hill area.

"Officers attended and subsequently stopped a vehicle in the Darras Hall area and seized a bow and arrows. At this stage, it is understood they were for recreational use and there was no threat to the public. Enquiries are ongoing."

The Daily Mail report also claimed that Dedic will not face disciplinary action from Newcastle over the incident. That said, there is the internal feeling within the club that the player was naive to believe he could walk around the countryside carrying a bow and arrow.

The Bosnian is expected to be available for Saturday's Premier League trip to Fulham.

#1301. Agony of tragic footballer's girlfriend, stuck alone, while he died in hospital: How family could not reach Jesus de Miguel's partner - after his father burst into tears at a bar watching the horror collision on TV

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER and GERARD COUZENS

Published: 20:03 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 08:03 EDT, 5 November 2026

A friend of the Spanish footballer who died after a horror tackle this week has spoken of the heartbreak of the late sportsman's girlfriend, who had been watching the game with their one-year-old daughter.

Tenerife striker Jesus De Miguel, 30, died on Tuesday morning hours after receiving a flying knee to the chest from Andorra FC goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off before the match in Spain's second division was abandoned.

Yesterday, a post-mortem found De Miguel died from 'accidental chest trauma'. It is described in the preliminary report as a 'cause consistent with the player's death.' His funeral is due to be held today.

De Miguel's close friend Fernando Roman offered a tribute on social media and in an interview with Vamos a Ver.

Roman, who plays for Spanish side Talavera, explained that he had not been watching the match on Monday, but was alerted to it by his girlfriend after De Miguel had been injured by the tackle.

Roman had then been in contact with De Miguel's girlfriend Maria, who had been at the stadium with their one-year-old daughter Carla. Roman revealed she had been alone at the hospital and has been hit 'very hard' by the tragedy.

She was eventually joined by the De Miguel's parents, who travelled to Tenerife after being informed their son was in intensive care.

Close friend Fernando Roman (left) has revealed Jesus De Miguel's girlfriend Maria had been alone in hospital prior to de Miguel's death on Tuesday. Source: X/@ferroman9

A neighbour has said De Miguel's father (pictured right, with his mother, girlfriend and sister R-L) burst into tears after seeing the impact of the collision on television. (Source: Instagram/martitamig)

De Miguel died on Tuesday morning following a horrifying clash with Andorra FC goalkeeper Jesus Owono in a Spanish second division match

A neighbour of De Miguel's parents in Navahermosa told Y ahora Sonsoles that his father 'started crying' as soon as he saw the impact of the collision on television at his bar and immediately gathered his family to travel to Tenerife.

Roman told Vamos a Ver: 'Yesterday, my girlfriend and I were talking all afternoon and all night with María, his girlfriend, who was alone in the hospital.

'I've spoken with his girlfriend, and you can imagine how she is. Now we have to be with the family.

'We have to send our love to his family, to María, to his daughter Carla, who is a year and a few months old.

'It was unbelievable because we were talking about traveling to Disney with the girls, with my daughter too, and look what's happened.'

Roman also shared a letter on social media in tribute to De Miguel, reflecting on their friendship and stating he had 'brought happiness to everyone'.

'My friend... I can’t believe you’re gone... you have no idea how much I’m going to miss you. I didn’t just consider you a friend; I considered you a member of my own family,' Roman wrote.

'You were always there to help me when I was struggling—you were by my side during my worst moments.

'Many people didn’t truly know you, but having known you, I can say you were one of the best people I’ve ever had in my life: humble, hardworking, never one to look for trouble. You brought happiness to everyone around you, and above all, you were a truly good person.

The striker was struck in the chest by Owono's flying knee as he attempted to clear the ball near the halfway line

De Miguel was stretchered off the field following the collision with Owono

'All the moments we shared keep coming to mind... that trip to Punta Cana with the four of us - a trip I will never forget... all the lunches and dinners we enjoyed together, the time we spent with our daughters, the escape rooms we both loved so much...

'Tamara and I are absolutely devastated right now, but we know that from up above, you’ll still be with us—and, most importantly, with your daughter, with María, and with your entire family.

'My friend, I’m going to miss you so much... I love you dearly! REST IN PEACE!!'

Confirming receipt of the preliminary autopsy report yesterday and the authorisation of the transfer of the footballer's body, the Canary Islands High Court of Justice said: 'The court investigating the footballer's death, which is Court of Investigation Number Two of the Santa Cruz de Tenerife Court of First Instance, received the preliminary autopsy report today.

'The court has authorized the transport of the young man's remains to the mainland for burial.'

Police investigating De Miguel's death are probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility rival goalie Jesus Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged on Tuesday that homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

The goalkeeper shared a statement on Wednesday, revealing he is in 'enormous pain' over the death of De Miguel.

Owono said: 'These are being the most difficult days of my life. I am struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to assimilate anything that has happened.

'I feel an enormous pain for the loss of Jesús. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address; I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesús.'

Thirty-year-old father-of-one De Miguel died on Tuesday morning at Nuestra Senora Candelaria University Hospital after his second-division club revealed his neurological condition had worsened.

Medical personnel involved in the footballer's care are expected to be questioned and detectives will sift through medical reports as part of the probe.

Police investigating the death of CD Tenerife footballer Jesus De Miguel are probing the emergency medical response

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono

Equatorial Guinea international Owono, who has lived in Spain since he was eight, was red-carded for kneeing Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel in the chest near the halfway line late into stoppage time. The match was suspended when the two sides were drawing 2-2.

De Miguel, whose partner Maria and one-year-old daughter Carla were watching from the stands, was reportedly revived by paramedics on the pitch after going into cardiac arrest before being rushed to hospital.

His club confirmed around 9.30am local time yesterday morning he had died at a hospital in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz about 8am, saying they were 'heartbroken' and had a 'lump in their throats'.

It said in a statement, after revealing earlier the footballer's neurological condition had worsened: 'Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats, and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, which occurred this Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8am.

'There are no words of comfort, there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow.

'We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire 'tinerfeñismo' community, who today mourn this cruel outcome.

Owono is reportedly seeking to apologise to De Miguel's family before making any kind of public statement.

FC Andorra, reacting to news of the Tenerife striker's death in hospital, said yesterday morning: 'Heartbroken and devastated, we wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife.

#1300. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Champions League fixture as Aston Villa host Viking in the Midlands.

Villa made history in their previous home Champions League outing last week, thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 to seal the club’s biggest-ever European win. This emphatic victory, coupled with the hard-fought 3-2 triumph over Club Brugge at the start of September, means that Unai Emery’s side have made a 100% winning start to the league phase. The well-deserved 1-0 Premier League victory over Newcastle United at St James’ Park on Saturday evening has amplified the positivity, with Emery’s new-look squad beginning to meaningfully gel and now boast a five-match unbeaten streak across all competitions.

Prepared for another night on Europe's biggest stage ✨ https://t.co/oZYiIiGvRg

Despite their Viking’s lack of European pedigree, Villa should be wary of their Norwegian opponents, who secured an unforgettable 3-3 draw with Bayern Munich in Stavanger last time out in the Champions League. The hosts initially flew into a two-goal lead at the break, before a double from Harry Kane and a strike from Luiz Diaz hauled the Bavarians ahead. However, after Michael Olise was sent off, Herman Haugen’s 90th-minute headed equaliser rescued a thrilling draw to give Viking their European point this season following a 3-1 loss to Stuttgart on MD1. Domestically, the reigning champions of Norway are joint top of the Eliteserien with Bodo/Glimt and embroiled in a nailbiting title race with just seven games remaining.

Villa’s injury list includes Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Johan Manzambi, who both picked up issues against Newcastle, as well as Amadou Onana and Matteo Ruggeri. Still, the hosts possess more than enough quality to dismantle Viking, particularly with Nicolas Jackson, who has been in effective form recently and netted a brilliant brace against Fenerbahce.

We’ll bring you the latest updates and drama. Kick-off is at 20:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1299. Tottenham Are Officially The Second Most Dominant Premier League Team

How quickly things can change in the football world.

Just three-and-a-half weeks ago, Tottenham were rock bottom of the Premier League table and without a win to their name, with pressure building on Roberto De Zerbi's shoulders after he had pulled off the great escape last season to guide the Lilywhites to safety in the Premier League.

Fast forward to now, however, and everything is looking rosy for Spurs. They have enjoyed three straight victories to move into the top half of the table and, playing early on Saturday, they could move as high as fifth ahead of the other matches taking place.

De Zerbi splashed the cash in the summer transfer window to put his imprint on the squad he inherited from Thomas Frank and Igor Tudor, spending more than £300million, with that figure to rise to the £400million mark when Omar Marmoush's loan move is made permanent next summer.

It took a while for the players to gel, which is hardly surprising, given ten new faces arrived at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, and to get used to De Zerbi's style of football. But things appear to have clicked now, as evidenced by those wins against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace.

De Zerbi's philosophy is based around high intensity, possession-based football. The Italian expects his teams to play out from the back, through a ball-playing goalkeeper and centre-backs, playing through a midfield duo and into wingers and a No.10 behind a main striker.

Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke have been crucial to this strategy, with the duo of Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes - both new arrivals in the summer - ahead of them key in the midfield double pivot too.

De Zerbi, who ranks highly among current Premier League managers, was described by Pep Guardiola as "one of the most influential managers in the last 20 years" when he was at Brighton in 2023, and it has become clear that his influence is steadily growing on Tottenham too.

Spurs had 34 shots against Palace on Saturday, the most they have had in a match in the Premier League since 2016. It is a far cry from the shot-shy outfit of the last 12 months.

Heatmap graphs from before Spurs moved up the table suggested the side were on the right track unde the Italian, without picking up results, with some suggestions that they were dominating games just like top two Manchester City and Arsenal, despite being in the bottom three.

And, now the players are starting to click, that has proven to be true.

Tottenham are second in the table when it comes to possession so far this season, with only Manchester City averaging more in their nine games of the season.

It is no surprise to know that a De Zerbi team likes to have the ball, but it is perhaps somewhat surprising that Spurs are already the second most dominant team in the Premier League when it comes to having the ball, particularly given how they started the season.

What they have done in the last three matches is found a way to win, to turn their dominance into goals and subsequently three points. If they continue to do that, they could become a force to be reckoned with in the top flight, particularly without the sitraction of European football.

Despite signing a new five-year contract at Tottenham in the summer, he is subject to strong transfer interest from Barcelona

#1298. Italy confirm Cassano and Lontani will not earn debuts in November despite first call-ups

Roberto Mancini has named Como and Parma teenagers Riccardo Cassano and Simone Lontani in his Italy national team squad for November’s Nations League fixtures, but the FIGC has confirmed that they will both be with the senior side for a few days before returning to the U18s and U19s squads.

Mancini announced his squad of 31 Italy national team players on Thursday evening: The Azzurri will be in action against France in San Siro next Thursday, November 12, and away against Belgium on Sunday, November 15.

As things stand, Italy sit in second place in their Nations League group on seven points after four matches. France lead the way on 10, Belgium are in third on six and Turkiye are bottom on zero.

Among the surprise selections were 17-year-old Cassano, who has not yet featured competitively at club level for Como, and 18-year-old Lontani, who has just 10 Serie A appearances, but three league goals to his name with Parma.

The FIGC has confirmed that both players have been called up so that Mancini can have an up-close look at them for the first few days of the training camp. However, Cassano will then return to the U18s squad and Lontani to the U19s after the first few days.

“As for Cassano and Lontani, Mancini wanted to call them up to have the opportunity to observe them closely and to give them a valuable opportunity to impress: They will not remain attached to the group for the duration of the camp.” the FIGC confirmed in their statement announcing the latest Italy squad.

“Instead, they will join the U18 and U19 teams, engaged respectively in the World Cup starting on November 19 in Qatar and the second phase of European Championship qualifiers scheduled for November 11 until November 17.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1297. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta (Pan Macmillan, RRP £22).

This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1296. Now will the FA put their money where their mouth is? England chiefs and UEFA must decide whether to back rival Japanese bid to FIFA president Gianni Infantino after slamming World Cup controversial sell-off plan

Published: 08:23 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 11:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

The FA and UEFA face a dilemma over whether to support a bid to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency after honorary Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima announced his decision to stand.

Alongside the FA, UEFA have spearheaded opposition to Infantino following the collapse of his botched deal to sell stakes in the World Cup.

However, despite declaring Infantino 'has lost the confidence of UEFA' and threatening to boycott the World Cup, the European governing body have so far failed to come up with a candidate to challenge him at the March election in Rabat.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin decided against a run for the FIFA presidency, opting instead to focus on securing another term at the top of European football.

At a meeting of the FA Council last month FA chair Debbie Hewitt demanded answers over the World Cup sell-off plan - and decision to suspend the ban of US striker Folarin Balogun after pressure from Donald Trump. She said: 'The man has to answer those questions, and if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president, and that was what was shared in the meeting.'

But there is a growing feeling that a European candidate would struggle to secure sufficient support from the rest of the world, while Infantino believes he already has enough votes to secure re-election, making it difficult to find a credible challenger.

Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima has announced a decision to stand for FIFA presidency

Tashima will run against the controversial current president Gianni Infantino (left)

That said, FIFA Council member and Japanese FA bigwig Tashima could split the Asian vote and is well respected in Europe.

With Tashima - the first candidate to secure the backing of a national association - declaring his intention to run, pressure is now mounting on the FA and UEFA to either support his bid or put forward a candidate of their own, having called for Infantino to step down.

It follows former Tottenham and Switzerland footballer Ramon Vega making a public leadership bid on Wednesday, though it is unclear whether he could obtain the backing of enough national associations.

Candidates require the support of five football associations to run for the presidency and must pass eligibility checks by November 18.

Tashima is the first candidate with a realistic chance to announce an intention to run before the November 18 deadline, where the support of five national associations is required.

Speaking to Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon, Tashima said: ‘I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association.

‘It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.’

#1295. Portuguese Journalist Makes Bombshell Claim About Cristiano Ronaldo’s Retirement

The farewell Cristiano Ronaldo had envisioned for when he finally waved goodbye to international football with Portugal hasn't quite gone like the fairytale many expected.

Having hoped to hang up his international boots with a World Cup under his belt, things instead ended in tears for the 41-year-old, who spent the final month of his international career at loggerheads with new manager Jorge Jesus, received a fine for his public outburst and was subsequently handed a ban.

The Euro 2016 winner seemingly left it too late to call time on his international career, finding it increasingly difficult to accept that he was no longer the same player who had claimed five Ballon d'Or titles during his spells at Real Madrid and Manchester United.

But now, his farewell could be set for an even more sorrowful twist, should the bombshell claims made by a Portuguese journalist about plans for his send-off prove to be true.

Journalist Pedro Sepulveda told talkSPORT that Jesus had intended to call-up Ronaldo during the next international break, in an attempt to rebuild bridges, after the Al-Nassr superstar was left fuming over a decision that saw him benched during a 2-1 win against Norway and did not come on.

Sepulveda now claims that Ronaldo is still so caught up in that drama that the then-captain will be blocked from having a farewell match, though it might be because he doesn't want to either. He said:

“I can guarantee you that Ronaldo won't dress officially, let's say like that, in the Portuguese jersey again. I can guarantee you that until Jorge Jesus leaves the national team of Portugal that last friendly game for everyone to say goodbye to Cristiano Ronaldo won't happen.”

Ronaldo's exit comes after he dramatically fell out with Portugal boss Jorge Jesus.

He added: “The thing is, Ronaldo feels that he wanted to retire after the World Cup. He made that decision and then Pedro Proenca, the new president of the federation, with Jorge Jesus, they both convinced him to stay. In the head of Ronaldo, after they convinced him, they took the decision to make this to Ronaldo without defending him.”

That would be in stark contrast to his Argentine adversary, Lionel Messi, who played his 208th and final international match in Buenos Aires in October.

Interestingly, the journalist's comments seem to contradict the Portugal FA's initial statement, which concludes: “Cristiano Ronaldo has elevated Portugal’s name and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps, being, for many of us, the best player of all time!

“Therefore, the Portuguese Football Federation refuses to let this farewell take place without due tribute. It is our firm and immense desire to organise, plan, participate and actively collaborate in what will always be a fitting tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo’s immense career, in which fans and the country can applaud and celebrate, once again, the player who has given us so much.”

A date, time, and official agreement has not yet been reached as rumours of Ronaldo's desire not to take part in another game continuing to flutter. But as Portugal's greatest-ever player, and up there among the best players in world football, it would surely be inconceivable that CR7 doesn't get a proper goodbye.

#1294. Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1,2,3,4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5,6,7,8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

Numerical simulations for a 1D chain of N = 16 atoms with periodic boundary conditions and Rb/a = 1.4. a,b. Simulations including the full experimentally relevant noise model. a. Time evolution of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) at Δ/Ω = 0.2 and 3.7. Solid curves show noisy numerics including readout confusion; shaded regions indicate the total 1σ uncertainty obtained by combining trajectory and shot-noise errors in quadrature. Noiseless numerics and experimental data are shown for comparison. b. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning, averaged over 0≤t≤4 μs; shading indicates the corresponding total 1σ uncertainty. The noisy numerics use the Aquila-relevant noise model of Extended Data Table 1, with 20 stochastic trajectories, 120 shots per time point, and a sampling interval of 0.01 μs. c,d. Simulations including only positional atom disorder. c. Increase of the resonance peak width near Δ/Ω ≈ 3.7, relative to the zero-disorder case, as a function of the positional disorder strength σp, extracted from Lorentzian fits, together with a simple classical estimate. d. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning for several values of σp. Increasing positional disorder selectively broadens and smooths the resonance peaks, while leaving the rest of the long-time response comparatively unchanged under experimentally relevant noise.

Experimental results for 180 atoms on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. a. The time-averaged expectation values of several k-island observables, namely the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable for k = 1, 2, 3, over time intervals with (top) different initial times ti and fixed final time tf = 4.0 μs, and (bottom) fixed initial time ti = 0.8 μs and different final times tf. The grey dashed vertical lines mark the quench parameters of the time series in panel b, namely the peaks of each island operator (Δ/Ω = 0.0, 1.2, 3.6, 4.8) and the point close to the right exit of the xy 1-island operator region (Δ/Ω = 2.0). b. The time evolution of the expectation values of the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable with k = 1, 2, 3. The drawing on the right shows an example of island conversion processes possible in the 2D system (equivalent to the 1D island conversion Hamiltonian discussed in the Supplementary Information). The arrows in the panels indicate the time series segments for the main resonance at Δ/Ω = 3.6 that tentatively reveal island conversion dynamics: two-islands are rapidly created and then slowly converted into a mix of one- and three-islands. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The time-averaged expectation values of the island operator sum on the cut Rb/a = 1.4 for 16 atoms, and the thermal expectation values of the observable for the effective temperature of the quench using the nearest-neighbor blockade subspace (thermal xy blockade) and the full Hilbert space (thermal full). b. The dependence of the time-averaged blockade violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(1)}\) (also shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a) on V1/Ω at representative constant detuning cuts for 144 atoms. To normalize the blockade violation density to the connectivity and boundary conditions, we scale it by N/NB, where NB = 2NxNy − Nx − Ny is the number of nearest-neighbor bonds. The states along these cuts are prethermal, and thus over a fixed time interval the time averages after peak exhibit exponential scaling [equation (22)], as evidenced by the dashed lines showing fits \(\propto {e}^{-c({V}_{1}/\varOmega )}\). As shown in the Supplementary Information, the upward curvature observed in the experiments relative to the clean exponential scalings at large V1/Ω can be explained by the position disorder, while the calibrated readout errors set the final saturation floor. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The dependence of Δc/Ω (as extracted from \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{L}^{(1)}\rangle }\) using the procedure described in Methods) on inverse linear system size for Rb/a = 1.4 cut. The classical prediction, given by Δc/V2 = 2 − 2(1/Nx + 1/Ny) + 2/(NxNy), is shown for comparison. b. The dependence of the conjugate variable jump ratio (\({\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}\rangle }/{\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}{\hat{n}}_{\langle \langle i\rangle \rangle }\rangle }\)) on the inverse linear system size. The jump ratio is used to probe the Clausius-Clapeyron relation at the DPT. Both the transition point and the jump ratio converge as the system size increases, consistent with a first-order transition. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting statistical and fitting uncertainties as described in Methods.

The classical spin dynamics model is described in the Supplementary Information, where the 2D square lattice has coordination numbers z1 = z2 = z3 = 4. a. Dynamical phase diagram in terms of the long-time averages of the (squared) spin component \({S}_{z}^{2}\). Panels b,c show the three (squared) spin components on b. the cut Rb/a = 1.4 across the phase transition and c. the cut Rb/a = 0.7 across the crossover, each indicated by a grey dashed horizontal line in panel a. The black dashed lines in panels a,b show the phase transition from the approximate analytic solution of the Stoner-Wohlfarth model.

Experimental phase diagrams extended down to Rb/a = 1.0 for 144 atoms. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the Rydberg density observable \({\hat{O}}_{n}\) and the k-neighbor correlation observables \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2 (defined in the main text). Besides the crossover, at low Rb and Δ ≈ 2V1 we observe another distinct dynamical regime, which corresponds to antiblockade dynamics73 characterized by expanding excitation loops74. b. The time-averaged expectation values of the xyk-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3 (equation (4) and surrounding text). The atom schematics in the upper corners show the types and sizes of Rydberg excitations that the observables measure. The grey horizontal line indicates the lower bound Rb/a = 1.2 of the phase diagrams for 180 atoms shown in Fig. 4a. The first-order DPT smooths to a crossover at low Rb, in analogy with the classical Stoner-Wohlfarth scenario (Extended Data Fig. 5). The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

The lattices are shown for Rb/a = 1.4. 1D lattice with a. 52 atoms; and b. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 2 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. 2D square lattice with c. 180 atoms; and d. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 6 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. e. Pulse sequences. (Top) The Rabi frequency Ω is set to a constant value Ω/2π = 2.5 MHz. (Bottom) The detuning Δ is set in the range Δ/Ω ∈ [−4.0, 6.0], and shown here for Δ/Ω = 0.4.

Experimental results on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. Panels a-c show experiments with (left) N = 52 atoms and (right) N = 16 atoms. The geometries are shown in Extended Data Fig. 7. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) observables and the k-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3. Experimental \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) data is equivalent to Fig. 3b. b. The time evolution of the expectation value of the 1-island observable for several values of Δ/Ω on the right exit from the central region, shown as dotted vertical lines in a. c. The time-average \(\bar{p}(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega )=\frac{1}{T}{\sum }_{i}p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,{t}_{i})\) of the Hamming weight probability distribution \(p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,t)={\rm{Tr}}\,(\rho (t){\hat{P}}_{\alpha })\). Projectors \({\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\) arise from the spectral decomposition of the (unnormalized) Hamming weight operator \({\hat{Q}}_{n}\equiv N{\hat{O}}_{n}={\sum }_{\alpha }{\lambda }_{\alpha }{\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\), where λα = 0, …, N denote the possible Hamming weights. The time average is equivalent to marginalization over ti with p(ti) = 1/T. The grey dashed vertical lines identify the distribution at Δ/Ω = 0. d. The mean and variance of the time-averaged Hamming weight probability distribution at Δ/Ω = 0, measured in experiments with different system sizes N. The data are linear, with fits yielding the slope of ~0.275 ± 0.002 for the mean and ~0.106 ± 0.006 for the variance, shown respectively by the red and green solid lines. The approximate scalings are 1/4 and 1/8, shown respectively by the red and green dashed lines, consistent with a state that ergodically explores the blockade subspace. e. The time-averaged Hamming weight probability from numerical simulations with 16 atoms. The experimental data shown are derived from 120 samples per time evolution for 52 atom experiments and 100 samples per time evolution for 16 atom experiments, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

Numerical studies of multiple observables, scaling, and averaging for the 1D chain in a circular geometry on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. The time-averaged expectation values are computed as \(\overline{\langle \hat{O}\rangle }=\frac{1}{{t}_{f}}{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{f}}{\rm{d}}t\langle \hat{O}(t)\rangle \). a. The time averages of the blockade-violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) operator, the diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\) operator (also presented in the main text Fig. 2d), and the off-diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) operator. The \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) response vanishes at the main peak, but captures the resonances, suggesting their origin from blockade violations; the \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) response showcases non-analyticities at points where the dynamics is expected to change abruptly. b. The time averages for different system sizes N = 10, …, 20 and final time tf = 10 μs. The curves are nearly identical, indicating a weak system size dependence. c. The time averages for N = 16 atoms and different final times tf. The curves rapidly converge in tf ≈ 0.5 μs. The dashed line denotes the curve for tf = 100 μs, which is the longest time examined in the numerics, while the squares denote the diagonal ensemble averages, which are equal to the time averages in the strictly infinite-time limit. d. The time averages of the blockade-violation operator for N = 16 atoms and different quench parameters Δ/Ω, reflecting the 1D experiments in Fig. 3a. Similar to the experimental results, the curves show exponential decay, corroborating prethermal dynamics even at small system sizes.

Numerical results obtained using the time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) method for a chain of N = 52 Rydberg atoms with open boundary conditions. The blockade radius is Rb/a = 1.4. The system is evolved up to \({t}_{\max }=4.0\,\mu {\rm{s}}\) with a time step Δt = 0.01 μs, and the Hamiltonian includes nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions, with longer-range terms truncated. a. Real-time dynamics of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) for two representative detunings, (top) Δ/Ω = 0.0 and (bottom) Δ/Ω = 0.5, illustrating convergence of the oscillatory behavior with increasing maximum MPS bond dimension \({\chi }_{\max }\). b. Time-averaged value \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle }\) as a function of detuning Δ/Ω, where the plotted values are averaged over the final 2.0 μs of the evolution. The curves correspond to different maximum bond dimensions \({\chi }_{\max }\). Both the real-time dynamics and the time-averaged observables exhibit rapid convergence as \({\chi }_{\max }\) increases, with \({\chi }_{\max }\gtrsim 256\) yielding nearly indistinguishable results, indicating that the dynamics are well converged with respect to entanglement truncation at the probed times.

This Supplementary Information file contains the following sections: I. Supplementary experimental data on dynamical regimes in 1D; II. Characterization of dynamical regimes in 1D; III. Perturbation theory of the resonances; IV. Characterization of dynamical regimes in 2D; V. Classical Stoner–Wohlfarth transition; and Supplementary References.

#1293. UEL | Milan 0-2 Ferencvaros: Dismal Rossoneri risk quick Europa exit

Milan risk crashing out of the Europa League after a third defeat in four games, capitulating 2-0 at home to leaders Ferencvaros with a Lenny Joseph brace.

The Rossoneri had their confidence restored by Saturday’s 3-1 Derby della Madonnina victory, but were trailing in Europe after losing two of the first three games. Mike Maignan was sent off in the 3-0 defeat at Bournemouth, so was suspended here and third choice Lorenzo Torriani stepped in, with Pietro Terracciano, Fikayo Tomori, Matteo Gabbia, Samuel Chukwueze, Ruben Loftus-Cheek and Alexis Saelemaekers injured, plus Strahinja Pavlovic rested after playing almost every minute this season.

Ferencvaros had a perfect Europa League record after beating Celtic, Viktoria Plzen and Torreense, but missed Krisztian Lisztes, Franko Kovacevic and Daniel Radnoti, with Gergo Szecsi, Bence Otvos, Barnabas Nagy and Isaac Pappoe ineligible.

The Hungarians started the better team and tested Torriani with a Kristoffer Zachariassen angled drive, but Ardon Jashari almost gifted them the opener with a misplaced back-pass to send Lenny Joseph clear, the striker scuffing the finish one-on-one with Torriani.

Milan’s first chance was on 39 minutes with Alphadjo Cisse unable to keep the half-volley down on a Goncalo Ramos knockdown from 12 yards, but Joseph tested Torriani at the near post after blazing past Sankhoun Diawara.

Torriani was again forced into a tough save on the Joseph angled drive from 10 yards at the end of a very sluggish first half performance.

Ruben Amorim was as unimpressed as the fans, so made a triple substitution at the break, introducing Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira and Mario Gila.

They seemed immediately brighter, Omari Hutchinson hitting the side-netting from a tricky angle and Goncalo Ramos with an effort deflected wide.

However, it was Ferencvaros who broke the deadlock when Torriani had a heavy touch, Zachariassen tried to pounce and was perhaps fouled by the goalkeeper, but Joseph turned the loose ball into the empty net to resolve the situation. The defending was again sluggish with nobody warning Torriani that he was under pressure.

Hutchinson’s angled drive shaved a coat of paint off the far post, while Diego Moreira caused problems with a couple of cross-shots and a curler over the bar.

Just as they were pouring forward, they left huge gaps in defence and were caught out on another rapid counter-attack. Zachariasson sprinted from his own half and drew out Torriani, laying it off for the simple Joseph tap-in.

Francesco Camarda came on and turned wide of the near post on a Diego Moreira roll across from the left.

Zachariasson was a constant danger, forcing a great one-handed Torriani save at the near post, and the Gomez free header inches over on the resulting corner.

Ferencvaros went down to 10 men, as Bamidele Yusuf foolishly raised an elbow to Mario Gila’s face in an off the ball incident that was spotted by VAR.

Milan tried to take advantage, but Denes Dibusz stuck out a boot to parry the Hutchinson low drive.

Down to 10 men, Ferencvaros nearly scored a third in stoppages with Madarasz unable to make the most of another defensive error, hitting the side-netting.

Abysmal and embarrassing. De Winter mouthing off how we can beat anyone then immediately get turned over again. Can’t see us winning in Greece then Sunderland will come and have their dream night at San Siro.

These teams should be eliminated and if possible finish the league in mid table and below,not to play in uefa club competitions in near future

Well, we learned two things: 1. It is quite astonishing the consistency of results one can get by only preparing just for one match in a year! 2. Ferencvaros > Inter!

Thank heavens Como got into the CL over these clowns. Almost 20 years since Milan were a European force. European farce now.

What happened to the battleship we read about last week? Came a Hungarian dinghy and sank it. Could have been worse , luck and poor finishing saved them from a bigger embarrassment

This is the Milan we all know and love. It’s too bad Inter always sleeps when they play together. It gives Paramount+ And Susy false hope.

#1292. Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history

Eighteen years ago, Bournemouth were minutes away from being liquidated and playing in the fourth tier. On Thursday night, Bournemouth not only welcomed AC Milan in Europe; they did so as favourites, and then pummelled them.

When Amine Adli curled in an 84-minute free-kick with his left foot at the Vitality Stadium, it put the seal on the most extraordinary evening in Bournemouth’s history. On a brutally windy and wet night, Bournemouth trounced AC Milan 3-0.

Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

Evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench showed the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1291. Ex-Man Utd Ace Apologises For Mason Greenwood Comments

Former Manchester United defender Clayton Blackmore has issued a public apology after sparking a backlash with comments about Mason Greenwood. The 25-year-old scored for Fenerbahce against Liverpool this week.

The Turkish giants beat their English opposition 3-2 in the Champions League, with Greenwood deflected equaliser levelling the scores after Trey Nyoni had opened the scoring. Alexander Isak then put Liverpool ahead in the 69th minute, but goals from Archie Brown and Vedat Muriqi saw Fenerbahce come away with all three points.

Greenwood joined the Istanbul-based club this summer, having spent the past two seasons in France with Marseille. He came through the Man Utd academy but left in 2024, two years after being arrested on suspicion of sexual assault.

Despite the circumstances around Greenwood's move away from the Premier League, former Wales and Man Utd defender Blackmore seemed desperate for the English winger to make a return to Old Trafford. He wrote on social media:

"Well done Mason Greenwood [for] beating Liverpool. Come home to us please."

The comments drew a lot of attention on social media as Blackmore – who played 241 times for the Red Devils, winning the Premier League and the FA Cup under Sir Alex Ferguson in the early 1990s – was widely criticised for his post. The 62-year-old then wrote a follow-up message, stating:

"Sorry I've offended anyone but I heard he had been cleared of any wrongdoing I apologise to everyone I've upset with my comments like I said I thought he had been cleared of everything and he’s had a baby with his girlfriend. Big sorry."

Perhaps Blackmore was confused by Greenwood, who claimed he had been 'cleared of all charges' in 2023. This wasn't quite the case. Rather, the charges were dropped by the Crown Prosecution Service when witnesses withdrew their involvement and new material came to light.

Ronaldo's exit comes after he dramatically fell out with Portugal boss Jorge Jesus.

It's little wonder many fans felt uneasy with Blackmore calling for Greenwood to come back to Man Utd. Although once the most talented prospect emerging at the Carrington academy, the winger's career was derailed in 2022 amid allegations of attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour, and assault, per Goal.

The Crown Prosecution Service ultimately dropped all charges in early 2023, citing the withdrawal of key witnesses as new material that also came to light. After separately conducting a lengthy internal investigation, however, Man Utd decided it was best for both parties if he continued his career elsewhere. That call came amid significant pressure from fans.

Greenwood scored 35 goals in 129 games for Man Utd. He was then loaned out to Getafe in 2023/24, before being sold to Marseille. With 48 goals in 81 games for the French club, Fenerbahce spent £33.27m to sign the Englishman in July 2026. He has eight goals in his first 19 games for the Turkish team.

#1290. How Declan Rice's new role has turned him into the Premier League assist king, saves him from burnout and reduces Arsenal's reliance on set-piece goals

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

For so long, Declan Rice was Mikel Arteta’s lighthouse. ‘You just look at him and you know where to head,’ said the Arsenal boss. ‘A focal point giving clarity and direction to everybody.’

Only, not any more. Arteta had a chat with his midfield general at the start of the season, one Rice described as a ‘really honest conversation’, to discuss how he wanted his role to evolve.

After setting up Kai Havertz’s winner against Liverpool with a superb overlap run and cross on Sunday, Rice revealed what Arteta had told him.

‘I’ve done well but he believes I can still do more and he's drilled that into me,’ said Rice. ‘This season I've really tried to attack that part going forward, trying to come up with assists, create chances, create moments. Being behind the ball as well, linking the play. Being involved with all aspects, for me, is my best position.’

He’s certainly doing the creative part of that assignment. Rice’s assist for Havertz at Anfield was his fifth of the season, the most of any player in the Premier League, and puts him on track to obliterate his previous high of eight in 2023-24. Remarkably, for the corner specialist at the league's renowned set-piece kings, all five have come from open play.

Rice, too, revealed he’d discussed overlapping before the Liverpool game and told Havertz to attack balls into the box. That’s just what they both did.

Arsenal's Declan Rice is top of the assist charts in the Premier League this season with five

His latest came at Anfield on Sunday when he made an overlapping run around Noni Madueke who picks up the ball on the edge of the box...

...Madueke plays the ball into Rice's path and he crosses for Kai Havertz (arm raised) to finish at the back post

In truth, Rice’s role has evolved throughout his time at Arsenal.

In the very early days at the Emirates, Rice spent most of his time sitting in a defensive midfield role.

As the seasons have progressed, especially after Martin Zubimendi’s arrival last summer, Rice has been freed to drive further up the pitch, and occupy that space in the left channel.

You can see from his heat map over his Arsenal career, where the redder zones reflect more touches in that area, how much that role has shifted.

In his first season at Arsenal, Rice pops up all over the pitch...

...the following year he appears as an attacking force on the left side of the pitch...

...as he did again last season alongside Martin Zubimendi when Arsenal went on to win the title...

...but this season he is popping up more on the right-hand side, as seen at Anfield for Havertz's winning goal

What’s most noticeable about this season, following the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes and Arteta’s ability to use converted left back Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield, is that Rice has now shifted to the right.

That has enabled him to link up more effectively with Bukayo Saka or Noni Madueke on that side.

What is perhaps less obvious, but even more telling, is that despite the sight of Rice bursting into the box on the overlap down the right to set up Havertz, he is actually doing most of his creative work and tempo-setting from deeper on the pitch.

As Rice put it, ‘Being behind the ball as well’.

Early in this campaign, he spent a large portion of games picking up possession between Arsenal's centre backs, allowing the champions to create overloads when building up play and bypass an opposition press.

He’s averaging just one touch in the opposition box per game in the league, the lowest number in any season of his Arsenal career. He’s only played a handful of passes all season beyond the edge of the 18-yard box.

In Arsenal’s victory over Sunderland, in which Rice set up one goal and created another two chances, he was the deepest sitting of all Arteta’s midfielders (No 41)

And yet it’s making him more influential than ever. He’s playing more forward passes than in any season at the club. More passes into the final third, more line-breaking passes. And he's carrying the ball towards goal more frequently than at any point in his Arsenal career.

At the same time, he’s having less defensive responsibility, averaging the fewest ball recoveries and possession wins in the final third of any of his seasons at the club.

There is a small caveat to add here. For as clearly effective and influential as he has been in this evolved role, Rice is still overperforming his numbers a little.

His five assists have come from a total open-play expected assists (xA) tally of just 1.07. No one has overperformed that metric – which measures how likely the chances you’ve created are to result in a goal – as much as Rice.

You only need to look back at a few of those assists this season. His one for Madueke against Nottingham Forest was a simple pass out to the touchline where the winger then did all the work to cut inside and bend a beauty into the far corner.

He did the same for Havertz on the other flank for his equaliser against Chelsea. And it was a little sideways pass to Guimaraes against Sunderland that his midfield partner then whacked into the top corner from long range.

By contrast, Martin Odegaard, for so long his side’s creative hub, is yet to claim an assist from open play despite having an xA of 1.9, the fourth-highest in the division.

But that is not to take away from the superb work Rice is doing. Where he’s really showing his expertise is in how simply he’s making those forward creative passes look. Take these examples:

After his assist at Anfield, Rice creates another chance for Jurrien Timber, poking a little pass that cuts out two Liverpool players to open up space for a long-range shot

Against Everton, he knocks another through the lines into space for Madueke to turn and run on to

And even though Havertz still had everything to do for his goal against Chelsea, Rice’s pass to him takes out four blue shirts

The xA on the above pass might not be high but it creates the opportunity for Havertz to conjure some magic. Short, simple passes that help open up defences.

Rice is doing all this while running less, too. He’s averaging 6.8 miles per game. Over the previous two campaigns, he travelled 7.1.

Perhaps it was always going to have to be this way. It was over the World Cup this summer that the sheer weight of games Rice had played in 2025-26 – 69 for club and country – finally took its toll.

He played through a hamstring injury from Christmas onwards and was substituted early in England’s victory over Croatia with ‘neural pain’ in his back.

'The body's been through a lot this season,’ he said after the semi-final defeat by Argentina. 'I think you can see I'm mentally done, physically done. I need a break now.’

Now, with the likes of Guimaraes and Lewis-Skelly as well as Zubimendi around him, Rice is able to keep starting every game but also do what great midfield metronomes like Rodri and Paul Scholes did before him: control matches without having to bust a gut.

It has allowed Rice to be more selective in his runs forward. Guimaraes, especially, is dynamic enough to sit in for those moments – like at Anfield – when Rice spots the opportunity to make his move.

Rice's movement and backheel allowed space for Bruno Guimaraes to fire in the winning goal against Leeds last month

He did similar against Leeds to set up Guimaraes’ winner, charging into the box to play a neat little backheel to the Brazilian, who fired into the bottom corner.

It allows Arteta, too, to find different ways to open up defences in open play, whether they are sitting deep or pressing man-to-man. Rice is now able to exploit the gaps or pick the locks.

Arsenal have not always had this luxury and, when they frequently struggled to do so in the past, had to turn to set-pieces. Not any more.

Rice may no longer be Arteta's lighthouse but he continues to find new ways to lead Arsenal to glory.
